senses.d: A rod or stick used by masons in mixing hair with mortar.
Master; lord; teacher; — a Jewish title of respect or honor for a teacher or doctor of the law.
q: Be not ye called Rabbi, for one is your Master, even Christ, and all ye are brethren.

Rabbi.etym: [L., fr. Gr. ραββἵ, Heb. rabī my master, from rab master, lord, teacher, akin to Ar. rabb.]

senses.d: A term of reproach used by the Jews of our Savior's time, meaning “worthless.”
q: Whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council.

senses.d: To raze.
A root.
The descendants of a common ancestor; a family, tribe, people, or nation, believed or presumed to belong to the same stock; a lineage; a breed.
q: The whole race of mankind.
Whence the long race of Alban fathers come.

senses.d: Company; herd; breed.
q: For do but note a wild and wanton herd, Or race of youthful and unhandled colts, Fetching mad bounds.

senses.d: A variety of such fixed character that it may be propagated by seed.
Peculiar flavor, taste, or strength, as of wine; that quality, or assemblage of qualities, which indicates origin or kind, as in wine; hence, characteristic flavor; smack.
q: Is it of the right race ?

senses.d: Hence, characteristic quality or disposition.
q: And now I give my sensual race the rein.
Some . . . great race of fancy or judgment.

Race.syn: Lineage; line; family; house; breed; offspring; progeny; issue.
Race.etym: [F. race; cf. Pr. & Sp. raza, It. razza; all from OHG. reiza line, akin to E. write. See Write.]

senses.d: A progress; a course; a movement or progression.
Esp., swift progress; rapid course; a running.
q: The flight of many birds is swifter than the race of any beasts.

senses.d: Hence: The act or process of running in competition; a contest of speed in any way, as in running, riding, driving, skating, rowing, sailing; in the plural, usually, a meeting for contests in the running of horses; as, he attended the races.
q: The race is not to the swift.
I wield the gauntlet, and I run the race.

senses.d: Competitive action of any kind, especially when prolonged; hence, career; course of life.
q: My race of glory run, and race of shame.

senses.d: A strong or rapid current of water, or the channel or passage for such a current; a powerful current or heavy sea, sometimes produced by the meeting of two tides; as, the Portland Race; the Race of Alderney.
The current of water that turns a water wheel, or the channel in which it flows; a mill race.
A channel or guide along which a shuttle is driven back and forth, as in a loom, sewing machine, etc.

Race.etym: [OE. ras, res, rees, AS. rǣs a rush, running; akin to Icel. rās course, race. √118.]

senses.d: To run swiftly; to contend in a race; as, the animals raced over the ground; the ships raced from port to port.
To run too fast at times, as a marine engine or screw, when the screw is lifted out of water by the action of a heavy sea.
To cause to contend in a race; to drive at high speed; as, to race horses.
To run a race with.
A raftsman.
Originally, any rough and somewhat heavy piece of timber. Now, commonly, one of the timbers of a roof which are put on sloping, according to the inclination of the roof. See Illust. of Queen-post.
q: oft is sooner found in lowly sheds, With smoky rafters, than in tapestry halls.

Rafter.etym: [AS. ræfter; akin to E. raft, n. See Raft.]

senses.d: To make into rafters, as timber.
To furnish with rafters, as a house.
To plow so as to turn the grass side of each furrow upon an unplowed ridge; to ridge.
To scold or rail at; to rate; to tease; to torment; to banter.

Rag.etym: [Cf. Icel. rægja to calumniate, OHG. ruogen to accuse, G. rügen to censure, AS. wrēgan, Goth. wrōhjan to accuse.]

senses.d: A piece of cloth torn off; a tattered piece of cloth; a shred; a tatter; a fragment.
q: Cowls, hoods, and habits, with their wearers, tossed. And fluttered into rags.
Not having otherwise any rag of legality to cover the shame of their cruelty.

senses.d: Hence, mean or tattered attire; worn-out dress.
q: And virtue, though in rags, will keep me warm.

senses.d: A shabby, beggarly fellow; a ragamuffin.
q: The other zealous rag is the compositor.
Upon the proclamation, they all came in, both tag and rag.

senses.d: A coarse kind of rock, somewhat cellular in texture.
A ragged edge.
A sail, or any piece of canvas.
q: Our ship was a clipper with every rag set.

Rag.etym: [OE. ragge, probably of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. rögg a tuft, shagginess, Sw. ragg rough hair. Cf. Rug, n.]

senses.d: To become tattered.
To break (ore) into lumps for sorting.
To cut or dress roughly, as a grindstone.
To play or compose (a piece, melody, etc.) in syncopated time.
To dance to ragtime music, esp. in some manner considered indecorous.
Violent excitement; eager passion; extreme vehemence of desire, emotion, or suffering, mastering the will.
q: He appeased the rage of hunger with some scraps of broken meat.
Convulsed with a rage of grief.

senses.d: Especially, anger accompanied with raving; overmastering wrath; violent anger; fury.
q: Torment, and loud lament, and furious rage.

senses.d: A violent or raging wind.
The subject of eager desire; that which is sought after, or prosecuted, with unreasonable or excessive passion; as, to be all the rage.

Rage.syn: Anger; vehemence; excitement; passion; fury. See Anger.
Rage.etym: [F., fr. L. rabies, fr. rabere to rave; cf. Skr. rabh to seize, rabhas violence. Cf. Rabid, Rabies, Rave.]

senses.d: To be furious with anger; to be exasperated to fury; to be violently agitated with passion.
q: When one so great begins to rage, he is hunted Even to falling.

senses.d: To be violent and tumultuous; to be violently driven or agitated; to act or move furiously; as, the raging sea or winds.
q: Why do the heathen rage?
The madding wheels Of brazen chariots raged; dire was the noise.

senses.d: To ravage; to prevail without restraint, or with destruction or fatal effect; as, the plague raged in Cairo.
To toy or act wantonly; to sport.
To enrage.
Rent or worn into tatters, or till the texture is broken; as, a ragged coat; a ragged sail.
Broken with rough edges; having jags; uneven; rough; jagged; as, ragged rocks.
Hence, harsh and disagreeable to the ear; dissonant.
Wearing tattered clothes; as, a ragged fellow.
Rough; shaggy; rugged.
q: What shepherd owns those ragged sheep?

senses.d: An outer cloak or covering; a neckerchief for women.

Rail.etym: [OE. reil, re”el, AS. hrægel, hrægl, a garment; akin to OHG. hregil, OFries. hreil.]

senses.d: To flow forth; to roll out; to course.
q: Streams of tears from her fair eyes forth railing.

senses.d: A bar of timber or metal, usually horizontal or nearly so, extending from one post or support to another, as in fences, balustrades, staircases, etc.
A horizontal piece in a frame or paneling. See Illust. of Style.
A bar of steel or iron, forming part of the track on which the wheels roll. It is usually shaped with reference to vertical strength, and is held in place by chairs, splices, etc.
The stout, narrow plank that forms the top of the bulwarks.

Rail.etym: [Akin to LG. & Sw. regel bar, bolt, G. riegel a rail, bar, or bolt, OHG. rigil, rigel, bar, bolt, and possibly to E. row a line.]

senses.d: To inclose with rails or a railing.
q: It ought to be fenced in and railed.

senses.d: To range in a line.
q: They were brought to London all railed in ropes, like a team of horses in a cart.

senses.d: Any one of numerous species of limicoline birds of the family Rallidæ, especially those of the genus Rallus, and of closely allied genera. They are prized as game birds.

Rail.etym: [F. râle, fr. râler to have a rattling in the throat; of German origin, and akin to E. rattle. See Rattle, v.]

senses.d: To use insolent and reproachful language; to utter reproaches; to scoff; — followed by at or against, formerly by on.
q: And rail at arts he did not understand.
Lesbia forever on me rails.

Rail.etym: [F. railler; cf. Sp. rallar to grate, scrape, molest; perhaps fr. (assumed) LL. radiculare, fr. L. radere to scrape, grate. Cf. Rally to banter, Rase.]

senses.d: To rail at.
To move or influence by railing.
q: Rail the seal from off my bond.

senses.d: A railroad as a means of transportation; as, to go by rail; a place not accesible by rail.
One who rails; one who scoffs, insults, censures, or reproaches with opprobrious language.
Expressing reproach; insulting.
q: Angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them.

senses.d: A barrier made of a rail or of rails.
Rails in general; also, material for making rails.
Clothing in general; vesture; garments; — usually singular in form, with a collective sense.
q: Living, both food and raiment she supplies.

senses.d: An article of dress.
Reign.
Water falling in drops from the clouds; the descent of water from the clouds in drops.
q: Rain is water by the heat of the sun divided into very small parts ascending in the air, till, encountering the cold, it be condensed into clouds, and descends in drops.
Fair days have oft contracted wind and rain.

Rain.etym: [OE. rein, AS. regen; akin to OFries. rein, D. & G. regen, OS. & OHG. regan, Icel., Dan., & Sw. regn, Goth. rign, and prob. to L. rigare to water, to wet; cf. Gr. βρέχειν to wet, to rain.]

senses.d: To fall in drops from the clouds, as water; — used mostly with it for a nominative; as, it rains.
q: The rain it raineth every day.

senses.d: To fall or drop like water from the clouds; as, tears rained from their eyes.

Rain.etym: [AS. regnian, akin to G. regnen, Goth. rignjan. See Rain, n.]

senses.d: To pour or shower down from above, like rain from the clouds.
q: Then said the Lord unto Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you.

senses.d: To bestow in a profuse or abundant manner; as, to rain favors upon a person.

A bow or arch exhibiting, in concentric bands, the several colors of the spectrum, and formed in the part of the hemisphere opposite to the sun by the refraction and reflection of the sun's rays in drops of falling rain.

Rainbow.etym: [AS. regenboga, akin to G. regenbogen. See Rain, and Bow anything bent.]

senses.d: Abounding with rain; wet; showery; as, rainy weather; a rainy day or season.
Same as 2d Reis.
To cause to rise; to bring from a lower to a higher place; to lift upward; to elevate; to heave; as, to raise a stone or weight.

To bring to a higher condition or situation; to elevate in rank, dignity, and the like; to increase the value or estimation of; to promote; to exalt; to advance; to enhance; as, to raise from a low estate; to raise to office; to raise the price, and the like.
q: This gentleman came to be raised to great titles.
The plate pieces of eight were raised three pence in the piece.

senses.d: To increase the strength, vigor, or vehemence of; to excite; to intensify; to invigorate; to heighten; as, to raise the pulse; to raise the voice; to raise the spirits or the courage; to raise the heat of a furnace.
To elevate in degree according to some scale; as, to raise the pitch of the voice; to raise the temperature of a room.
To cause to rise up, or assume an erect position or posture; to set up; to make upright; as, to raise a mast or flagstaff.
To cause to spring up from a recumbent position, from a state of quiet, or the like; to awaken; to arouse.
q: They shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep.

senses.d: To rouse to action; to stir up; to incite to tumult, struggle, or war; to excite.
q: He commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind.
Æneas . . . employs his pains, In parts remote, to raise the Tuscan swains.

senses.d: To bring up from the lower world; to call up, as a spirit from the world of spirits; to recall from death; to give life to.
q: Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead ?

senses.d: To cause to arise, grow up, or come into being or to appear; to give rise to; to originate, produce, cause, effect, or the like.
To form by the accumulation of materials or constituent parts; to build up; to erect; as, to raise a lofty structure, a wall, a heap of stones.
q: I will raise forts against thee.

senses.d: To bring together; to collect; to levy; to get together or obtain for use or service; as, to raise money, troops, and the like.
To cause to grow; to procure to be produced, bred, or propagated; to grow; as, to raise corn, barley, hops, etc.; toraise cattle.
q: I was raised, as they say in Virginia, among the mountains of the North.

Raise.syn: To lift; exalt; elevate; erect; originate; cause; produce; grow; heighten; aggravate; excite.
Raise.etym: [OE. reisen, Icel. reisa, causative of rīsa to rise. See Rise, and cf. Rear to raise.]

senses.d: Lifted up; showing above the surroundings; as, raised or embossed metal work.
Leavened; made with leaven, or yeast; — used of bread, cake, etc., as distinguished from that made with cream of tartar, soda, etc. See Raise, v. t., 4.
One who, or that which, raises (in various senses of the verb).
A grape, or a bunch of grapes.
A grape dried in the sun or by artificial heat.

Raisin.etym: [F. raisin grape, raisin, L. racemus cluster of grapes or berries; cf. Gr. ρἅξ, ραγὅσ, berry, grape. Cf. Raceme.]

senses.d: The act of lifting, setting up, elevating, exalting, producing, or restoring to life.
Specifically, the operation or work of setting up the frame of a building; as, to help at a raising.
The operation of embossing sheet metal, or of forming it into cup-shaped or hollow articles, by hammering, stamping, or spinning.
The male of the sheep and allied animals. In some parts of England a ram is called a tup.
Aries, the sign of the zodiac which the sun enters about the 21st of March.
An engine of war used for butting or battering.
A hydraulic ram. See under Hydraulic.
The weight which strikes the blow, in a pile driver, steam hammer, stamp mill, or the like.
The plunger of a hydraulic press.

Ram.etym: [AS. ramm, ram; akin to OHG. & D. ram, Prov. G. ramm, and perh. to Icel. ramr strong.]

senses.d: To butt or strike against; to drive a ram against or through; to thrust or drive with violence; to force in; to drive together; to cram; as, to ram an enemy's vessel; to ram piles, cartridges, etc.
q: rammed me in with foul shirts, and smocks, socks, foul stockings, greasy napkins.

senses.d: To fill or compact by pounding or driving.
q: A ditch . . . was filled with some sound materials, and rammed to make the foundation solid.

senses.d: That which fortifies and defends from assault; that which secures safety; a defense or bulwark.
A broad embankment of earth round a place, upon which the parapet is raised. It forms the substratum of every permanent fortification.

Rampart.etym: [F. rempart, OF. rempar, fr. remparer to fortify, se remparer to fence or intrench one's self; pref. re- re- + pref. en- (L. in) + parer to defend, parry, prepare, L. parare to prepare. See Pare.]

senses.d: To surround or protect with, or as with, a rampart or ramparts.
q: Those grassy hills, those glittering dells, Proudly ramparted with rocks.

senses.d: Open robbery.
Yarns coiled on a spun-yarn winch.
To set in a row, or in rows; to place in a regular line or lines, or in ranks; to dispose in the proper order; to rank; as, to range soldiers in line.
q: Maccabeus ranged his army by bands.

senses.d: To place (as a single individual) among others in a line, row, or order, as in the ranks of an army; — usually, reflexively and figuratively, (in the sense) to espouse a cause, to join a party, etc.
q: It would be absurd in me to range myself on the side of the Duke of Bedford and the corresponding society.

senses.d: To separate into parts; to sift.
To dispose in a classified or in systematic order; to arrange regularly; as, to range plants and animals in genera and species.
To rove over or through; as, to range the fields.
q: Teach him to range the ditch, and force the brake.

senses.d: To sail or pass in a direction parallel to or near; as, to range the coast.
To be native to, or to live in; to frequent.

Range.etym: [OE. rengen, OF. rengier, F. ranger, OF. renc row, rank, F. rang; of German origin. See Rank, n.]

senses.d: To rove at large; to wander without restraint or direction; to roam.
q: Like a ranging spaniel that barks at every bird he sees.

senses.d: To have range; to change or differ within limits; to be capable of projecting, or to admit of being projected, especially as to horizontal distance; as, the temperature ranged through seventy degrees Fahrenheit; the gun ranges three miles; the shot ranged four miles.
To be placed in order; to be ranked; to admit of arrangement or classification; to rank.
q: And range with humble livers in content.

senses.d: To have a certain direction; to correspond in direction; to be or keep in a corresponding line; to trend or run; — often followed by with; as, the front of a house ranges with the street; to range along the coast.
q: Which way the forests range.

senses.d: To be native to, or live in, a certain district or region; as, the peba ranges from Texas to Paraguay.

Range.syn: To rove; roam; ramble; wander; stroll.

senses.d: A series of things in a line; a row; a rank; as, a range of buildings; a range of mountains.
An aggregate of individuals in one rank or degree; an order; a class.
q: The next range of beings above him are the immaterial intelligences.

senses.d: The step of a ladder; a rung.
A kitchen grate.
q: He was bid at his first coming to take off the range, and let down the cinders.

senses.d: An extended cooking apparatus of cast iron, set in brickwork, and affording conveniences for various ways of cooking; also, a kind of cooking stove.
A bolting sieve to sift meal.
A wandering or roving; a going to and fro; an excursion; a ramble; an expedition.
q: He may take a range all the world over.

senses.d: That which may be ranged over; place or room for excursion; especially, a region of country in which cattle or sheep may wander and pasture.
Extent or space taken in by anything excursive; compass or extent of excursion; reach; scope; discursive power; as, the range of one's voice, or authority.
q: Far as creation's ample range extends.
The range and compass of Hammond's knowledge filled the whole circle of the arts.
A man has not enough range of thought.

senses.d: The region within which a plant or animal naturally lives.
The horizontal distance to which a shot or other projectile is carried.
In the public land system of the United States, a row or line of townships lying between two successive meridian lines six miles apart.
Luxuriant in growth; of vigorous growth; exuberant; grown to immoderate height; as, rank grass; rank weeds.
q: And, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good.

senses.d: Raised to a high degree; violent; extreme; gross; utter; as, rank heresy.
Causing vigorous growth; producing luxuriantly; very rich and fertile; as, rank land.
Strong-scented; rancid; musty; as, oil of a rank smell; rank-smelling rue.
Strong to the taste.
Inflamed with venereal appetite.

Rank.etym: [AS. ranc strong, proud; cf. D. rank slender, Dan. rank upright, erect, Prov. G. rank slender, Icel. rakkr slender, bold. The meaning seems to have been influenced by L. rancidus, E. rancid.]

senses.d: Rankly; stoutly; violently.
q: That rides so rank and bends his lance so fell.

senses.d: A row or line; a range; an order; a tier; as, a rank of osiers.
q: Many a mountain nigh Rising in lofty ranks, and loftier still.

senses.d: A line of soldiers ranged side by side; — opposed to file. See 1st File, 1 (a).
q: Fierce, fiery warriors fought upon the clouds, In ranks and squadrons and right form of war.

senses.d: Grade of official standing, as in the army, navy, or nobility; as, the rank of general; the rank of admiral.
An aggregate of individuals classed together; a permanent social class; an order; a division; as, ranks and orders of men; the highest and the lowest ranks of men, or of other intelligent beings.
Degree of dignity, eminence, or excellence; position in civil or social life; station; degree; grade; as, a writer of the first rank; a lawyer of high rank.
q: These all are virtues of a meaner rank.

senses.d: Elevated grade or standing; high degree; high social position; distinction; eminence; as, a man of rank.

Rank.etym: [OE. renk, reng, OF. renc, F. rang, fr. OHG. hring a circle, a circular row, G. ring. See Ring, and cf. Range, n. & v.]

senses.d: To place abreast, or in a line.
To range in a particular class, order, or division; to class; also, to dispose methodically; to place in suitable classes or order; to classify.
q: Ranking all things under general and special heads.
Poets were ranked in the class of philosophers.
Heresy is ranked with idolatry and witchcraft.

senses.d: To take rank of; to outrank.
To be ranged; to be set or disposed, as in a particular degree, class, order, or division.
q: Let that one article rank with the rest.

senses.d: To have a certain grade or degree of elevation in the orders of civil or military life; to have a certain degree of esteem or consideration; as, he ranks with the first class of poets; he ranks high in public estimation.
The release of a captive, or of captured property, by payment of a consideration; redemption; as, prisoners hopeless of ransom.
The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner, or for goods captured by an enemy; payment for freedom from restraint, penalty, or forfeit.
q: Thy ransom paid, which man from death redeems.
His captivity in Austria, and the heavy ransom he paid for his liberty.

senses.d: A sum paid for the pardon of some great offense and the discharge of the offender; also, a fine paid in lieu of corporal punishment.

Ransom.etym: [OE. raunson, raunsoun, OF. rançon, raençon, raançon, F. rançon, fr. L. redemptio, fr. redimere to redeem. See Redeem, and cf. Redemption.]

senses.d: To redeem from captivity, servitude, punishment, or forfeit, by paying a price; to buy out of servitude or penalty; to rescue; to deliver; as, to ransom prisoners from an enemy.
To exact a ransom for, or a payment on.
q: Such lands as he had rule of he ransomed them so grievously, and would tax the men two or three times in a year.

senses.d: Early.
q: Rude mechanicals that rare and late Work in the market place.

senses.d: Nearly raw; partially cooked; not thoroughly cooked; underdone; as, rare beef or mutton.
q: New-laid eggs, which Baucis' busy care Turned by a gentle fire, and roasted rare.

Rare.etym: [Cf. AS. hrēr, or E. rare early. √18.]

senses.d: Not frequent; seldom met with or occurring; unusual; as, a rare event.
Of an uncommon nature; unusually excellent; valuable to a degree seldom found.
q: Rare work, all filled with terror and delight.
Above the rest I judge one beauty rare.

senses.d: Thinly scattered; dispersed.
q: Those rare and solitary, these in flocks.

senses.d: Characterized by wide separation of parts; of loose texture; not thick or dense; thin; as, a rare atmosphere at high elevations.
q: Water is nineteen times lighter, and by consequence nineteen times rarer, than gold.
A perfect union of wit and judgment is one of the rarest things in the world.
When any particular piece of money grew very scarce, it was often recoined by a succeeding emperor.

Rare.syn: Scarce; infrequent; unusual; uncommon; singular; extraordinary; incomparable.

senses.d: To rub along the surface of; to graze.
q: Was he not in the . . . neighborhood to death? and might not the bullet which rased his cheek have gone into his head?
Sometimes his feet rased the surface of the water, and at others the skylight almost flattened his nose.

senses.d: To rub or scratch out; to erase.
q: Except we rase the faculty of memory, root and branch, out of our mind.

senses.d: To level with the ground; to overthrow; to destroy; to raze.
q: Till Troy were by their brave hands rased, They would not turn home.

Rase.syn: To erase; efface; obliterate; expunge; cancel; level; prostrate; overthrow; subvert; destroy; demolish; ruin.
Rase.etym: [F. raser, LL. rasare to scrape often, v. freq. fr. L. radere, rasum, to scrape, shave; cf. Skr. rad to scratch, gnaw, L. rodere to gnaw. Cf. Raze, Razee, Razor, Rodent.]

senses.d: To be leveled with the ground; to fall; to suffer overthrow.
A scratching out, or erasure.
A slight wound; a scratch.
A way of measuring in which the commodity measured was made even with the top of the measuring vessel by rasing, or striking off, all that was above it.
To pull off or pluck violently.
To slash; to hack; to cut; to slice.
q: Rashing off helms and riving plates asunder.

senses.d: A fine eruption or efflorescence on the body, with little or no elevation.

Rash.etym: [OF. rasche an eruption, scurf, F. rache; fr. (assumed) LL. rasicare to scratch, fr. L. radere, rasum, to scrape, scratch, shave. See Rase, and cf. Rascal.]

senses.d: An inferior kind of silk, or mixture of silk and worsted.

Rash.etym: [Cf. F. ras short-nap cloth, It. & Sp. raso satin (cf. Rase); or cf. It. rascia serge, G. rasch, probably fr. Arras in France (cf. Arras).]

senses.d: Sudden in action; quick; hasty.
Requiring sudden action; pressing; urgent.
q: I scarce have leisure to salute you, My matter is so rash.

senses.d: Esp., overhasty in counsel or action; precipitate; resolving or entering on a project or measure without due deliberation and caution; opposed to prudent; said of persons; as, a rash statesman or commander.
Uttered or undertaken with too much haste or too little reflection; as, rash words; rash measures.
So dry as to fall out of the ear with handling, as corn.
q: Was never known a more adventurous knight.
Her rash hand in evil hour Forth reaching to the fruit, she plucked, she eat.
If any yet be so foolhardy To expose themselves to vain jeopardy; If they come wounded off, and lame, No honor 's got by such a maim.

Rash.syn: Precipitate; headlong; headstrong; foolhardy; hasty; indiscreet; heedless; thoughtless; incautious; careless; inconsiderate; unwary.
Rash.etym: [Probably of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. rask quick, brisk, rash, Icel. röskr vigorous, brave, akin to D. & G. rasch quick, of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To prepare with haste.
In a rash manner; with precipitation.
q: He that doth anything rashly, must do it willingly; for he was free to deliberate or not.

senses.d: To chide with vehemence; to scold; to censure violently.
q: Go, rate thy minions, proud, insulting boy!
Conscience is a check to beginners in sin, reclaiming them from it, and rating them for it.

Rate.etym: [Perh. fr. E. rate, v. t., to value at a certain rate, to estimate, but more prob. fr. Sw. rata to find fault, to blame, to despise, to hold cheap; cf. Icel. hrat refuse, hrati rubbish.]

senses.d: Established portion or measure; fixed allowance.
q: The one right feeble through the evil rate Of food which in her duress she had found.

senses.d: That which is established as a measure or criterion; degree; standard; rank; proportion; ratio; as, a slow rate of movement; rate of interest is the ratio of the interest to the principal, per annum.
q: Heretofore the rate and standard of wit was different from what it is nowadays.
In this did his holiness and godliness appear above the rate and pitch of other men's, in that he was so . . . merciful.
Many of the horse could not march at that rate, nor come up soon enough.

senses.d: Valuation; price fixed with relation to a standard; cost; charge; as, high or low rates of transportation.
q: They come at dear rates from Japan.

senses.d: A tax or sum assessed by authority on property for public use, according to its income or value; esp., in England, a local tax; as, parish rates; town rates.
Order; arrangement.
q: Thus sat they all around in seemly rate.

senses.d: Ratification; approval.
The gain or loss of a timepiece in a unit of time; as, daily rate; hourly rate; etc.
The order or class to which a war vessel belongs, determined according to its size, armament, etc.; as, first rate, second rate, etc.

Rate.etym: [OF., fr. L. rata (sc. pars), fr. ratus reckoned, fixed by calculation, p. p. of reri to reckon, to calculate. Cf. Reason.]

senses.d: To set a certain estimate on; to value at a certain price or degree.
q: To rate a man by the nature of his companions is a rule frequent indeed, but not infallible.
You seem not high enough your joys to rate.

senses.d: To assess for the payment of a rate or tax.
To settle the relative scale, rank, position, amount, value, or quality of; as, to rate a ship; to rate a seaman; to rate a pension.
To ratify.
To be set or considered in a class; to have rank; as, the ship rates as a ship of the line.
To make an estimate.
A hill or mound.
A kind of ancient fortification found in Ireland.
Coming before others, or before the usual time; early.
q: Bring the rathe primrose that forsaken dies.

Rath.etym: [AS. hræð, hræd, quick, akin to OHG. hrad, Icel. hraðr.]

senses.d: Early; soon; betimes.
q: Why rise ye up so rathe?
Too rathe cut off by practice criminal.

senses.d: Prior; earlier; former.
q: Now no man dwelleth at the rather town.

senses.d: Earlier; sooner; before.
q: Thou shalt, quod he, be rather false than I.
A good mean to come the rather to grace.

senses.d: More readily or willingly; preferably.
q: My soul chooseth . . . death rather than my life.

senses.d: On the other hand; to the contrary of what was said or suggested; instead.
q: Was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse.

senses.d: Of two alternatives conceived of, this by preference to, or as more likely than, the other; somewhat.
q: He sought throughout the world, but sought in vain, And nowhere finding, rather feared her slain.

senses.d: More properly; more correctly speaking.
q: This is an art Which does mend nature, change it rather, but The art itself is nature.

senses.d: In some degree; somewhat; as, the day is rather warm; the house is rather damp.

Rather.etym: [AS. hraðor, compar. of hraðe, hræðe, quickly, immediately. See Rath, a.]

senses.d: To make a quick succession of sharp, inharmonious noises, as by the collision of hard and not very sonorous bodies shaken together; to clatter.
q: And the rude hail in rattling tempest forms.
'T was but the wind, Or the car rattling o'er the stony street.

senses.d: To drive or ride briskly, so as to make a clattering; as, we rattled along for a couple of miles.
To make a clatter with the voice; to talk rapidly and idly; to clatter; — with on or away; as, she rattled on for an hour.

Rattle.etym: [Akin to D. ratelen, G. rasseln, AS. hrætele a rattle, in hrætelwyrt rattlewort; cf. Gr. κραδαίνειν to swing, wave. Cf. Rail a bird.]

senses.d: To cause to make a rattling or clattering sound; as, to rattle a chain.
To assail, annoy, or stun with a rattling noise.
q: Sound but another , and another shall As loud as thine rattle the welkin's ear.

senses.d: Hence, to disconcert; to confuse; as, to rattle one's judgment; to rattle a player in a game.
To scold; to rail at.
A rapid succession of sharp, clattering sounds; as, the rattle of a drum.
Noisy, rapid talk.
q: All this ado about the golden age is but an empty rattle and frivolous conceit.

senses.d: An instrument with which a rattling sound is made; especially, a child's toy that rattles when shaken.
q: The rattles of Isis and the cymbals of Brasilea nearly enough resemble each other.
Pleased with a rattle, tickled with a straw.

senses.d: A noisy, senseless talker; a jabberer.
q: It may seem strange that a man who wrote with so much perspicuity, vivacity, and grace, should have been, whenever he took a part in conversation, an empty, noisy, blundering rattle.

senses.d: A scolding; a sharp rebuke.
Any organ of an animal having a structure adapted to produce a rattling sound.
The noise in the throat produced by the air in passing through mucus which the lungs are unable to expel; — chiefly observable at the approach of death, when it is called the death rattle. See Râle.
A large black passerine bird (Corvus corax), similar to the crow, but larger. It is native of the northern parts of Europe, Asia, and America, and is noted for its sagacity.

Raven.etym: [AS. hræfn; akin to D. raaf, G. rabe, OHG. hraban, Icel. hrafn, Dan. ravn, and perhaps to L. corvus, Gr. κόραξ. √19.]

senses.d: Of the color of the raven; jet black; as, raven curls; raven darkness.
Rapine; rapacity.
Prey; plunder; food obtained by violence.

Raven.etym: [OF. raviné impetuosity, violence, F. ravine ravine. See Ravine, Rapine.]

senses.d: To obtain or seize by violence.
To devour with great eagerness.
q: Like rats that ravin down their proper bane.

senses.d: To prey with rapacity; to be greedy; to show rapacity.
q: Benjamin shall raven as a wolf.

senses.d: Eagerness for plunder; rapacity; extortion.
Greedily devouring; rapacious; as, ravening wolves.
Devouring with rapacious eagerness; furiously voracious; hungry even to rage; as, a ravenous wolf or vulture.
Eager for prey or gratification; as, a ravenous appetite or desire.
Ravenous.
Food obtained by violence; plunder; prey; raven.
q: Though Nature, red in tooth and claw With ravine, shrieked against his creed.

senses.d: To seize and carry away by violence; to snatch by force.
q: These hairs which thou dost ravish from my chin Will quicken, and accuse thee.
This hand shall ravish thy pretended right.

senses.d: To transport with joy or delight; to delight to ecstasy.
q: Thou hast ravished my heart.

senses.d: To have carnal knowledge of (a woman) by force, and against her consent; to rape.

Ravish.syn: To transport; entrance; enrapture; delight; violate; deflour; force.
Ravish.etym: [OE. ravissen, F. ravir, fr. L. rapere to snatch or tear away, to ravish. See Rapacious, Rapid, and -ish.]

senses.d: Not altered from its natural state; not prepared by the action of heat; as, raw sienna; specifically, not cooked; not changed by heat to a state suitable for eating; not done; as, raw meat.
Hence: Unprepared for use or enjoyment; immature; unripe; unseasoned; inexperienced; unpracticed; untried; as, raw soldiers; a raw recruit.
q: Approved himself to the raw judgment of the multitude.

senses.d: Not worked in due form; in the natural state; untouched by art; unwrought.
Not covered; bare.
q: And all his sinews waxen weak and raw Through long imprisonment.

senses.d: Disagreeably damp or cold; chilly; bleak; as, a raw wind.

Raw.etym: [AS. hreáw; akin to D. raauw, LG. rau, G. roh, OHG. rō, Icel. hrār, Dan. raa, Sw. rå, L. crudus, Gr. κρέασ flesh, Skr. kravis raw flesh. √18. Cf. Crude, Cruel.]

senses.d: A raw, sore, or galled place; a sensitive spot; as, to touch one on the raw.
q: Like savage hackney coachmen, they know where there is a raw.

senses.d: A keen-edged knife of peculiar shape, used in shaving the hair from the face or the head.
A tusk of a wild boar.

Razor.etym: [OE. rasour, OF. rasur, LL. rasor: cf. F. rasoir, LL. rasorium. See Raze, v. t., Rase, v. t.]

senses.d: A syllable applied in solmization to the second tone of the diatonic scale of C; in the American system, to the second tone of any diatonic scale.
To retch.
An effort to vomit.
To extend; to stretch; to thrust out; to put forth, as a limb, a member, something held, or the like.
q: Her tresses yellow, and long straughten, Unto her heeles down they raughten.
Reach hither thy hand and thrust it into my side.
Fruit trees, over woody, reached too far Their pampered boughs.

senses.d: Hence, to deliver by stretching out a member, especially the hand; to give with the hand; to pass to another; to hand over; as, to reach one a book.
q: He reached me a full cup.

senses.d: To attain or obtain by stretching forth the hand; to extend some part of the body, or something held by one, so as to touch, strike, grasp, or the like; as, to reach an object with the hand, or with a spear.
q: O patron power, . . . thy present aid afford, Than I may reach the beast.

senses.d: To strike, hit, or touch with a missile; as, to reach an object with an arrow, a bullet, or a shell.
Hence, to extend an action, effort, or influence to; to penetrate to; to pierce, or cut, as far as.
q: If these examples of grown men reach not the case of children, let them examine.

senses.d: To extend to; to stretch out as far as; to touch by virtue of extent; as, his land reaches the river.
q: Thy desire . . . leads to no excess That reaches blame.

senses.d: To arrive at; to come to; to get as far as.
q: Before this letter reaches your hands.

senses.d: To arrive at by effort of any kind; to attain to; to gain; to be advanced to.
q: The best account of the appearances of nature which human penetration can reach, comes short of its reality.

senses.d: To understand; to comprehend.
q: Do what, sir? I reach you not.

senses.d: To overreach; to deceive.

Reach.etym: [OE. rechen, AS. rǣcan, rǣcean, to extend, stretch out; akin to D. reiken, G. reichen, and possibly to AS. rīce powerful, rich, E. rich. √115.]

senses.d: To stretch out the hand.
q: Goddess humane, reach, then, and freely taste!

senses.d: To strain after something; to make efforts.
q: Reaching above our nature does no good.

senses.d: To extend in dimension, time, amount, action, influence, etc., so as to touch, attain to, or be equal to, something.
q: And behold, a ladder set upon the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven.
The new world reaches quite across the torrid zone.

senses.d: To sail on the wind, as from one point of tacking to another, or with the wind nearly abeam.
q: He would be in the posture of the mind reaching after a positive idea of infinity.

senses.d: The act of stretching or extending; extension; power of reaching or touching with the person, or a limb, or something held or thrown; as, the fruit is beyond my reach; to be within reach of cannon shot.
The power of stretching out or extending action, influence, or the like; power of attainment or management; extent of force or capacity.
q: Drawn by others who had deeper reaches than themselves to matters which they least intended.
Be sure yourself and your own reach to know.

senses.d: Extent; stretch; expanse; hence, application; influence; result; scope.
q: And on the left hand, hell, With long reach, interposed.
I am to pray you not to strain my speech To grosser issues, nor to larger reach Than to suspicion.

senses.d: An extended portion of land or water; a stretch; a straight portion of a stream or river, as from one turn to another; a level stretch, as between locks in a canal; an arm of the sea extending up into the land.
q: The coast . . . is very full of creeks and reaches.

senses.d: An artifice to obtain an advantage.
q: The Duke of Parma had particular reaches and ends of his own underhand to cross the design.

senses.d: The pole or rod which connects the hind axle with the forward bolster of a wagon.
Rennet. See 3d Reed.
To advise; to counsel.
q: Therefore, I read thee, get thee to God's word, and thereby try all doctrine.

senses.d: To interpret; to explain; as, to read a riddle.
To tell; to declare; to recite.
q: But read how art thou named, and of what kin.

senses.d: To go over, as characters or words, and utter aloud, or recite to one's self inaudibly; to take in the sense of, as of language, by interpreting the characters with which it is expressed; to peruse; as, to read a discourse; to read the letters of an alphabet; to read figures; to read the notes of music, or to read music; to read a book.
q: Redeth the great poet of Itaille.
Well could he rede a lesson or a story.

senses.d: Hence, to know fully; to comprehend.
q: Who is't can read a woman?

senses.d: To discover or understand by characters, marks, features, etc.; to learn by observation.
q: An armed corse did lie, In whose dead face he read great magnanimity.
Those about her From her shall read the perfect ways of honor.

senses.d: To make a special study of, as by perusing textbooks; as, to read theology or law.

Read.etym: [OE. reden, ræden, AS. rǣdan to read, advise, counsel, fr. rǣd advice, counsel, rǣdan (imperf. reord) to advise, counsel, guess; akin to D. raden to advise, G. raten, rathen, Icel. rāða, Goth. rēdan (in comp.), and perh. also to Skr. rādh to succeed. √116. Cf. Riddle.]

senses.d: To give advice or counsel.
To tell; to declare.
To perform the act of reading; to peruse, or to go over and utter aloud, the words of a book or other like document.
q: So they read in the book of the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense.

senses.d: To study by reading; as, he read for the bar.
To learn by reading.
q: I have read of an Eastern king who put a judge to death for an iniquitous sentence.

senses.d: To appear in writing or print; to be expressed by, or consist of, certain words or characters; as, the passage reads thus in the early manuscripts.
To produce a certain effect when read; as, that sentence reads queerly.
Saying; sentence; maxim; hence, word; advice; counsel. See Rede.
Reading.
q: One newswoman here lets magazines for a penny a read.

Read.etym: [AS. rǣd counsel, fr. rǣdan to counsel. See Read, v. t.]

senses.d: Instructed or knowing by reading; versed in books; learned.
q: A poet . . . well read in Longinus.

senses.d: The state or quality of being ready; preparation; promptness; aptitude; willingness.
q: They received the word with all readiness of mind.

Readiness.syn: Facility; quickness; expedition; promptitude; promptness; aptitude; aptness; knack; skill; expertness; dexterity; ease; cheerfulness. See Facility.

senses.d: The act of one who reads; perusal; also, printed or written matter to be read.
Study of books; literary scholarship; as, a man of extensive reading.
A lecture or prelection; public recital.
q: The Jews had their weekly readings of the law.

senses.d: The way in which anything reads; force of a word or passage presented by a documentary authority; lection; version.
Manner of reciting, or acting a part, on the stage; way of rendering.
An observation read from the scale of a graduated instrument; as, the reading of a barometer.
Of or pertaining to the act of reading; used in reading.
Addicted to reading; as, a reading community.

Prepared for what one is about to do or experience; equipped or supplied with what is needed for some act or event; prepared for immediate movement or action; as, the troops are ready to march; ready for the journey.
Fitted or arranged for immediate use; causing no delay for lack of being prepared or furnished.
q: My oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage.

senses.d: Prepared in mind or disposition; not reluctant; willing; free; inclined; disposed.
q: I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem, for the name of the Lord Jesus.
If need be, I am ready to forego And quit.

senses.d: Not slow or hesitating; quick in action or perception of any kind; dexterous; prompt; easy; expert; as, a ready apprehension; ready wit; a ready writer or workman.
q: Gurth, whose temper was ready, though surly.

senses.d: Offering itself at once; at hand; opportune; convenient; near; easy.
q: A sapling pine he wrenched from out the ground, The readiest weapon that his fury found.

senses.d: On the point; about; on the brink; near; — with a following infinitive.
q: My heart is ready to crack.

senses.d: A word of command, or a position, in the manual of arms, at which the piece is cocked and held in position to execute promptly the next command, which is, aim.

Ready.syn: Prompt; expeditious; speedy; unhesitating; dexterous; apt; skillful; handy; expert; facile; easy; opportune; fitted; prepared; disposed; willing; free; cheerful. See Prompt.
Ready.etym: [AS. rǣde; akin to D. gereed, bereid, G. bereit, Goth. garáids fixed, arranged, and possibly to E. ride, as meaning originally, prepared for riding. Cf. Array, 1st Curry.]

senses.d: In a state of preparation for immediate action; so as to need no delay.
q: We ourselves will go ready armed.

senses.d: Ready money; cash; — commonly with the; as, he was well supplied with the ready.
q: Lord Strut was not flush in ready, either to go to law, or to clear old debts.

senses.d: To dispose in order.
A royal jurisdiction or domain; a region which is under the dominion of a king; a kingdom.
q: The absolute master of realms on which the sun perpetually shone.

senses.d: Hence, in general, province; region; country; domain; department; division; as, the realm of fancy.

Realm.etym: [OE. realme, ream, reaume, OF. reialme, roialme, F. royaume, fr. (assumed) LL. regalimen, from L. regalis royal. See Regal.]

senses.d: To cut with a sickle, scythe, or reaping machine, as grain; to gather, as a harvest, by cutting.
q: When ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field.

senses.d: To gather; to obtain; to receive as a reward or harvest, or as the fruit of labor or of works; — in a good or a bad sense; as, to reap a benefit from exertions.
q: Why do I humble thus myself, and, suing For peace, reap nothing but repulse and hate?

senses.d: To clear of a crop by reaping; as, to reap a field.
To deprive of the beard; to shave.

Reap.etym: [OE. repen, AS. rīpan to seize, reap; cf. D. rapen to glean, reap, G. raufen to pluck, Goth. raupjan, or E. ripe.]

senses.d: To perform the act or operation of reaping; to gather a harvest.
q: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

senses.d: A bundle of grain; a handful of grain laid down by the reaper as it is cut.

Reap.etym: [Cf. AS. rīp harvest. See Reap, v.]

senses.d: One who reaps.
q: The sun-burned reapers wiping their foreheads.

senses.d: A reaping machine.
Early; soon.
q: Then why does Cuddy leave his cot so rear?

senses.d: The back or hindmost part; that which is behind, or last in order; — opposed to front.
q: Nipped with the lagging rear of winter's frost.

senses.d: Specifically, the part of an army or fleet which comes last, or is stationed behind the rest.
q: When the fierce foe hung on our broken rear.

Rear.etym: [OF. riere behind, backward, fr. L. retro. Cf. Arrear.]

senses.d: Being behind, or in the hindmost part; hindmost; as, the rear rank of a company.
To place in the rear; to secure the rear of.
To raise; to lift up; to cause to rise, become erect, etc.; to elevate; as, to rear a monolith.
q: In adoration at his feet I fell Submiss; he reared me.
It reareth our hearts from vain thoughts.
Mine the first hand to rear her banner.

senses.d: To erect by building; to set up; to construct; as, to rear defenses or houses; to rear one government on the ruins of another.
q: One reared a font of stone.

senses.d: To lift and take up.
q: And having her from Trompart lightly reared, Upon his courser set the lovely load.

senses.d: To bring up to maturity, as young; to educate; to instruct; to foster; as, to rear offspring.
q: He wants a father to protect his youth, And rear him up to virtue.

senses.d: To breed and raise; as, to rear cattle.
To rouse; to stir up.
q: And seeks the tusky boar to rear.

Rear.syn: To lift; elevate; erect; raise; build; establish. See the Note under Raise, 3 (c).
Rear.etym: [AS. rǣran to raise, rear, elevate, for rǣsan, causative of rīsan to rise. See Rise, and cf. Raise.]

senses.d: To rise up on the hind legs, as a horse; to become erect.

A thought or a consideration offered in support of a determination or an opinion; a just ground for a conclusion or an action; that which is offered or accepted as an explanation; the efficient cause of an occurrence or a phenomenon; a motive for an action or a determination; proof, more or less decisive, for an opinion or a conclusion; principle; efficient cause; final cause; ground of argument.
q: I 'll give him reasons for it.
The reason of the motion of the balance in a wheel watch is by the motion of the next wheel.
This reason did the ancient fathers render, why the church was called “catholic.”
Virtue and vice are not arbitrary things; but there is a natural and eternal reason for that goodness and virtue, and against vice and wickedness.

senses.d: The faculty or capacity of the human mind by which it is distinguished from the intelligence of the inferior animals; the higher as distinguished from the lower cognitive faculties, sense, imagination, and memory, and in contrast to the feelings and desires. Reason comprises conception, judgment, reasoning, and the intuitional faculty. Specifically, it is the intuitional faculty, or the faculty of first truths, as distinguished from the understanding, which is called the discursive or ratiocinative faculty.
q: We have no other faculties of perceiving or knowing anything divine or human, but by our five senses and our reason.

In common and popular discourse, reason denotes that power by which we distinguish truth from falsehood, and right from wrong, and by which we are enabled to combine means for the attainment of particular ends.

Reason is used sometimes to express the whole of those powers which elevate man above the brutes, and constitute his rational nature, more especially, perhaps, his intellectual powers; sometimes to express the power of deduction or argumentation.
By the pure reason I mean the power by which we become possessed of principles.
The sense perceives; the understanding, in its own peculiar operation, conceives; the reason, or rationalized understanding, comprehends.

senses.d: Due exercise of the reasoning faculty; accordance with, or that which is accordant with and ratified by, the mind rightly exercised; right intellectual judgment; clear and fair deductions from true principles; that which is dictated or supported by the common sense of mankind; right conduct; right; propriety; justice.
q: I was promised, on a time, To have reason for my rhyme.

But law in a free nation hath been ever public reason; the enacted reason of a parliament, which he denying to enact, denies to govern us by that which ought to be our law; interposing his own private reason, which to us is no law.
The most probable way of bringing France to reason would be by the making an attempt on the Spanish West Indies.

senses.d: Ratio; proportion.

Reason.syn: Motive; argument; ground; consideration; principle; sake; account; object; purpose; design. See Motive, Sense.
Reason.etym: [OE. resoun, F. raison, fr. L. ratio (akin to Goth. raþjō number, account, garaþjan to count, G. rede speech, reden to speak), fr. reri, ratus, to reckon, believe, think. Cf. Arraign, Rate, Ratio, Ration.]

senses.d: To exercise the rational faculty; to deduce inferences from premises; to perform the process of deduction or of induction; to ratiocinate; to reach conclusions by a systematic comparison of facts.
Hence: To carry on a process of deduction or of induction, in order to convince or to confute; to formulate and set forth propositions and the inferences from them; to argue.
q: Stand still, that I may reason with you, before the Lord, of all the righteous acts of the Lord.

senses.d: To converse; to compare opinions.
To arrange and present the reasons for or against; to examine or discuss by arguments; to debate or discuss; as, I reasoned the matter with my friend.
q: When they are clearly discovered, well digested, and well reasoned in every part, there is beauty in such a theory.

senses.d: To support with reasons, as a request.
To persuade by reasoning or argument; as, to reason one into a belief; to reason one out of his plan.
q: Men that will not be reasoned into their senses.

senses.d: To overcome or conquer by adducing reasons; — with down; as, to reason down a passion.
To find by logical processes; to explain or justify by reason or argument; — usually with out; as, to reason out the causes of the librations of the moon.
Having the faculty of reason; endued with reason; rational; as, a reasonable being.

Governed by reason; being under the influence of reason; thinking, speaking, or acting rationally, or according to the dictates of reason; agreeable to reason; just; rational; as, the measure must satisfy all reasonable men.
q: By indubitable certainty, I mean that which doth not admit of any reasonable cause of doubting.
Men have no right to what is not reasonable.

senses.d: Not excessive or immoderate; within due limits; proper; as, a reasonable demand, amount, price.
q: Let . . . all things be thought upon That may, with reasonable swiftness, add More feathers to our wings.

Reasonable.syn: Rational; just; honest; equitable; fair; suitable; moderate; tolerable. See Rational.
Reasonable.etym: [OE. resonable, F. raisonnable, fr. L. rationabilis. See Reason, n.]

senses.d: Reasonably; tolerably.
q: I have a reasonable good ear in music.

senses.d: The act or process of adducing a reason or reasons; manner of presenting one's reasons.
That which is offered in argument; proofs or reasons when arranged and developed; course of argument.
q: His reasoning was sufficiently profound.

senses.d: Pertaining to rebels or rebellion; acting in revolt; rebellious; as, rebel troops.
q: Whoso be rebel to my judgment.
Convict by flight, and rebel to all law.

Rebel.etym: [F. rebelle, fr. L. rebellis. See Rebel, v. i.]

senses.d: One who rebels.
To renounce, and resist by force, the authority of the ruler or government to which one owes obedience. See Rebellion.
q: The murmur and the churls' rebelling.
Ye have builded you an altar, that ye might rebel this day against the Lord.

senses.d: To be disobedient to authority; to assume a hostile or insubordinate attitude; to revolt.
q: How could my hand rebel against my heart? How could your heart rebel against your reason?

Rebel.etym: [F. rebeller, fr. L. rebellare to make war again; pref. re- again + bellare to make war, fr. bellum war. See Bellicose, and cf. Revel to carouse.]

senses.d: The act of rebelling; open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes obedience, and resistance to its officers and laws, either by levying war, or by aiding others to do so; an organized uprising of subjects for the purpose of coercing or overthrowing their lawful ruler or government by force; revolt; insurrection.
q: No sooner is the standard of rebellion displayed than men of desperate principles resort to it.

senses.d: Open resistance to, or defiance of, lawful authority.

Rebellion.syn: Insurrection; sedition; revolt; mutiny; resistance; contumacy. See Insurrection.
Rebellion.etym: [F. rébellion, L. rebellio. See Rebel, v. i. Among the Romans rebellion was originally a revolt or open resistance to their government by nations that had been subdued in war. It was a renewed war.]

senses.d: Engaged in rebellion; disposed to rebel; of the nature of rebels or of rebellion; resisting government or lawful authority by force.
To check, silence, or put down, with reproof; to restrain by expression of disapprobation; to reprehend sharply and summarily; to chide; to reprove; to admonish.
q: The proud he tamed, the penitent he cheered, Nor to rebuke the rich offender feared.

Rebuke.syn: To reprove; chide; check; chasten; restrain; silence. See Reprove.
Rebuke.etym: [OF. rebouquier to dull, blunt, F. reboucher; perhaps fr. pref. re- re- + bouche mouth, OF. also bouque, L. bucca cheek; if so, the original sense was, to stop the mouth of; hence, to stop, obstruct.]

senses.d: A direct and pointed reproof; a reprimand; also, chastisement; punishment.
q: For thy sake I have suffered rebuke.
Why bear you these rebukes and answer not?

senses.d: Check; rebuff.
One who rebukes.
To call back; to summon to return; as, to recall troops; to recall an ambassador.
q: If Henry were recalled to life again.

senses.d: To revoke; to annul by a subsequent act; to take back; to withdraw; as, to recall words, or a decree.
q: Passed sentence may not be recall'd.

senses.d: To call back to mind; to revive in memory; to recollect; to remember; as, to recall bygone days.
A calling back; a revocation.
q: 'T is done, and since 't is done, 't is past recall.

senses.d: A call on the trumpet, bugle, or drum, by which soldiers are recalled from duty, labor, etc.

The right or procedure by which a public official, commonly a legislative or executive official, may be removed from office, before the end of his term of office, by a vote of the people to be taken on the filing of a petition signed by a required number or percentage of qualified voters.

Short for recall of judicial decisions, the right or procedure by which the decision of a court may be directly reversed or annulled by popular vote, as was advocated, in 1912, in the platform of the Progressive party for certain cases involving the police power of the state.
The act of receiving; reception.
Reception, as an act of hospitality.
q: Thy kind receipt of me.

senses.d: Capability of receiving; capacity.
q: It has become a place of great receipt.

senses.d: Place of receiving.
q: He saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom.

senses.d: Hence, a recess; a retired place.
A formulary according to the directions of which things are to be taken or combined; a recipe; as, a receipt for making sponge cake.
q: She had a receipt to make white hair black.

senses.d: A writing acknowledging the taking or receiving of goods delivered; an acknowledgment of money paid.
That which is received; that which comes in, in distinction from what is expended, paid out, sent away, and the like; — usually in the plural; as, the receipts amounted to a thousand dollars.

Receipt.etym: [OE. receite, OF. recete, recepte, F. recette, fr. L. recipere, receptum, to receive. See Receive.]

senses.d: To give a receipt for; as, to receipt goods delivered by a sheriff.
To put a receipt on, as by writing or stamping; as, to receipt a bill.
To give a receipt, as for money paid.
To take, as something that is offered, given, committed, sent, paid, or the like; to accept; as, to receive money offered in payment of a debt; to receive a gift, a message, or a letter.
q: Receyven all in gree that God us sent.

senses.d: Hence: To gain the knowledge of; to take into the mind by assent to; to give admission to; to accept, as an opinion, notion, etc.; to embrace.
q: Our hearts receive your warnings.
The idea of solidity we receive by our touch.

senses.d: To allow, as a custom, tradition, or the like; to give credence or acceptance to.
q: Many other things there be which they have received to hold, as the washing of cups, and pots.

senses.d: To give admittance to; to permit to enter, as into one's house, presence, company, and the like; as, to receive a lodger, visitor, ambassador, messenger, etc.
q: They kindled a fire, and received us every one.

senses.d: To admit; to take in; to hold; to contain; to have capacity for; to be able to take in.
q: The brazen altar that was before the Lord was too little to receive the burnt offerings.

senses.d: To be affected by something; to suffer; to be subjected to; as, to receive pleasure or pain; to receive a wound or a blow; to receive damage.
q: Against his will he can receive no harm.

senses.d: To take from a thief, as goods known to be stolen.
To bat back (the ball) when served.
q: Who, if we knew What we receive, would either not accept Life offered, or soon beg to lay it down.

Receive.syn: To accept; take; allow; hold; retain; admit.
Receive.etym: [OF. receveir, recevoir, F. recevoir, fr. L. recipere; pref. re- re- + capere to take, seize. See Capable, Heave, and cf. Receipt, Reception, Recipe.]

senses.d: To receive visitors; to be at home to receive calls; as, she receives on Tuesdays.
To return, or bat back, the ball when served; as, it is your turn to receive.
One who takes or receives in any manner.

A person appointed, ordinarily by a court, to receive, and hold in trust, money or other property which is the subject of litigation, pending the suit; a person appointed to take charge of the estate and effects of a corporation, and to do other acts necessary to winding up its affairs, in certain cases.
One who takes or buys stolen goods from a thief, knowing them to be stolen.
A vessel connected with an alembic, a retort, or the like, for receiving and condensing the product of distillation.
The glass vessel in which the vacuum is produced, and the objects of experiment are put, in experiments with an air pump. Cf. Bell jar, and see Illust. of Air pump.
A vessel for receiving the exhaust steam from the high-pressure cylinder before it enters the low-pressure cylinder, in a compound engine.
That portion of a telephonic apparatus, or similar system, at which the message is received and made audible; — opposed to transmitter.

In portable breech-loading firearms, the steel frame screwed to the breech end of the barrel, which receives the bolt or block, gives means of securing for firing, facilitates loading, and holds the ejector, cut-off, etc.

One of the descendants of Jonadab, the son of Rechab, all of whom by his injunction abstained from the use of intoxicating drinks and even from planting the vine. Jer. xxxv. 2-19. Also, in modern times, a member of a certain society of abstainers from alcoholic liquors.
To count; to enumerate; to number; also, to compute; to calculate.
q: The priest shall reckon to him the money according to the years that remain.
I reckoned above two hundred and fifty on the outside of the church.

senses.d: To count as in a number, rank, or series; to estimate by rank or quality; to place by estimation; to account; to esteem; to repute.
q: He was reckoned among the transgressors.
For him I reckon not in high estate.

senses.d: To charge, attribute, or adjudge to one, as having a certain quality or value.
q: Faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness.
Without her eccentricities being reckoned to her for a crime.

senses.d: To conclude, as by an enumeration and balancing of chances; hence, to think; to suppose; — followed by an objective clause; as, I reckon he won't try that again.

Reckon.syn: To number; enumerate; compute; calculate; estimate; value; esteem; account; repute. See Calculate, Guess.
Reckon.etym: [OE. rekenen, AS. gerecenian to explain; akin to D. rekenen to reckon, G. rechnen, OHG. rehhanōn (cf. Goth. rahnjan), and to E. reck, rake an implement; the original sense probably being, to bring together, count together. See Reck, v. t.]

senses.d: To make an enumeration or computation; to engage in numbering or computing.
To come to an accounting; to make up accounts; to settle; to examine and strike the balance of debt and credit; to adjust relations of desert or penalty.
q: “Parfay,” sayst thou, “sometime he reckon shall.”

senses.d: The act of one who reckons, counts, or computes; the result of reckoning or counting; calculation.
q: Even reckoning makes lasting friends, and the way to make reckonings even is to make them often.
He quitted London, never to return till the day of a terrible and memorable reckoning had arrived.

senses.d: The charge or account made by a host at an inn.
q: A coin would have a nobler use than to pay a reckoning.

senses.d: Esteem; account; estimation.
q: You make no further reckoning of it than of an outward fading benefit nature bestowed.

senses.d: The calculation of a ship's position, either from astronomical observations, or from the record of the courses steered and distances sailed as shown by compass and log, — in the latter case called dead reckoning (see under Dead); — also used for dead reckoning in contradistinction to observation.

To commend to the favorable notice of another; to commit to another's care, confidence, or acceptance, with favoring representations; to put in a favorable light before any one; to bestow commendation on; as, he recommended resting the mind and exercising the body.
q: Mæcenas recommended Virgil and Horace to Augustus, whose praises . . . have made him precious to posterity.

senses.d: To make acceptable; to attract favor to.
q: A decent boldness ever meets with friends, Succeeds, and e'en a stranger recommends.

senses.d: To commit; to give in charge; to commend.
q: Paul chose Silas and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God.

senses.d: To render an equivalent to, for service, loss, etc.; to requite; to remunerate; to compensate.
q: He can not recompense me better.

senses.d: To return an equivalent for; to give compensation for; to atone for; to pay for.
q: God recompenseth the gift.
To recompense My rash, but more unfortunate, misdeed.

senses.d: To give in return; to pay back; to pay, as something earned or deserved.
q: Recompense to no man evil for evil.

Recompense.syn: To repay; requite; compensate; reward; remunerate.
Recompense.etym: [F. récompenser, LL. recompensare, fr.L. pref. re- re- + compensare to compensate. See Compensate.]

senses.d: To give recompense; to make amends or requital.
An equivalent returned for anything done, suffered, or given; compensation; requital; suitable return.
q: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompense.
And every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward.

Recompense.syn: Repayment; compensation; remuneration; amends; satisfaction; reward; requital.

senses.d: To cause to be friendly again; to conciliate anew; to restore to friendship; to bring back to harmony; to cause to be no longer at variance; as, to reconcile persons who have quarreled.
q: Propitious now and reconciled by prayer.
The church is interdicted till it be reconciled by the bishop.
We pray you . . . be ye reconciled to God.

senses.d: To bring to acquiescence, content, or quiet submission; as, to reconcile one's self to affictions.
To make consistent or congruous; to bring to agreement or suitableness; — followed by with or to.
q: The great men among the ancients understood how to reconcile manual labor with affairs of state.
Some figures monstrous and misshaped appear, Considered singly, or beheld too near; Which, but proportioned to their light or place, Due distance reconciles to form and grace.

senses.d: To adjust; to settle; as, to reconcile differences.

Reconcile.syn: To reunite; conciliate; placate; propitiate; pacify; appease.
Reconcile.etym: [F. réconcilier, L. reconciliare; pref. re- re- + conciliare to bring together, to unite. See Conciliate.]

senses.d: To become reconciled.
The act of reconciling, or the state of being reconciled; reconcilenment; restoration to harmony; renewal of friendship.
q: Reconciliation and friendship with God really form the basis of all rational and true enjoyment.

senses.d: Reduction to congruence or consistency; removal of inconsistency; harmony.
q: A clear and easy reconciliation of those seeming inconsistencies of Scripture.

Reconciliation.syn: Reconcilement; reunion; pacification; appeasement; propitiation; atonement; expiation.

senses.d: To recall to mind; to recollect; to remember; to meditate.
To repeat; to recite; to sing or play.
q: They longed to see the day, to hear the lark Record her hymns, and chant her carols blest.

senses.d: To preserve the memory of, by committing to writing, to printing, to inscription, or the like; to make note of; to write or enter in a book or on parchment, for the purpose of preserving authentic evidence of; to register; to enroll; as, to record the proceedings of a court; to record historical events.
q: Those things that are recorded of him . . . are written in the chronicles of the kings.

Record.etym: [OE. recorden to repeat, remind, F. recorder, fr. L. recordari to remember; pref. re- re- + cor, cordis, the heart or mind. See Cordial, Heart.]

senses.d: To reflect; to ponder.
q: Praying all the way, and recording upon the words which he before had read.

senses.d: To sing or repeat a tune.
q: Whether the birds or she recorded best.

senses.d: A writing by which some act or event, or a number of acts or events, is recorded; a register; as, a record of the acts of the Hebrew kings; a record of the variations of temperature during a certain time; a family record.
An official contemporaneous writing by which the acts of some public body, or public officer, are recorded; as, a record of city ordinances; the records of the receiver of taxes.
Testimony; witness; attestation.
q: John bare record, saying.

senses.d: That which serves to perpetuate a knowledge of acts or events; a monument; a memorial.
That which has been, or might be, recorded; the known facts in the course, progress, or duration of anything, as in the life of a public man; as, a politician with a good or a bad record.
That which has been publicly achieved in any kind of competitive sport as recorded in some authoritative manner, as the time made by a winning horse in a race.

Record.etym: [OF. recort, record, remembrance, attestation, record. See Record, v. t.]

senses.d: One who records; specifically, a person whose official duty it is to make a record of writings or transactions.

The title of the chief judical officer of some cities and boroughs; also, of the chief justice of an East Indian settlement. The Recorder of London is judge of the Lord Mayor's Court, and one of the commissioners of the Central Criminal Court.
A kind of wind instrument resembling the flageolet.
To count or reckon again.
A counting again, as of votes.
To tell over; to relate in detail; to recite; to tell or narrate the particulars of; to rehearse; to enumerate; as, to recount one's blessings.
q: To all his angels, who, with true applause, Recount his praises.

Recount.etym: [F. raconter to relate, to recount; pref. re- again + � (L. ad.) + conter to relate. See Count, v.]

senses.d: To cover again.
To get or obtain again; to get renewed possession of; to win back; to regain.
q: David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away.

senses.d: To make good by reparation; to make up for; to retrieve; to repair the loss or injury of; as, to recover lost time.
q: Even good men have many failings and lapses to lament and recover.

senses.d: To restore from sickness, faintness, or the like; to bring back to life or health; to cure; to heal.
q: The wine in my bottle will recover him.

senses.d: To overcome; to get the better of, — as a state of mind or body.
q: I do hope to recover my late hurt.
When I had recovered a little my first surprise.

senses.d: To rescue; to deliver.
q: That they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him.

senses.d: To gain by motion or effort; to obtain; to reach; to come to.
q: The forest is not three leagues off; If we recover that, we're sure enough.
Except he could recover one of the Cities of Refuge he was to die.

senses.d: To gain as a compensation; to obtain in return for injury or debt; as, to recover damages in trespass; to recover debt and costs in a suit at law; to obtain title to by judgement in a court of law; as, to recover lands in ejectment or common recovery; to gain by legal process; as, to recover judgement against a defendant.

Recover.syn: To regain; repossess; resume; retrieve; recruit; heal; cure.
Recover.etym: [OE. recoveren, OF. recovrer, F. recouvrer, from L. recuperare; pref. re- re + a word of unknown origin. Cf.Recuperate.]

senses.d: To regain health after sickness; to grow well; to be restored or cured; hence, to regain a former state or condition after misfortune, alarm, etc.; — often followed by of or from; as, to recover from a state of poverty; to recover from fright.
q: Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover of this disease.

senses.d: To make one's way; to come; to arrive.
q: With much ado the Christians recovered to Antioch.

senses.d: To obtain a judgement; to succeed in a lawsuit; as, the plaintiff has recovered in his suit.
Recovery.
To put on order; to make tidy; also, to free from entanglement or embarrassement; — generally with up; as, to red up a house.
Of the color of blood, or of a tint resembling that color; of the hue of that part of the rainbow, or of the solar spectrum, which is furthest from the violet part.
q: Your color, I warrant you, is as red as any rose.

Red.etym: [OE. red, reed, AS. reád, reód; akin to OS. rōd, OFries. rād, D. rood, G. roht, rot, OHG. rōt, Dan. & Sw. röd, Icel. rauðr, rjōðr, Goth. ráuds, W. rhudd, Armor. ruz, Ir. & Gael. ruadh, L. ruber, rufus, Gr. ερυθρὄσ, Skr. rudhira, rohita; cf. L. rutilus. √113. Cf. Erysipelas, Rouge, Rubric, Ruby, Rudd

senses.d: The color of blood, or of that part of the spectrum farthest from violet, or a tint resembling these.
A red pigment.
An abbreviation for Red Republican. See under Red, a.
The menses.
Somewhat red; moderately red.
To purchase back; to regain possession of by payment of a stipulated price; to repurchase.
q: If a man sell a dwelling house in a walled city, then he may redeem it within a whole year after it is sold.

senses.d: To recall, as an estate, or to regain, as mortgaged property, by paying what may be due by force of the mortgage.

To ransom, liberate, or rescue from captivity or bondage, or from any obligation or liability to suffer or to be forfeited, by paying a price or ransom; to ransom; to rescue; to recover; as, to redeem a captive, a pledge, and the like.
q: Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.
The Almighty from the grave Hath me redeemed.

senses.d: Hence, to rescue and deliver from the bondage of sin and the penalties of God's violated law.
q: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.

senses.d: To make good by performing fully; to fulfill; as, to redeem one's promises.
q: I will redeem all this on Percy's head.

senses.d: To pay the penalty of; to make amends for; to serve as an equivalent or offset for; to atone for; to compensate; as, to redeem an error.
q: Which of ye will be mortal, to redeem Man's mortal crime?
It is a chance which does redeem all sorrows.

Redeem.etym: [F. rédimer, L. redimere; pref. red-, re- re- + emere, emptum, to buy, originally, to take, cf. OIr. em (in comp.), Lith. imti. Cf. Assume, Consume, Exempt, Premium, Prompt, Ransom.]

senses.d: One who redeems.
Specifically, the Savior of the world, Jesus Christ.
The quality or state of being red; red color.
To roll back, as a wave or flood; to be sent or driven back; to flow back, as a consequence or effect; to conduce; to contribute; to result.
q: The evil, soon Driven back, redounded as a flood on those From whom it sprung.
The honor done to our religion ultimately redounds to God, the author of it.
both . . . will devour great quantities of paper, there will no small use redound from them to that manufacture.

senses.d: To be in excess; to remain over and above; to be redundant; to overflow.
q: For every dram of honey therein found, A pound of gall doth over it redound.

Redound.etym: [F. redonder, L. redundare; pref. red-, re-, re- + undare to rise in waves or surges, fr. unda a wave. See Undulate, and cf. Redundant.]

senses.d: The coming back, as of consequence or effect; result; return; requital.
q: We give you welcome; not without redound Of use and glory to yourselves ye come.

senses.d: Rebound; reverberation.
To riddle; to sift; to separate or throw off.

Ree.etym: [Cf. Prov. G. räden, raden, raiten. Cf. Riddle a sieve.]

senses.d: Red.
Same as Rede.
The fourth stomach of a ruminant; rennet.

A name given to many tall and coarse grasses or grasslike plants, and their slender, often jointed, stems, such as the various kinds of bamboo, and especially the common reed of Europe and North America (Phragmites communis).
A musical instrument made of the hollow joint of some plant; a rustic or pastoral pipe.
q: Arcadian pipe, the pastoral reed Of Hermes.

senses.d: An arrow, as made of a reed.
Straw prepared for thatching a roof.

A small piece of cane or wood attached to the mouthpiece of certain instruments, and set in vibration by the breath. In the clarinet it is a single fiat reed; in the oboe and bassoon it is double, forming a compressed tube.
A frame having parallel flat stripe of metal or reed, between which the warp threads pass, set in the swinging lathe or batten of a loom for beating up the weft; a sley. See Batten.
A tube containing the train of powder for igniting the charge in blasting.
Same as Reeding.

Reed.etym: [AS. hreód; akin to D. riet, G. riet, ried, OHG. kriot, riot.]

senses.d: A lively dance of the Highlanders of Scotland; also, the music to the dance; — often called Scotch reel.
A frame with radial arms, or a kind of spool, turning on an axis, on which yarn, threads, lines, or the like, are wound; as, a log reel, used by seamen; an angler's reel; a garden reel.
A machine on which yarn is wound and measured into lays and hanks, — for cotton or linen it is fifty-four inches in circuit; for worsted, thirty inches.
A device consisting of radial arms with horizontal stats, connected with a harvesting machine, for holding the stalks of grain in position to be cut by the knives.

Reel.etym: [AS. kre�l: cf. Icel. kr�ll a weaver's reed or sley.]

senses.d: To roll.
q: And Sisyphus an huge round stone did reel.

senses.d: To wind upon a reel, as yarn or thread.
To incline, in walking, from one side to the other; to stagger.
q: They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man.
He, with heavy fumes oppressed, Reeled from the palace, and retired to rest.
The wagons reeling under the yellow sheaves.

senses.d: To have a whirling sensation; to be giddy.
q: In these lengthened vigils his brain often reeled.

senses.d: The act or motion of reeling or staggering; as, a drunken reel.

To reduce to a fine, unmixed, or pure state; to free from impurities; to free from dross or alloy; to separate from extraneous matter; to purify; to defecate; as, to refine gold or silver; to refine iron; to refine wine or sugar.
q: I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined.

senses.d: To purify from what is gross, coarse, vulgar, inelegant, low, and the like; to make elegant or exellent; to polish; as, to refine the manners, the language, the style, the taste, the intellect, or the moral feelings.
q: Love refines The thoughts, and heart enlarges.

Refine.etym: [Pref. re- + fine to make fine: cf. F. raffiner.]

senses.d: To become pure; to be cleared of feculent matter.
q: So the pure, limpid stream, when foul with stains, Works itself clear, and, as it runs, refines.

senses.d: To improve in accuracy, delicacy, or excellence.
q: Chaucer refined on Boccace, and mended his stories.
But let a lord once own the happy lines, How the wit brightens! How the style refines!

senses.d: To affect nicety or subtilty in thought or language.
Freed from impurities or alloy; purifed; polished; cultured; delicate; as; refined gold; refined language; refined sentiments.
q: Refined wits who honored poesy with their pens.

senses.d: One who, or that which, refines.

To put into a new and improved form or condition; to restore to a former good state, or bring from bad to good; to change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; as, to reform a profligate man; to reform corrupt manners or morals.
q: The example alone of a vicious prince will corrupt an age; but that of a good one will not reform it.

Reform.syn: To amend; correct; emend; rectify; mend; repair; better; improve; restore; reclaim.
Reform.etym: [F. réformer, L. reformare; pref. re- re- + formare to form, from forma form. See Form.]

senses.d: To return to a good state; to amend or correct one's own character or habits; as, a man of settled habits of vice will seldom reform.
Amendment of what is defective, vicious, corrupt, or depraved; reformation; as, reform of elections; reform of government.

Reform.syn: Reformation; amendment; rectification; correction. See Reformation.

senses.d: The act of reforming, or the state of being reformed; change from worse to better; correction or amendment of life, manners, or of anything vicious or corrupt; as, the reformation of manners; reformation of the age; reformation of abuses.
q: Satire lashes vice into reformation.
