senses.d: Specifically (Eccl. Hist.), the important religious movement commenced by Luther early in the sixteenth century, which resulted in the formation of the various Protestant churches.

Corrected; amended; restored to purity or excellence; said, specifically, of the whole body of Protestant churches originating in the Reformation. Also, in a more restricted sense, of those who separated from Luther on the doctrine of consubstantiation, etc., and carried the Reformation, as they claimed, to a higher point. The Protestant churches founded by them in Switzerland, France, Holland, and part of Germany, were called the Reformed churches.
q: The town was one of the strongholds of the Reformed faith.

senses.d: Amended in character and life; as, a reformed gambler or drunkard.
Retained in service on half or full pay after the disbandment of the company or troop; — said of an officer.
To hold back; to restrain; to keep within prescribed bounds; to curb; to govern.
q: His reason refraineth not his foul delight or talent.
Refrain thy foot from their path.

senses.d: To abstain from.
q: Who, requiring a remedy for his gout, received no other counsel than to refrain cold drink.

Refrain.etym: [OE. refreinen, OF. refrener, F. refréner, fr. L. refrenare; influenced by OF. refraindre to restrain, moderate, fr. LL. refrangere, for L. refringere to break up, break (see Refract). L. refrenare is fr. pref. re- back + frenum bridle; cf. Skr. dhṛ to hold.]

senses.d: To keep one's self from action or interference; to hold aloof; to forbear; to abstain.
q: Refrain from these men, and let them alone.
They refrained therefrom some time after.

Refrain.syn: To hold back; forbear; abstain; withhold.

senses.d: The burden of a song; a phrase or verse which recurs at the end of each of the separate stanzas or divisions of a poetic composition.
q: We hear the wild refrain.

Refrain.etym: [F. refrain, fr. OF. refraindre; cf. Pr. refranhs a refrain, refranher to repeat. See Refract,Refrain, v.]

senses.d: To make fresh again; to restore strength, spirit, animation, or the like, to; to relieve from fatigue or depression; to reinvigorate; to enliven anew; to reanimate; as, sleep refreshes the body and the mind.
q: Foer they have refreshed my spirit and yours.
And labor shall refresh itself with hope.

senses.d: To make as if new; to repair; to restore.
q: The rest refresh the scaly snakes that fol� The shield of Pallas, and renew their gold.

Refresh.syn: To cool; refrigerate; invigorate; revive; reanimate; renovate; renew; restore; recreate; enliven; cheer.
Refresh.etym: [OE. refreshen, refreschen, OF. refreschir (cf. OF. rafraischir, rafreschir, F. rafra�chir); pref. re- re- + fres fresh. F. frais. See Fresh, a.]

senses.d: The act of refreshing.
Reviving; reanimating.
Shelter or protection from danger or distress.
q: Rocks, dens, and caves! But I in none of these Find place or refuge.
We might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us.

senses.d: That which shelters or protects from danger, or from distress or calamity; a stronghold which protects by its strength, or a sanctuary which secures safety by its sacredness; a place inaccessible to an enemy.
q: The high hills are a refuger the wild goats.
The Lord also will be a refuge for the oppressed.

senses.d: An expedient to secure protection or defense; a device or contrivance.
q: Their latest refuge Was to send him.
Light must be supplied, among gracefulrefuges, by terracing ��� story in danger of darkness.

Refuge.etym: [F. réfuge, L. refugium, fr. refugere to flee back; pref. re- + figere. SEe Fugitive.]

senses.d: To shelter; to protect.
To deny, as a request, demand, invitation, or command; to decline to do or grant.
q: That never yet refused your hest.

senses.d: To throw back, or cause to keep back (as the center, a wing, or a flank), out of the regular aligment when troops ar� about to engage the enemy; as, to refuse the right wing while the left wing attacks.
To decline to accept; to reject; to deny the request or petition of; as, to refuse a suitor.
q: The cunning workman never doth refuse The meanest tool that he may chance to use.

senses.d: To disown.

Refuse.etym: [F. refuser, either from (assumed) LL. refusare to refuse, v. freq. of L. refundere to pour back, give back, restore (see Refund to repay), or. fr. L. recusare to decline, refuse cf. Accuse, Ruse), influenced by L. refutare to drive back, repel, refute. Cf. Refute.]

senses.d: To deny compliance; not to comply.
q: Too proud to ask, too humble to refuse.
If ye refuse . . . ye shall be devoured with the sword.

senses.d: Refusal.
That which is refused or rejected as useless; waste or worthless matter.

Refuse.etym: [F. refus refusal, also, that which is refused. See Refuse to deny.]

senses.d: Refused; rejected; hence; left as unworthy of acceptance; of no value; worthless.
q: Everything that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.

senses.d: To keep in view; to behold; to look at; to view; to gaze upon.
q: Your niece regards me with an eye of favor.

senses.d: Hence, to look or front toward; to face.
q: It is peninsula which regardeth the mainland.
That exceedingly beatiful seat, on the ass�ent of a hill, flanked with wood and regarding the river.

senses.d: To look closely at; to observe attentively; to pay attention to; to notice or remark particularly.
q: If much you note him, You offened him; . . . feed, and regard him not.

senses.d: To look upon, as in a certain relation; to hold as an popinion; to consider; as, to regard abstinence from wine as a duty; to regard another as a friend or enemy.
To consider and treat; to have a certain feeling toward; as, to regard one with favor or dislike.
q: His associates seem to have regarded him with kindness.

senses.d: To pay respect to; to treat as something of peculiar value, sanctity, or the like; to care for; to esteem.
q: He that regardeth thae day, regardeth it into the LOrd.
Here's Beaufort, that regards nor God nor king.

senses.d: To take into consideration; to take account of, as a fact or condition.
To have relation to, as bearing upon; to respect; to relate to; to touch; as, an argument does not regard the question; — often used impersonally; as, I agree with you as regards this or that.

Regard.syn: To consider; observe; remark; heed; mind; respect; esteem; estimate; value. See Attend.
Regard.etym: [F. regarder; pref. re- re + garder to guard, heed, keep. See Guard, and cf. Reward.]

senses.d: To look attentively; to consider; to notice.
A look; aspect directed to another; view; gaze.
q: But her, with stern regard, he thus repelled.

senses.d: Attention of the mind with a feeling of interest; observation; heed; notice.
q: Full many a lady I have eyed with best regard.

senses.d: That view of the mind which springs from perception of value, estimable qualities, or anything that excites admiration; respect; esteem; reverence; affection; as, to have a high regard for a person; — often in the plural.
q: He has rendered himself worthy of their most favorable regards.
Save the long-sought regards of woman, nothing is sweeter than those marks of childish preference.

senses.d: State of being regarded, whether favorably or otherwise; estimation; repute; note; account.
q: A man of meanest regard amongst them, neither having wealth or power.

senses.d: Consideration; thought; reflection; heed.
q: Sad pause and deep regard become the sage.

senses.d: Matter for consideration; account; condition.
Respect; relation; reference.
q: Persuade them to pursue and persevere in virtue, with regard to themselves; in justice and goodness with regard to their neighbors; and piefy toward God.
Change was thought necessary in regard of the injury the church did receive by a number of things then in use.
In regard of its security, it had a great advantage over the bandboxes.

senses.d: Object of sight; scene; view; aspect.
q: Throw out our eyes for brave Othello, Even till we make the main and the aërial blue An indistinct regard.

senses.d: Supervision; inspection.

Regard.syn: Respect; consideration; notice; observance; heed; care; concern; estimation; esteem; attachment; reverence.

senses.d: Concerning; respecting.
The act of regenerating, or the state of being regenerated.
The entering into a new spiritual life; the act of becoming, or of being made, Christian; that change by which holy affectations and purposes are substituted for the opposite motives in the heart.
q: He saved us by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Chost.

senses.d: The reproduction of a part which has been removed or destroyed; re-formation; — a process especially characteristic of a many of the lower animals; as, the regeneration of lost feelers, limbs, and claws by spiders and crabs.

The reproduction or renewal of tissues, cells, etc., which have been used up and destroyed by the ordinary processes of life; as, the continual regeneration of the epithelial cells of the body, or the regeneration of the contractile substance of muscle.

One of the grand districts or quarters into which any space or surface, as of the earth or the heavens, is conceived of as divided; hence, in general, a portion of space or territory of indefinite extent; country; province; district; tract.
q: If thence he 'scappe, into whatever world, Or unknown region.

senses.d: Tract, part, or space, lying about and including anything; neighborhood; vicinity; sphere.
q: Philip, tetrarch of .. the region of Trachonitis.

senses.d: The upper air; the sky; the heavens.
q: Anon the dreadful thunder Doth rend the region.

senses.d: The inhabitants of a district.
Place; rank; station.
q: He is of too high a region.

Region.etym: [F. région, from L. regio a direction, a boundary line, region, fr. regere to guide, direct. See Regimen.]

senses.d: A written account or entry; an official or formal enumeration, description, or record; a memorial record; a list or roll; a schedule.
q: As you have one eye upon my follies, . . . turn another into the register of your own.

senses.d: A record containing a list and description of the merchant vessels belonging to a port or customs district.
One who registers or records; a registrar; a recorder; especially, a public officer charged with the duty of recording certain transactions or events; as, a register of deeds.
That which registers or records.

A lid, stopper, or sliding plate, in a furnace, stove, etc., for regulating the admission of air to the fuel; also, an arrangement containing dampers or shutters, as in the floor or wall of a room or passage, or in a chimney, for admitting or excluding heated air, or for regulating ventilation.
The inner part of the mold in which types are cast.

The compass of a voice or instrument; a specified portion of the compass of a voice, or a series of vocal tones of a given compass; as, the upper, middle, or lower register; the soprano register; the tenor register.
A stop or set of pipes in an organ.

Register.syn: List; catalogue; roll; record; archives; chronicle; annals. See List.
Register.etym: [OE. registre, F. registre, LL. registrum,regestum, L. regesta, pl., fr. regerere, regestum, to carry back, to register; pref. re- re- + gerere to carry. See Jest, and cf. Regest.]

senses.d: To enter in a register; to record formally and distinctly, as for future use or service.
To enroll; to enter in a list.
q: Such follow him as shall be registered.

Register.etym: [Cf. F. regisrer, exregistrer, LL. registrare. See Register, n.]

senses.d: To enroll one's name in a register.

To correspond in relative position; as, two pages, columns, etc. , register when the corresponding parts fall in the same line, or when line falls exactly upon line in reverse pages, or (as in chromatic printing) where the various colors of the design are printed consecutively, and perfect adjustment of parts is necessary.

To enter the name of the owner of (a share of stock, a bond, or other security) in a register, or record book. A registered security is transferable only on the written assignment of the owner of record and on surrender of his bond, stock certificate, or the like.
To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite.
q: When the words were heard which David spake, they rehearsed them before Saul.

senses.d: To narrate; to relate; to tell.
q: Rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord.

senses.d: To recite or repeat in private for experiment and improvement, before a public representation; as, to rehearse a tragedy.
To cause to rehearse; to instruct by rehearsal.
q: He has been rehearsed by Madame Defarge as to his having seen her.

Rehearse.syn: To recite; recapitulate; recount; detail; describe; tell; relate; narrate.
Rehearse.etym: [OE. rehercen, rehersen, OF. reherser, rehercier, to harrow over again; pref. re- re- + hercier to harrow, fr. herce a harrow, F. herse. See Hearse.]

senses.d: To recite or repeat something for practice.
A portuguese money of account, in value about one tenth of a cent.

Rei.etym: [Pg. real, pl. reis. See Real a coin.]

senses.d: Royal authority; supreme power; sovereignty; rule; dominion.
q: He who like a father held his reign.
Saturn's sons received the threefold reign Of heaven, of ocean, and deep hell beneath.

senses.d: The territory or sphere which is reigned over; kingdom; empire; realm; dominion.
q: him bereft the regne that he had.

senses.d: The time during which a king, queen, or emperor possesses the supreme authority; as, it happened in the reign of Elizabeth.

Reign.etym: [OE. regne, OF. reigne, regne, F. règne, fr. L. regnum, fr. rex, regis, a king, fr. regere to guide, rule. See Regal, Regimen.]

senses.d: To possess or exercise sovereign power or authority; to exercise government, as a king or emperor;; to hold supreme power; to rule.
q: We will not have this man to reign over us.
Shall Banquo's issue ever Reign in this kingdom?

senses.d: Hence, to be predominant; to prevail.
To have superior or uncontrolled dominion; to rule.
q: Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body.

Reign.syn: To rule; govern; direct; control; prevail.
Reign.etym: [OE. regnen, reinen, OF. regner, F. régner, fr. L. regnare, fr. regnum. See Reign, n.]

senses.d: The strap of a bridle, fastened to the curb or snaffle on each side, by which the rider or driver governs the horse.
q: This knight laid hold upon his reyne.

senses.d: Hence, an instrument or means of curbing, restraining, or governing; government; restraint.

Rein.etym: [F. rêne, fr. (assumed) LL. retina, fr. L. retinere to hold back. See Retain.]

senses.d: To govern or direct with the reins; as, to rein a horse one way or another.
q: He mounts and reins his horse.

senses.d: To restrain; to control; to check.
q: Being once chafed, he can not Be reined again to temperance.

senses.d: To be guided by reins.
The kidneys; also, the region of the kidneys; the loins.
The inward impulses; the affections and passions; — so called because formerly supposed to have their seat in the part of the body where the kidneys are.
q: My reins rejoice, when thy lips speak right things.
I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts.

Reins.etym: [F. rein, pl. reins, fr. L. ren, pl. renes.]

senses.d: To cast from one; to throw away; to discard.
q: Therefore all this exercise of hunting . . . the Utopians have rejected to their butchers.
Reject me not from among thy children.

senses.d: To refuse to receive or to acknowledge; to decline haughtily or harshly; to repudiate.
q: That golden scepter which thou didst reject.
Because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me.

senses.d: To refuse to grant; as, to reject a prayer or request.

Reject.syn: To repel; renounce; discard; rebuff; refuse; decline.
Reject.etym: [L. rejectus, p. p. of reicere, rejicere; pref. re- re- + jacere to throw: cf. F. rejeter, formerly also spelt rejecter. See Jet a shooting forth.]

senses.d: To feel joy; to experience gladness in a high degree; to have pleasurable satisfaction; to be delighted.
q: I will be glad and rejoice in thy mercy.

Rejoice.etym: [OE. rejoissen, OF. resjouir, resjoir, F. réjouir; pref. re- re- + OF, esjouir, esjoir, F. éjouir, to rejoice; pref. es- (L. ex-) + OF. jouir, joir, F. jouir, from L. gaudere to rejoice. See Joy.]

senses.d: To enjoy.
To give joy to; to make joyful; to gladden.
q: I me rejoysed of my liberty.
While she, great saint, rejoices heaven.
Were he alive, it would rejoice his soul to see what mischief it had made.

senses.d: The act of rejoicing.
Joy; gladness; delight.
q: We should particularly express our rejoicing by love and charity to our neighbors.

senses.d: The expression of joy or gladness.
q: The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tabernacles of the righteous.

senses.d: That which causes to rejoice; occasion of joy.
q: Thy testimonies have I taken as an heritage forever, for they are the rejoicing of my heart.

senses.d: To lease again; to grant a new lease of; to let back.
To let loose again; to set free from restraint, confinement, or servitude; to give liberty to, or to set at liberty; to let go.
q: Now at that feast he released unto them one prisoner, whomsoever they desired.

senses.d: To relieve from something that confines, burdens, or oppresses, as from pain, trouble, obligation, penalty.

To let go, as a legal claim; to discharge or relinquish a right to, as lands or tenements, by conveying to another who has some right or estate in possession, as when the person in remainder releases his right to the tenant in possession; to quit.
To loosen; to relax; to remove the obligation of; as, to release an ordinance.
q: A sacred vow that none should aye release.

Release.syn: To free; liberate; loose; discharge; disengage; extricate; let go; quit; acquit.
Release.etym: [OE. relessen, OF. relassier, to release, to let free. See Relay, n., Relax, and cf. Release to lease again.]

senses.d: The act of letting loose or freeing, or the state of being let loose or freed; liberation or discharge from restraint of any kind, as from confinement or bondage.
Relief from care, pain, or any burden.
Discharge from obligation or responsibility, as from debt, penalty, or claim of any kind; acquittance.
A giving up or relinquishment of some right or claim; a conveyance of a man's right in lands or tenements to another who has some estate in possession; a quitclaim.
The act of opening the exhaust port to allow the steam to escape.
A device adapted to hold or release a device or mechanism as required;
The act or manner of ending a sound.
In the block-signaling system, a printed card conveying information and instructions to be used at intermediate sidings without telegraphic stations.

The act of relieving, or the state of being relieved; the removal, or partial removal, of any evil, or of anything oppressive or burdensome, by which some ease is obtained; succor; alleviation; comfort; ease; redress.
q: He sees the dire contagion spread so fast, That, where it seizes, all relief is vain.

senses.d: Release from a post, or from the performance of duty, by the intervention of others, by discharge, or by relay; as, a relief of a sentry.
q: For this relief much thanks; 'tis bitter cold.

senses.d: That which removes or lessens evil, pain, discomfort, uneasiness, etc.; that which gives succor, aid, or comfort; also, the person who relieves from performance of duty by taking the place of another; a relay.

A fine or composition which the heir of a deceased tenant paid to the lord for the privilege of taking up the estate, which, on strict feudal principles, had lapsed or fallen to the lord on the death of the tenant.
The projection of a figure above the ground or plane on which it is formed.
The appearance of projection given by shading, shadow, etc., to any figure.
The height to which works are raised above the bottom of the ditch.
The elevations and surface undulations of a country.

Relief.syn: Alleviation; mitigation; aid; help; succor; assistance; remedy; redress; indemnification.
Relief.etym: [OE. relef, F. relief, properly, a lifting up, a standing out. See Relieve, and cf. Basrelief, Rilievi.]

senses.d: To lift up; to raise again, as one who has fallen; to cause to rise.
To cause to seem to rise; to put in relief; to give prominence or conspicuousness to; to set off by contrast.
q: Her tall figure relieved against the blue sky; seemed almost of supernatural height.

senses.d: To raise up something in; to introduce a contrast or variety into; to remove the monotony or sameness of.
q: The poet must . . . sometimes relieve the subject with a moral reflection.

senses.d: To raise or remove, as anything which depresses, weighs down, or crushes; to render less burdensome or afflicting; to alleviate; to abate; to mitigate; to lessen; as, to relieve pain; to relieve the wants of the poor.

To free, wholly or partly, from any burden, trial, evil, distress, or the like; to give ease, comfort, or consolation to; to give aid, help, or succor to; to support, strengthen, or deliver; as, to relieve a besieged town.
q: Now lend assistance and relieve the poor.

senses.d: To release from a post, station, or duty; to put another in place of, or to take the place of, in the bearing of any burden, or discharge of any duty.
q: Who hath relieved you?

senses.d: To ease of any imposition, burden, wrong, or oppression, by judicial or legislative interposition, as by the removal of a grievance, by indemnification for losses, or the like; to right.

Relieve.syn: To alleviate; assuage; succor; assist; aid; help; support; substain; ease; mitigate; lighten; diminish; remove; free; remedy; redress; indemnify.
Relieve.etym: [OE. releven, F. relever to raise again, discharge, relieve, fr. L. relevare to lift up, raise, make light, relieve; pref. re- re- + levare to raise, fr. levis light. See Levity, and cf. Relevant, Relief.]

senses.d: The outward act or form by which men indicate their recognition of the existence of a god or of gods having power over their destiny, to whom obedience, service, and honor are due; the feeling or expression of human love, fear, or awe of some superhuman and overruling power, whether by profession of belief, by observance of rites and ceremonies, or by the conduct of life; a system of faith and worship; a manifestation of piety; as, ethical religions; monotheistic religions; natural religion; revealed religion; the religion of the Jews; the religion of idol worshipers.
q: An orderly life so far as others are able to observe us is now and then produced by prudential motives or by dint of habit; but without seriousness there can be no religious principle at the bottom, no course of conduct from religious motives; in a word, there can be no religion.
Religion not, as too often now, used as equivalent for godliness; but . . . it expressed the outer form and embodiment which the inward spirit of a true or a false devotion assumed.

Religions, by which are meant the modes of divine worship proper to different tribes, nations, or communities, and based on the belief held in common by the members of them severally. . . . There is no living religion without something like a doctrine. On the other hand, a doctrine, however elaborate, does not constitute a religion.
Religion . . . means the conscious relation between man and God, and the expression of that relation in human conduct.
After the most straitest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
The image of a brute, adorned With gay religions full of pomp and gold.

senses.d: Specifically, conformity in faith and life to the precepts inculcated in the Bible, respecting the conduct of life and duty toward God and man; the Christian faith and practice.
q: Let us with caution indulge the supposition that morality can be maintained without religion.
Religion will attend you . . . as a pleasant and useful companion in every proper place, and every temperate occupation of life.

senses.d: A monastic or religious order subject to a regulated mode of life; the religious state; as, to enter religion.
q: A good man was there of religion.

senses.d: Strictness of fidelity in conforming to any practice, as if it were an enjoined rule of conduct.
q: Those parts of pleading which in ancient times might perhaps be material, but at this time are become only mere styles and forms, are still continued with much religion.

Religion.etym: [F., from L. religio; cf. religens pious, revering the gods, Gr. αλἔγειν to heed, have a care. Cf. Neglect.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to religion; concerned with religion; teaching, or setting forth, religion; set apart to religion; as, a religious society; a religious sect; a religious place; religious subjects, books, teachers, houses, wars.
q: Our law forbids at their religious rites My presence.

senses.d: Possessing, or conforming to, religion; pious; godly; as, a religious man, life, behavior, etc.
q: Men whose lives Religious titled them the sons of God.

senses.d: Scrupulously faithful or exact; strict.
q: Thus, Indianlike, Religious in my error, I adore The sun, that looks upon his worshiper.

senses.d: Belonging to a religious order; bound by vows.
q: One of them is religious.

Religious.syn: Pious; godly; holy; devout; devotional; conscientious; strict; rogod; exact.
Religious.etym: [OF. religius, religious, F. religieux, from L. religiosus. See Religion.]

senses.d: A person bound by monastic vows, or sequestered from secular concern, and devoted to a life of piety and religion; a monk or friar; a nun.

To rest with confidence, as when fully satisfied of the veracity, integrity, or ability of persons, or of the certainty of facts or of evidence; to have confidence; to trust; to depend; — with on, formerly also with in.
q: Go in thy native innocence; rely On what thou hast of virtue.
On some fond breast the parting soul relies.

senses.d: To stay behind while others withdraw; to be left after others have been removed or destroyed; to be left after a number or quantity has been subtracted or cut off; to be left as not included or comprised.
q: Gather up the fragments that remain.
Of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep.
That . . . remains to be proved.

senses.d: To continue unchanged in place, form, or condition, or undiminished in quantity; to abide; to stay; to endure; to last.
q: Remain a widow at thy father's house.
Childless thou art; childless remain.

Remain.syn: To continue; stay; wait; tarry; rest; sojourn; dwell; abide; last; endure.
Remain.etym: [OF. remaindre, remanoir, L. remanere; pref. re- re- + manere to stay, remain. See Mansion, and cf. Remainder, Remnant.]

senses.d: To await; to be left to.
q: The easier conquest now remains thee.

senses.d: State of remaining; stay.
q: Which often, since my here remain in England, I 've seen him do.

senses.d: That which is left; relic; remainder; — chiefly in the plural.
q: When this remain of horror has entirely subsided.

senses.d: That which is left of a human being after the life is gone; relics; a dead body.
q: Old warriors whose adored remains In weeping vaults her hallowed earth contains!

senses.d: The posthumous works or productions, esp. literary works, of one who is dead; as, Cecil's
Anything that remains, or is left, after the separation and removal of a part; residue; remnant.
q: If these decoctions be repeated till the water comes off clear, the remainder yields no salt.

senses.d: The quantity or sum that is left after subtraction, or after any deduction.

An estate in expectancy, generally in land, which becomes an estate in possession upon the determination of a particular prior estate, created at the same time, and by the same instrument; for example, if land be conveyed to A for life, and on his death to B, A's life interest is a particuar estate, and B's interest is a remainder, or estate in remainder.
Remaining; left; left over; refuse.
q: Which is as dry as the remainder biscuit After a voyage.

senses.d: Realm.
That which relieves or cures a disease; any medicine or application which puts an end to disease and restores health; — with for; as, a remedy for the gout.
That which corrects or counteracts an evil of any kind; a corrective; a counteractive; reparation; cure; — followed by for or against, formerly by to.
q: What may else be remedy or cure To evils which our own misdeeds have wrought, He will instruct us.

senses.d: The legal means to recover a right, or to obtain redress for a wrong.

Remedy.syn: Cure; restorative; counteraction; reparation; redress; relief; aid; help; assistance.
Remedy.etym: [L. remedium; pref. re- re- + mederi to heal, to cure: cf. F. remède remedy, remédier to remedy. See Medical.]

senses.d: To apply a remedy to; to relieve; to cure; to heal; to repair; to redress; to correct; to counteract.
q: I will remedy this gear ere long.

Remedy.etym: [L. remediare, remediari: cf. F. rem�dier. See Remedy, n.]

senses.d: To have ( a notion or idea) come into the mind again, as previously perceived, known, or felt; to have a renewed apprehension of; to bring to mind again; to think of again; to recollect; as, I remember the fact; he remembers the events of his childhood; I cannot remember dates.
q: We are said to remember anything, when the idea of it arises in the mind with the consciousness that we have had this idea before.

senses.d: To be capable of recalling when required; to keep in mind; to be continually aware or thoughtful of; to preserve fresh in the memory; to attend to; to think of with gratitude, affection, respect, or any other emotion.
q: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
That they may have their wages duly paid 'em, And something over to remember me by.
Remember what I warn thee; shun to taste.

senses.d: To put in mind; to remind; — also used reflexively and impersonally.
q: My friends remembered me of home.
Remember you of passed heaviness.
And well thou wost if it remember thee.

senses.d: To mention.
To recall to the mind of another, as in the friendly messages, remember me to him, he wishes to be remembered to you, etc.

Remember.etym: [OF. remebrer, L. rememorari; pref. re- re- + memorare to bring to remembrance, from memor mindful. See Memory, and cf. Rememorate.]

senses.d: To execise or have the power of memory; as, some remember better than others.
The act of remembering; a holding in mind, or bringing to mind; recollection.
q: Lest fierce remembrance wake my sudden rage.
Lest the remembrance of his grief should fail.

senses.d: The state of being remembered, or held in mind; memory; recollection.
q: This, ever grateful, in remembrance bear.

senses.d: Something remembered; a person or thing kept in memory.
That which serves to keep in or bring to mind; a memorial; a token; a memento; a souvenir; a memorandum or note of something to be remembered.
q: And on his breast a bloody cross he bore, The dear remembrance of his dying Lord.
Keep this remembrance for thy Julia's sake.

senses.d: Something to be remembered; counsel; admoni��on; instruction.
Power of remembering; reach of personal knowledge; period over which one's memory extends.
q: Thee I have heard relating what was done Ere my remembrance.

senses.d: The act of remitting, surrendering, resigning, or giving up.
Discharge from that which is due; relinquishment of a claim, right, or obligation; pardon of transgression; release from forfeiture, penalty, debt, etc.
q: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.
That ples, therefore, . . . Will gain thee no remission.

senses.d: Diminution of intensity; abatement; relaxation.
A temporary and incomplete subsidence of the force or violence of a disease or of pain, as destinguished from intermission, in which the disease completely leaves the patient for a time; abatement.
The act of sending back.
Act of sending in payment, as money; remittance.
To send back; to give up; to surrender; to resign.
q: In the case the law remits him to his ancient and more certain right.
In grevious and inhuman crimes, offenders should be remitted to their prince.
The prisoner was remitted to the guard.

senses.d: To restore.
q: The archbishop was . . . remitted to his liberty.

senses.d: To transmit or send, esp. to a distance, as money in payment of a demand, account, draft, etc.; as, he remitted the amount by mail.

To send off or away; hence: (a) To refer or direct (one) for information, guidance, help, etc. “Remitting them . . . to the works of Galen.” Sir T. Elyot. (b) To submit, refer, or leave (something) for judgment or decision.
To relax in intensity; to make less violent; to abate.
q: So willingly doth God remit his ire.

senses.d: To forgive; to pardon; to remove.
q: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them.

senses.d: To refrain from exacting or enforcing; as, to remit the performance of an obligation.

Remit.syn: To relax; release; abate; relinguish; forgive; pardon; absolve.
Remit.etym: [L. remittere, remissum, to send back, to slacken, relax; pref. re- re- + mittere to send. See Mission, and cf. Remise, Remiss.]

senses.d: To abate in force or in violence; to grow less intense; to become moderated; to abate; to relax; as, a fever remits; the severity of the weather remits.
To send money, as in payment.
Remaining; yet left.
q: And quiet dedicate her remnant life To the just duties of an humble wife.

Remnant.etym: [OF. remanant, p. pr. of remanoir, remaindre. See Remanent, Remain.]

senses.d: That which remains after a part is removed, destroyed, used up, performed, etc.; residue.
q: The remnant that are left of the captivity.
The remnant of my tale is of a length To tire your patience.

senses.d: A small portion; a slight trace; a fragment; a little bit; a scrap.
q: Some odd quirks and remnants of wit.

senses.d: An unsold end of piece goods, as cloth, ribbons, carpets, etc.
To move away from the position occupied; to cause to change place; to displace; as, to remove a building.
q: Thou shalt not remove thy neighbor's landmark.
When we had dined, to prevent the ladies' leaving us, I generally ordered the table to be removed.

senses.d: To cause to leave a person or thing; to cause to cease to be; to take away; hence, to banish; to destroy; to put an end to; to kill; as, to remove a disease.
To dismiss or discharge from office; as, the President removed many postmasters.

Remove.etym: [OF. removoir, remouvoir, L. removere, remotum; pref. re- re- + movere to move. See Move.]

senses.d: To change place in any manner, or to make a change in place; to move or go from one residence, position, or place to another.
q: Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane, I can not taint with fear.

senses.d: The act of removing; a removal.
q: This place should be at once both school and university, not needing a remove to any other house of scholarship.
And drags at each remove a lengthening chain.

senses.d: The transfer of one's business, or of one's domestic belongings, from one location or dwelling house to another; — in the United States usually called a move.
q: It is an English proverb that three removes are as bad as a fire.

senses.d: The state of being removed.
That which is removed, as a dish removed from table to make room for something else.

The distance or space through which anything is removed; interval; distance; stage; hence, a step or degree in any scale of gradation; specifically, a division in an English public school; as, the boy went up two removes last year.
q: A freeholder is but one remove from a legislator.

senses.d: The act of resetting a horse's shoe.
Changed in place.
Dismissed from office.
Distant in location; remote.
Distant by degrees in relationship; as, a cousin once removed.
To separate into parts with force or sudden violence; to tear asunder; to split; to burst; as, powder rends a rock in blasting; lightning rends an oak.
q: The dreadful thunder Doth rend the region.

senses.d: To part or tear off forcibly; to take away by force.
q: An empire from its old foundations rent.
I will surely rend the kingdom from thee.

Rend.syn: To tear; burst; break; rupture; lacerate; fracture; crack; split.
Rend.etym: [AS. rendan, hrendan; cf. OFries. renda, randa, Fries. renne to cut, rend, Icel. hrinda to push, thrust, AS. hrindan; or cf. Icel. r�na to rob, plunder, Ir. rannaim to divide, share, part, W. rhanu, Armor. ranna.]

senses.d: To be rent or torn; to become parted; to separate; to split.
One who rends.
To return; to pay back; to restore.
q: Whose smallest minute lost, no riches render may.

senses.d: To inflict, as a retribution; to requite.
q: I will render vengeance to mine enemies.

senses.d: To give up; to yield; to surrender.
q: I 'll make her render up her page to me.

senses.d: Hence, to furnish; to contribute.
q: Logic renders its daily service to wisdom and virtue.

senses.d: To furnish; to state; to deliver; as, to render an account; to render judgment.
To cause to be, or to become; as, to render a person more safe or more unsafe; to render a fortress secure.
To translate from one language into another; as, to render Latin into English.
To interpret; to set forth, represent, or exhibit; as, an actor renders his part poorly; a singer renders a passage of music with great effect; a painter renders a scene in a felicitous manner.
q: He did render him the most unnatural That lived amongst men.

senses.d: To try out or extract (oil, lard, tallow, etc.) from fatty animal substances; as, to render tallow.
To plaster, as a wall of masonry, without the use of lath.

Render.etym: [F. rendre, LL. rendre, fr. L. reddere; pref. red-, re-, re- + dare to give. See Datetime, and cf. Reddition, Rent.]

senses.d: To give an account; to make explanation or confession.
To pass; to run; — said of the passage of a rope through a block, eyelet, etc.; as, a rope renders well, that is, passes freely; also, to yield or give way.
A surrender.
A return; a payment of rent.
q: In those early times the king's household was supported by specific renders of corn and other victuals from the tenants of the demains.

senses.d: An account given; a statement.
The act of one who renders, or that which is rendered.
A version; translation; as, the rendering of the Hebrew text.
In art, the presentation, expression, or interpretation of an idea, theme, or part.
The act of laying the first coat of plaster on brickwork or stonework.
The coat of plaster thus laid on.
The process of trying out or extracting lard, tallow, etc., from animal fat.
To make new again; to restore to freshness, perfection, or vigor; to give new life to; to rejuvenate; to re�stablish; to recreate; to rebuild.
q: In such a night Medea gathered the enchanted herbs That did renew old �son.

senses.d: Specifically, to substitute for (an old obligation or right) a new one of the same nature; to continue in force; to make again; as, to renew a lease, note, or patent.
To begin again; to recommence.
q: The last great age . . . renews its finished course.

senses.d: To repeat; to go over again.
q: The birds-their notes renew.

senses.d: To make new spiritually; to regenerate.
q: Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.

senses.d: To become new, or as new; to grow or begin again.
To declare against; to reject or decline formally; to refuse to own or acknowledge as belonging to one; to disclaim; as, to renounce a title to land or to a throne.
To cast off or reject deliberately; to disown; to dismiss; to forswear.
q: This world I do renounce, and in your sights Shake patiently my great affliction off.

senses.d: To disclaim having a card of (the suit led) by playing a card of another suit.
q: From Thebes my birth I own; . . . since no disgrace Can force me to renounce the honor of my race.
Either to die the death, or to abjure Forever the society of man.
Ease would recant Vows made in pain, as violent and void.

Renounce.syn: To cast off; disavow; disown; disclaim; deny; abjure; recant; abandon; forsake; quit; forego; resign; relinquish; give up; abdicate.
Renounce.etym: [F. renoncer, L. renuntiare to bring back word, announce, revoke, retract, renounce; pref. re- re- + nuntiare to announce, fr. nuncius, a messenger. See Nuncio, and cf. Renunciation.]

senses.d: To make renunciation.
q: He of my sons who fails to make it good, By one rebellious act renounces to my blood.

senses.d: To decline formally, as an executor or a person entitled to letters of administration, to take out probate or letters.
q: Dryden died without a will, and his widow having renounced, his son Charles administered on June 10.

senses.d: Act of renouncing.
The state of being much known and talked of; exalted reputation derived from the extensive praise of great achievements or accomplishments; fame; celebrity; — always in a good sense.
q: Nor envy we Thy great renown, nor grudge thy victory.

senses.d: Report of nobleness or exploits; praise.
q: This famous duke of Milan, Of whom so often I have heard renown.

Renown.etym: [F. renom. See Noun, and cf. Renown, v.]

senses.d: To make famous; to give renown to.
q: For joy to hear me so renown his son.
The bard whom pilfered pastorals renown.

Renown.etym: [F. renommer to name again, celebrate, make famous; pref. re- re- + nommer to name, L. nominare , fr. nomen a name. See Noun.]

senses.d: Famous; celebrated for great achievements, for distinguished qualities, or for grandeur; eminent; as, a renowned king.
q: These were the renowned of the congregation.

Renowned.syn: Famous; famed; distinguished; noted; eminent; celebrated; remarkable; wonderful. See Famous.

senses.d: To rant.
An opening made by rending; a break or breach made by force; a tear.
q: See what a rent the envious Casca made.

senses.d: Figuratively, a schism; a rupture of harmony; a separation; as, a rent in the church.

Rent.syn: Fissure; breach; disrupture; rupture; tear; dilaceration; break; fracture.

senses.d: To tear. See Rend.
Income; revenue. See Catel.
q: a waster was and all his rent In wine and bordel he dispent.
So bought an annual rent or two, And liv'd, just as you see I do.

senses.d: Pay; reward; share; toll.
q: Death, that taketh of high and low his rent.

senses.d: A certain periodical profit, whether in money, provisions, chattels, or labor, issuing out of lands and tenements in payment for the use; commonly, a certain pecuniary sum agreed upon between a tenant and his landlord, paid at fixed intervals by the lessee to the lessor, for the use of land or its appendages; as, rent for a farm, a house, a park, etc.

Rent.etym: [F. rente, LL. renta, fr. L. reddita, fem. sing. or neut. pl. of redditus, p. p. of reddere to give back, pay. See Render.]

senses.d: To grant the possession and enjoyment of, for a rent; to lease; as, the owwner of an estate or house rents it.
To take and hold under an agreement to pay rent; as, the tennant rents an estate of the owner.
To be leased, or let for rent; as, an estate rents for five hundred dollars a year.

That portion of the produce of the earth paid to the landlord for the use of the “original and indestructible powers of the soil;” the excess of the return from a given piece of cultivated land over that from land of equal area at the “margin of cultivation.” Called also economic, or Ricardian, rent. Economic rent is due partly to differences of productivity, but chiefly to advantages of location; it is equivalent to ordinary or commercial rent less interest on improvements, and nearly equivalent to ground rent.
Loosely, a return or profit from a differential advantage for production, as in case of income or earnings due to rare natural gifts creating a natural monopoly.
In France, interest payable by government on indebtedness; the bonds, shares, stocks, etc., which represent government indebtedness.
To return.
q: I thought . . . that he repaire should again.

senses.d: To go; to betake one's self; to resort; ass, to repair to sanctuary for safety.
q: Go, mount the winds, and to the shades repair.

Repair.etym: [OE. repairen, OF. repairier to return, fr. L. repatriare to return to one's contry, to go home again; pref. re- re- + patria native country, fr. pater father. See Father, and cf. Repatriate.]

senses.d: The act of repairing or resorting to a place.
q: The king sent a proclamation for their repair to their houses.

senses.d: Place to which one repairs; a haunt; a resort.
q: There the fierce winds his tender force assail And beat him downward to his first repair.

Repair.etym: [OF. repaire retreat, asylum, abode. See Repair to go.]

senses.d: To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation, or partial destruction; to renew; to restore; to mend; as, to repair a house, a road, a shoe, or a ship; to repair a shattered fortune.
q: Secret refreshings that repair his strength.
Do thou, as thou art wont, repair My heart with gladness.

senses.d: To make amends for, as for an injury, by an equivalent; to indemnify for; as, to repair a loss or damage.
q: I 'll repair the misery thou dost bear.

Repair.syn: To restore, recover; renew; amend; mend; retrieve; recruit.
Repair.etym: [F. réparer, L. reparare; pref. re- re- + parare to prepare. See Pare, and cf. Reparation.]

senses.d: Restoration to a sound or good state after decay, waste, injury, or partial restruction; supply of loss; reparation; as, materials are collected for the repair of a church or of a city.
q: Sunk down and sought repair Of sleep, which instantly fell on me.

senses.d: Condition with respect to soundness, perfectness, etc.; as, a house in good, or bad, repair; the book is out of repair.
One who, or that which, repairs, restores, or makes amends.
To pay back; to refund; as, to repay money borrowed or advanced.
q: If you repay me not on such a day, In such a place, such sum or sums.

senses.d: To make return or requital for; to recompense; — in a good or bad sense; as, to repay kindness; to repay an injury.
q: Benefits which can not be repaid . . . are not commonly found to increase affection.

senses.d: To pay anew, or a second time, as a debt.

Repay.syn: To refund; restore; return; recompense; compensate; remunerate; satisfy; reimburse; requite.

senses.d: To go over again; to attempt, do, make, or utter again; to iterate; to recite; as, to repeat an effort, an order, or a poem.
q: Not well conceived of God; who, though his power Creation could repeat, yet would be loth Us to abolish.

senses.d: To make trial of again; to undergo or encounter again.
To repay or refund (an excess received).

Repeat.syn: To reiterate; iterate; renew; recite; relate; rehearse; recapitulate. See Reiterate.
Repeat.etym: [F. répéter, L. repetere; pref. re- re- + petere to fall upon, attack. See Petition.]

senses.d: The act of repeating; repetition.
That which is repeated; as, the repeat of a pattern; that is, the repetition of the engraved figure on a roller by which an impression is produced (as in calico printing, etc.).
A mark, or series of dots, placed before and after, or often only at the end of, a passage to be repeated in performance.
Prostrate and rooting; — said of stems.
Same as Reptant.

Repent.etym: [L. repens, -entis, creeping, p. pr. of repere to creep.]

senses.d: To feel pain, sorrow, or regret, for what one has done or omitted to do.
q: First she relents With pity; of that pity then repents.

senses.d: To change the mind, or the course of conduct, on account of regret or dissatisfaction.
q: Lest, peradventure, the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt.

senses.d: To be sorry for sin as morally evil, and to seek forgiveness; to cease to love and practice sin.
q: Except ye repent, ye shall likewise perish.

Repent.etym: [F. se repentir; L. pref. re- re- + poenitere to make repent, poenitet me it repents me, I repent. See Penitent.]

senses.d: To feel pain on account of; to remember with sorrow.
q: I do repent it from my very soul.

senses.d: To feel regret or sorrow; — used reflexively.
q: My father has repented him ere now.

senses.d: To cause to have sorrow or regret; — used impersonally.
The act of repenting, or the state of being penitent; sorrow for what one has done or omitted to do; especially, contrition for sin.
q: Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation.
Repentance is a change of mind, or a conversion from sin to God.

Repentance is the relinquishment of any practice from the conviction that it has offended God. Sorrow, fear, and anxiety are properly not parts, but adjuncts, of repentance; yet they are too closely connected with it to be easily separated.

Repentance.syn: Contrition; regret; penitence; contriteness; compunction. See Contrition.

senses.d: The act of repeating; a doing or saying again; iteration.
q: I need not be barren of accusations; he hath faults, with surplus to tire in repetition.

senses.d: Recital from memory; rehearsal.
The act of repeating, singing, or playing, the same piece or part a second time; reiteration of a note.
Reiteration, or repeating the same word, or the same sense in different words, for the purpose of making a deeper impression on the audience.
The measurement of an angle by successive observations with a repeating instrument.

Repetition.etym: [L. repetitio: cf. F. répétition. See Repeat.]

senses.d: To fill again after having been diminished or emptied; to stock anew; hence, to fill completely; to cause to abound.
q: Multiply and replenish the earth.
The waters thus With fish replenished, and the air with fowl.

senses.d: To finish; to complete; to perfect.
q: We smothered The most replenished sweet work of nature.

Replenish.etym: [OE. replenissen, OF. replenir; L. pref. re- re- + plenus full. See Full, -ish, and cf. Replete.]

senses.d: To recover former fullness.
q: The humors will not replenish so soon.

senses.d: To make a return in words or writing; to respond; to answer.
q: O man, who art thou that repliest against God?

senses.d: To answer a defendant's plea.
Figuratively, to do something in return for something done; as, to reply to a signal; to reply to the fire of a battery.

Reply.etym: [OE. replien, OF. replier, F. répliquer, fr. L. replicare to fold back, make a reply; pref. re- re- + plicare to fold. See Ply, and cf. Replica.]

senses.d: To return for an answer.
q: Lords, vouchsafe To give me hearing what I shall reply.

senses.d: That which is said, written, or done in answer to what is said, written, or done by another; an answer; a response.

Reply.etym: [See Reply, v. i., and cf. Replica.]

senses.d: To refer.
q: Baldwin, his son, . . . succeeded his father; so like unto him that we report the reader to the character of King Almeric, and will spare the repeating his description.

senses.d: To bring back, as an answer; to announce in return; to relate, as what has been discovered by a person sent to examine, explore, or investigate; as, a messenger reports to his employer what he has seen or ascertained; the committee reported progress.
q: There is no man that may reporten all.

senses.d: To give an account of; to relate; to tell; to circulate publicly, as a story; as, in the common phrase, it is reported.
q: It is reported among the heathen, and Gashmu saith it, that thou and the Jews think to rebel.

senses.d: To give an official account or statement of; as, a treasurer reports the receipts and expenditures.
To return or repeat, as sound; to echo.

To return or present as the result of an examination or consideration of any matter officially referred; as, the committee reported the bill witth amendments, or reported a new bill, or reported the results of an inquiry.
To make minutes of, as a speech, or the doings of a public body; to write down from the lips of a speaker.
To write an account of for publication, as in a newspaper; as, to report a public celebration or a horse race.
To make a statement of the conduct of, especially in an unfavorable sense; as, to report a servant to his employer.

Report.syn: To relate; narrate; tell; recite; describe.
Report.etym: [F. reporter to carry back, carry (cf. rapporter; see Rapport), L. reportare to bear or bring back; pref. re- re- + portare to bear or bring. See Port bearing, demeanor.]

senses.d: To make a report, or response, in respect of a matter inquired of, a duty enjoined, or information expected; as, the committee will report at twelve o'clock.
To furnish in writing an account of a speech, the proceedings at a meeting, the particulars of an occurrence, etc., for publication.

To present one's self, as to a superior officer, or to one to whom service is due, and to be in readiness for orders or to do service; also, to give information, as of one's address, condition, etc.; as, the officer reported to the general for duty; to report weekly by letter.
That which is reported.
q: It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom.
Cornelius the centurion, a just man, and . . . of good report among all the nation of the Jews.

senses.d: Sound; noise; as, the report of a pistol or cannon.

An official statement of facts, verbal or written; especially, a statement in writing of proceedings and facts exhibited by an officer to his superiors; as, the reports of the heads af departments to Congress, of a master in chancery to the court, of committees to a legislative body, and the like.

An account or statement of a judicial opinion or decision, or of case argued and determined in a court of law, chancery, etc.; also, in the plural, the volumes containing such reports; as, Coke's Reports.
A sketch, or a fully written account, of a speech, debate, or the proceedings of a public meeting, legislative body, etc.
Rapport; relation; connection; reference.
q: The corridors worse, having no report to the wings they join to.

Report.syn: Account; relation; narration; detail; description; recital; narrative; story; rumor; hearsay.

senses.d: To come back to, or come home to, as a matter of blame; to bring shame or disgrace upon; to disgrace.
q: I thought your marriage fit; else imputation, For that he knew you, might reproach your life.

senses.d: To attribute blame to; to allege something disgraceful against; to charge with a fault; to censure severely or contemptuously; to upbraid.
q: If ye be reproached for the name of Christ.
That this newcomer, Shame, There sit not, and reproach us as unclean.
Mezentius . . . with his ardor warmed His fainting friends, reproached their shameful flight. Repelled the victors.

Reproach.syn: To upbraid; censure; blame; chide; rebuke; condemn; revile; vilify.
Reproach.etym: [F. reprocher, OF. reprochier, (assumed) LL. reproriare; L. pref. re- again, against, back + prope near; hence, originally, to bring near to, throw in one's teeth. Cf. Approach.]

senses.d: The act of reproaching; censure mingled with contempt; contumelious or opprobrious language toward any person; abusive reflections; as, severe reproach.
q: No reproaches even, even when pointed and barbed with the sharpest wit, appeared to give him pain.
Give not thine heritage to reproach.

senses.d: A cause of blame or censure; shame; disgrace.
An object of blame, censure, scorn, or derision.
q: Come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.

Reproach.syn: Disrepute; discredit; dishonor; opprobrium; invective; contumely; reviling; abuse; vilification; scurrility; insolence; insult; scorn; contempt; ignominy; shame; scandal;; disgrace; infamy.

senses.d: Expressing or containing reproach; upbraiding; opprobrious; abusive.
q: The reproachful speeches . . . That he hath breathed in my dishonor here.

senses.d: Occasioning or deserving reproach; shameful; base; as, a reproachful life.

Reproachful.syn: Opprobrious; contumelious; abusive; offensive; insulting; contemptuous; scornful; insolent; scurrilous; disreputable; discreditable; dishonorable; shameful; disgraceful; scandalous; base; vile; infamous.

senses.d: Not enduring proof or trial; not of standard purity or fineness; disallowed; rejected.
q: Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the Lord hath rejected them.

senses.d: Abandoned to punishment; hence, morally abandoned and lost; given up to vice; depraved.
q: And strength, and art, are easily outdone By spirits reprobate.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to one who is given up to wickedness; as, reprobate conduct.

Reprobate.syn: Abandoned; vitiated; depraved; corrupt; wicked; profligate; base; vile. See Abandoned.
Reprobate.etym: [L. reprobatus, p. p. of reprobare to disapprove, condemn. See Reprieve, Reprove.]

senses.d: One morally abandoned and lost.
q: I acknowledge myself for a reprobate, a villain, a traitor to the king.

senses.d: To disapprove with detestation or marks of extreme dislike; to condemn as unworthy; to disallow; to reject.
q: Such an answer as this is reprobated and disallowed of in law; I do not believe it, unless the deed appears.
Every scheme, every person, recommended by one of them, was reprobated by the other.

senses.d: To abandon to punishment without hope of pardon.

Reprobate.syn: To condemn; reprehend; censure; disown; abandon; reject.

senses.d: Refutation; confutation; contradiction.
An expression of blame or censure; especially, blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; chiding; reproach.
q: Those best can bear reproof who merit praise.

Reproof.syn: Admonition; reprehension; chiding; reprimand; rebuke; censure; blame. See Admonition.

senses.d: To convince.
q: When he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment.

senses.d: To disprove; to refute.
q: Reprove my allegation, if you can.

senses.d: To chide to the face as blameworthy; to accuse as guilty; to censure.
q: What if thy son
Prove disobedient, and, reproved, retort, “Wherefore didst thou beget me?”

senses.d: To express disapprobation of; as, to reprove faults.
q: He neither reproved the ordinance of John, neither plainly condemned the fastings of the other men.

Reprove.syn: To reprehend; chide; rebuke; scold; blame censure.
Reprove.etym: [F. réprouver, OF. reprover, fr. L. reprobare. See Reprieve, Reprobate, and cf. Reproof.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, reproves.
The estimation in which one is held; character in public opinion; the character attributed to a person, thing, or action; repute.
q: The best evidence of reputation is a man's whole life.

senses.d: The character imputed to a person in the community in which he lives. It is admissible in evidence when he puts his character in issue, or when such reputation is otherwise part of the issue of a case.
Specifically: Good reputation; favorable regard; public esteem; general credit; good name.
q: I see my reputation is at stake.
The security of his reputation or good name.

senses.d: Account; value.
q: made himself of no reputation.

Reputation.syn: Credit; repute; regard; estimation; esteem; honor; fame. See the Note under Character.
Reputation.etym: [F. réputation, L. reputatio a reckoning, consideration. See Repute, v. t.]

senses.d: To hold in thought; to account; to estimate; to hold; to think; to reckon.
q: Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight?
The king your father was reputed for A prince most prudent.

Repute.etym: [F. réputer, L. reputare to count over, think over; pref. re- re- + putare to count, think. See Putative.]

senses.d: Character reputed or attributed; reputation, whether good or bad; established opinion; public estimate.
q: He who regns Monarch in heaven, till then as one secure Sat on his throne, upheld by old repute.

senses.d: Specifically: Good character or reputation; credit or honor derived from common or public opinion; — opposed to disrepute.
The act of asking for anything desired; expression of desire or demand; solicitation; prayer; petition; entreaty.
q: I will marry her, sir, at your request.

senses.d: That which is asked for or requested.
q: I will both hear and grant you your requests.

senses.d: A state of being desired or held in such estimation as to be sought after or asked for; demand.
q: Knowledge and fame were in as great request as wealth among us now.

Request.syn: Asking; solicitation; petition; prayer; supplication; entreaty; suit.
Request.etym: [OE. requeste, OF. requeste, F. requête, LL. requesta, for requisita, fr. L. requirere, requisitum, to seek again, ask for. See Require, and cf. Quest.]

senses.d: To ask for (something); to express desire ffor; to solicit; as, to request his presence, or a favor.
To address with a request; to ask.
q: I request you To give my poor host freedom.

Request.syn: To ask; solicit; entreat; beseech. See Beg.

senses.d: To demand; to insist upon having; to claim as by right and authority; to exact; as, to require the surrender of property.
q: Shall I say to Cæsar What you require of him?
By nature did what was by law required.

senses.d: To demand or exact as indispensable; to need.
q: Just gave what life required, and gave no more.
The two last require to be particularly noticed.

senses.d: To ask as a favor; to request.
q: I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way.

Require.syn: To claim; exact; enjoin; prescribe; direct; order; demand; need.
Require.etym: [OE. requeren, requiren, OF. requerre, F. requ�rir; L. pref. re- re- + quaerere to ask; cf. L. requirere. See Query, and cf. Request, Requisite.]

senses.d: To repay; in a good sense, to recompense; to return (an equivalent) in good; to reward; in a bad sense, to retaliate; to return (evil) for evil; to punish.
q: He can requite thee; for he knows the charma That call fame on such gentle acts as these.
Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand.

Requite.syn: To repay; reward; pay; compensate; remunerate; satisfy; recompense; punish; revenge.

senses.d: The rear guard of an army.

To free or deliver from any confinement, violence, danger, or evil; to liberate from actual restraint; to remove or withdraw from a state of exposure to evil; as, to rescue a prisoner from the enemy; to rescue seamen from destruction.
q: Had I been seized by a hungry lion, I would have been a breakfast to the best, Rather than have false Proteus rescue me.

Rescue.syn: To retake; recapture; free; deliver; liberate; release; save.
Rescue.etym: [OE. rescopuen, OF. rescourre, rescurre, rescorre; L. pref. re- re- + excutere to shake or drive out; ex out + quatere to shake. See Qtash to crush, Rercussion.]

senses.d: The act of rescuing; deliverance from restraint, violence, or danger; liberation.
q: Spur to the rescue of the noble Talbot.

senses.d: The forcible retaking, or taking away, against law, of things lawfully distrained.
q: The rescue of a prisoner from the court is punished with perpetual imprisonment and forfeiture of goods.

senses.d: The quality or state of resembling; likeness; similitude; similarity.
q: One main end of poetry and painting is to please; they bear a great resemblance to each other.

senses.d: That which resembles, or is similar; a representation; a likeness.
q: These sensible things, which religion hath allowed, are resemblances formed according to things spiritual.

senses.d: A comparison; a simile.
Probability; verisimilitude.

Resemblance.syn: Likeness; similarity; similitude; semblance; representation; image.

senses.d: To be like or similar to; to bear the similitude of, either in appearance or qualities; as, these brothers resemble each other.
q: We will resemble you in that.

senses.d: To liken; to compare; to represent as like.
q: The other . . . He did resemble to his lady bright.

senses.d: To counterfeit; to imitate.
To cause to imitate or be like.

Resemble.etym: [F. ressembler; pref. re- re- + sembler to seem, resemble, fr. L. similare, simulare, to imitate, fr. similis like, similar. See Similar.]

senses.d: To keep back; to retain; not to deliver, make over, or disclose.
Hence, to keep in store for future or special use; to withhold from present use for another purpose or time; to keep; to retain.
q: Hast thou seen the treasures of the hail, which I have reserved against the time of trouble?
Reserve your kind looks and language for private hours.

senses.d: To make an exception of; to except.

Reserve.etym: [F. réserver, L. reservare, reservatum; pref. re- re- + servare to keep. See Serve.]

senses.d: The act of reserving, or keeping back; reservation.
q: However any one may concur in the general scheme, it is still with certain reserves and deviations.

senses.d: That which is reserved, or kept back, as for future use.
q: The virgins, besides the oil in their lamps, carried likewise a reserve in some other vessel for a continual supply.

senses.d: That which is excepted; exception.
q: Each has some darling lust, which pleads for a reserve.

senses.d: Restraint of freedom in words or actions; backwardness; caution in personal behavior.
q: My soul, surprised, and from her sex disjoined, Left all reserve, and all the sex, behind.
The clergyman's shy and sensitive reserve had balked this scheme.

senses.d: A tract of land reserved, or set apart, for a particular purpose; as, the Connecticut Reserve in Ohio, originally set apart for the school fund of Connecticut; the Clergy Reserves in Canada, for the support of the clergy.
A body of troops in the rear of an army drawn up for battle, reserved to support the other lines as occasion may require; a force or body of troops kept for an exigency.
Funds kept on hand to meet liabilities.

Reserve.syn: Reservation; retention; limitation; backwardness; reservedness; coldness; restraint; shyness; coyness; modesty.

senses.d: That part of the assets of a bank or other financial institution specially kept in cash in a more or less liquid form as a reasonable provision for meeting all demands which may be made upon it;
In exhibitions, a distinction which indicates that the recipient will get a prize if another should be disqualified.
A resist.
A preparation used on an object being electroplated to fix the limits of the deposit.
Kept for future or special use, or for an exigency; as, reserved troops; a reserved seat in a theater.
Restrained from freedom in words or actions; backward, or cautious, in communicating one's thoughts and feelings; not free or frank.
q: To all obliging, yet reserved to all.
Nothing reserved or sullen was to see.

senses.d: That which remains after a part is taken, separated, removed, or designated; remnant; remainder.
q: The residue of them will I deliver to the sword.
If church power had then prevailed over its victims, not a residue of English liberty would have been saved.

senses.d: That part of a testeator's estate wwhich is not disposed of in his will by particular and special legacies and devises, and which remains after payment of debts and legacies.

That which remains of a molecule after the removal of a portion of its constituents; hence, an atom or group regarded as a portion of a molecule; — used as nearly equivalent to radical, but in a more general sense.
Any positive or negative number that differs from a given number by a multiple of a given modulus; thus, if 7 is the modulus, and 9 the given number, the numbers -5, 2, 16, 23, etc., are residues.

Residue.syn: Rest; remainder; remnant; balance; residuum; remains; leavings; relics.
Residue.etym: [F. résidu, L. residuum, fr. residuus that is left behind, remaining, fr. residere to remain behind. See Reside, and cf. Residuum.]

senses.d: To stand against; to withstand; to obstruct.
q: That mortal dint, Save He who reigns above, none can resist.

senses.d: To strive against; to endeavor to counteract, defeat, or frustrate; to act in opposition to; to oppose.
q: God resisteth the proud.
Contrary to his high will Whom we resist.

senses.d: To counteract, as a force, by inertia or reaction.
To be distasteful to.

Resist.syn: To withstand; oppose; hinder; obstruct; counteract; check; thwart; baffle; disappoint.
Resist.etym: [F. résister, L. resistere, pref. re- re- + sistere to stand, cause to stand, v. causative of stare to stand. See Stand.]

senses.d: To make opposition.

A substance used to prevent a color or mordant from fixing on those parts to which it has been applied, either by acting machanically in preventing the color, etc., from reaching the cloth, or chemically in changing the color so as to render it incapable of fixing itself in the fibers.. The pastes prepared for this purpose are called resist pastes.
Something that resists or prevents a certain action;
A substance applied to a surface, as of metal, to prevent the action on it of acid or other chemical agent.
To separate the component parts of; to reduce to the constituent elements; — said of compound substances; hence, sometimes, to melt, or dissolve.
q: O, that this too too solid flesh would melt, Thaw, and resolve itself into a dew!
Ye immortal souls, who once were men, And now resolved to elements again.

senses.d: To reduce to simple or intelligible notions; — said of complex ideas or obscure questions; to make clear or certain; to free from doubt; to disentangle; to unravel; to explain; hence, to clear up, or dispel, as doubt; as, to resolve a riddle.
q: To the resolving whereof we must first know that the Jews were commanded to divorce an unbelieving Gentile.

senses.d: To cause to perceive or understand; to acquaint; to inform; to convince; to assure; to make certain.
q: Sir, be resolved. I must and will come.
Resolve me, Reason, which of these is worse, Want with a full, or with an empty purse?
In health, good air, pleasure, riches, I am resolved it can not be equaled by any region.
We must be resolved how the law can be pure and perspicuous, and yet throw a polluted skirt over these Eleusinian mysteries.

senses.d: To determine or decide in purpose; to make ready in mind; to fix; to settle; as, he was resolved by an unexpected event.

To express, as an opinion or determination, by resolution and vote; to declare or decide by a formal vote; — followed by a clause; as, the house resolved (or, it was resolved by the house) that no money should be apropriated (or, to appropriate no money).
To change or convert by resolution or formal vote; — used only reflexively; as, the house resolved itself into a committee of the whole.
To solve, as a problem, by enumerating the several things to be done, in order to obtain what is required; to find the answer to, or the result of.
To dispere or scatter; to discuss, as an inflammation or a tumor.
To let the tones (as of a discord) follow their several tendencies, resulting in a concord.
To relax; to lay at ease.

Resolve.etym: [L. resolvere, resolutum, to untie, loosen, relax, enfeeble; pref. re- re- + solvere to loosen, dissolve: cf. F. résoudare to resolve. See Solve, and cf. Resolve, v. i., Resolute, Resolution.]

senses.d: To be separated into its component parts or distinct principles; to undergo resolution.
To melt; to dissolve; to become fluid.
q: When the blood stagnates in any part, it first coagulates, then resolves, and turns alkaline.

senses.d: To be settled in opinion; to be convinced.
q: Let men resolve of that as they plaease.

senses.d: To form a purpose; to make a decision; especially, to determine after reflection; as, to resolve on a better course of life.
The act of resolving or making clear; resolution; solution.
That which has been resolved on or determined; decisive conclusion; fixed purpose; determination; also, legal or official determination; a legislative declaration; a resolution.
q: Nor is your firm resolve unknown.
Cæsar's approach has summoned us together, And Rome attends her fate from our resolves.

senses.d: Having a fixed purpose; determined; resolute; — usually placed after its noun; as, a man resolved to be rich.
q: That makes him a resolved enemy.
I am resolved she shall not settle here.

senses.d: Active power or movement; spring.
q: Some . . . know the resorts and falls of business that can not sink into the main of it.

senses.d: To go; to repair; to betake one's self.
q: What men name resort to him?

senses.d: To fall back; to revert.
q: The inheritance of the son never resorted to the mother, or to any of her ancestors.

senses.d: To have recourse; to apply; to one's self for help, relief, or advantage.
q: The king thought it time to resort to other counsels.

Resort.etym: [OF. resortir to withdraw, take refuge, F. ressortir to be in the jurisdiction, LL. resortire; pref. re- re- + L. sortiri to draw lots, obtain by lot, from sors lot. See Sort. The meaning is first to reobtain (by lot), then to gain by appeal to a higher court (as a law term), to appeal, go for prote

senses.d: The act of going to, or making application; a betaking one's self; the act of visiting or seeking; recourse; as, a place of popular resort; — often figuratively; as, to have resort to force.
q: Join with me to forbid him her resort.

senses.d: A place to which one betakes himself habitually; a place of frequent assembly; a haunt.
q: Far from all resort of mirth.

senses.d: That to which one resorts or looks for help; resource; refuge.

Resort.etym: [Cf. F. ressort jurisdiction. See Resort, v.]

senses.d: To take notice of; to regard with special attention; to regard as worthy of special consideration; hence, to care for; to heed.
q: Thou respectest not spilling Edward's blood.
In orchards and gardens, we do not so much respect beauty as variety of ground for fruits, trees, and herbs.

senses.d: To consider worthy of esteem; to regard with honor.
To look toward; to front upon or toward.
q: Palladius adviseth the front of his house should so respect the ��uth.

senses.d: To regard; to consider; to deem.
q: To whom my father gave this name of Gaspar, And as his own respected him to death.

senses.d: To have regard to; to have reference to; to relate to; as, the treaty particularly respects our commerce.

Respect.syn: To regard; esteem; honor; revere; venerate.
Respect.etym: [L. respectare, v. intens. from respicere, respectum, to look back, respect; pref. re- re- + specere, spicere, to look, to view: cf. F. respecter. See Spy, and cf. Respite.]

senses.d: The act of noticing with attention; the giving particular consideration to; hence, care; caution.
q: But he it well did ward with wise respect.

senses.d: Esteem; regard; consideration; honor.
q: Seen without awe, and served without respect.
The same men treat the Lord's Day with as little respect.

senses.d: An expression of respect of deference; regards; as, to send one's respects to another.
Reputation; repute.
q: Many of the best respect in Rome.

senses.d: Relation; reference; regard.
q: They believed but one Supreme Deity, which, with respect to the various benefits men received from him, had several titles.

senses.d: Particular; point regarded; point of view; as, in this respect; in any respect; in all respects.
q: Everything which is imperfect, as the world must be acknowledged in many respects.
In one respect I'll be thy assistant.

senses.d: Consideration; motive; interest.
q: To the publik good Private respects must yield.

Respect.syn: Deference; attention; regard; consideration; estimation. See Deference.
Respect.etym: [L. respectus: cf. F. respect. See Respect, v., and cf. Respite.]

senses.d: One who respects.
q: Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.

senses.d: A putting off of that which was appointed; a postponement or delay.
q: I crave but four day's respite.

senses.d: Temporary intermission of labor, or of any process or operation; interval of rest; pause; delay.
q: Some pause and respite only I require.

senses.d: Temporary suspension of the execution of a capital offender; reprieve.

Respite.syn: Pause; interval; stop; cessation; delay; postponement; stay; reprieve.
Respite.etym: [OF. respit, F. répit, from L. respectus respect, regard, delay, in LL., the deferring of a day. See Respect.]

senses.d: To give or grant a respite to.
To delay or postpone; to put off.
To keep back from execution; to reprieve.
q: Forty days longer we do respite you.

senses.d: To relieve by a pause or interval of rest.

Respite.etym: [OF. respiter, LL. respectare. See Respite, n.]

senses.d: To arrest.
A state of quiet or repose; a cessation from motion or labor; tranquillity; as, rest from mental exertion; rest of body or mind.
q: Sleep give thee all his rest!

senses.d: Hence, freedom from everything which wearies or disturbs; peace; security.
q: And the land had rest fourscore years.

senses.d: Sleep; slumber; hence, poetically, death.
q: How sleep the brave who sink to rest, By all their country's wishes blest.

senses.d: That on which anything rests or leans for support; as, a rest in a lathe, for supporting the cutting tool or steadying the work.
q: He made narrowed rests round about, that the beams should not be fastened in the walls of the house.

senses.d: A projection from the right side of the cuirass, serving to support the lance.
q: Their visors closed, their lances in the rest.

senses.d: A place where one may rest, either temporarily, as in an inn, or permanently, as, in an abode.
q: In dust our final rest, and native home.
Ye are not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance which the Lord your God giveth you.

senses.d: A short pause in reading verse; a cæsura.
The striking of a balance at regular intervals in a running account.
A set or game at tennis.
Silence in music or in one of its parts; the name of the character that stands for such silence. They are named as notes are, whole, half, quarter,etc.

Rest.syn: Cessation; pause; intermission; stop; stay; repose; slumber; quiet; ease; quietness; stillness; tranquillity; peacefulness; peace.
Rest.etym: [AS. rest, ræst, rest; akin to D. rust, G. rast. OHG. rasta, Dan. & Sw. rast rest, repose, Icel. röst the distance between two resting places, a mole, Goth. rasta a mile, also to Goth. razn house, Icel. rann, and perhaps to G. ruhe rest, repose, AS. rōw, Gr. ερωἤ. Cf. Ransack.]

senses.d: To cease from action or motion, especially from action which has caused weariness; to desist from labor or exertion.
q: God . . . rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
Six days thou shalt do thy work, and on the seventh day thou shalt rest.

senses.d: To be free from whatever wearies or disturbs; to be quiet or still.
q: There rest, if any rest can harbor there.

senses.d: To lie; to repose; to recline; to lan; as, to rest on a couch.
To stand firm; to be fixed; to be supported; as, a column rests on its pedestal.
To sleep; to slumber; hence, poetically, to be dead.
q: Fancy . . . then retries Into her private cell when Nature rests.

senses.d: To lean in confidence; to trust; to rely; to repose without anxiety; as, to rest on a man's promise.
q: On him I rested, after long debate, And not without considering, fixed my fate.

senses.d: To be satisfied; to acquiesce.
q: To rest in Heaven's determination.

senses.d: To lay or place at rest; to quiet.
q: Your piety has paid All needful rites, to rest my wandering shade.

senses.d: To place, as on a support; to cause to lean.
q: Her weary head upon your bosom rest.

senses.d: That which is left, or which remains after the separation of a part, either in fact or in contemplation; remainder; residue.
q: Religion gives part of its reward in hand, the present comfort of having done our duty, and, for the rest, it offers us the best security that Heaven can give.

senses.d: Those not included in a proposition or description; the remainder; others.
q: Armed like the rest, the Trojan prince appears.

senses.d: A surplus held as a reserved fund by a bank to equalize its dividends, etc.; in the Bank of England, the balance of assets above liabilities.

Rest.syn: Remainder; overplus; surplus; remnant; residue; reserve; others.
