Rest.etym: [F. reste, fr. rester to remain, L. restare to stay back, remain; pref. re- re- + stare to stand, stay. See Stand, and cf. Arrest, Restive.]

senses.d: To be left; to remain; to continue to be.
q: The affairs of men rest still uncertain.

senses.d: The act of restoring anything to its rightful owner, or of making good, or of giving an equivalent for any loss, damage, or injury; indemnification.
q: A restitution of ancient rights unto the crown.
He restitution to the value makes.

senses.d: That which is offered or given in return for what has been lost, injured, or destroyed; compensation.
The act of returning to, or recovering, a former state; as, the restitution of an elastic body.

The movement of rotation which usually occurs in childbirth after the head has been delivered, and which causes the latter to point towards the side to which it was directed at the beginning of labor.

Restitution.syn: Restoration; return; indemnification; reparation; compensation; amends; remuneration.
Restitution.etym: [F. restitution, L. restitutio. See Restitute, v.]

senses.d: To bring back to its former state; to bring back from a state of ruin, decay, disease, or the like; to repair; to renew; to recover.
q: Our fortune restored after the severest afflictions.
And his hand was restored whole as the other.

senses.d: To give or bring back, as that which has been lost., or taken away; to bring back to the owner; to replace.
q: Now therefore restore the man his wife.
Loss of Eden, till one greater man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat.
The father banished virtue shall restore.

senses.d: To renew; to reëstablish; as, to restore harmony among those who are variance.
To give in place of, or as satisfaction for.
q: He shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.

senses.d: To make good; to make amends for.
q: But if the while I think on thee, dear friend, All losses are restored, and sorrows end.

senses.d: To bring back from a state of injury or decay, or from a changed condition; as, to restore a painting, statue, etc.

Restore.syn: To return; replace; refund; repay; reinstate; rebuild; reëstablish; renew; repair; revive; recover; heal; cure.
Restore.etym: [OE. restoren, OF. restorer, F. restaurer, fr. L. restaurare; pref. re- re- + an unused word; cf. Gr. σταυρόσ an upright pale or stake, Skr. sthāvara fixed, firm. Cf. Restaurant, Store.]

senses.d: Restoration.
One who, or that which, restores.
To draw back again; to hold back from acting, proceeding, or advancing, either by physical or moral force, or by any interposing obstacle; to repress or suppress; to keep down; to curb.
q: Restrain in me the cursed thoughts that nature Gives way to in repose!

senses.d: To draw back toghtly, as a rein.
To hinder from unlimited enjoiment; to abridge.
q: Though they two were committed, at least restrained of their liberty.

senses.d: To limit; to confine; to restrict.
q: Not only a metaphysical or natural, but a moral, universality also is to be restrained by a part of the predicate.

senses.d: To withhold; to forbear.
q: Thou restrained prayer before God.

Restrain.syn: To check; hinder; stop; withhold; repress; curb; suppress; coerce; restrict; limit; confine.
Restrain.etym: [OE. restreinen, F. restreindre, fr. L. restringere, restrictum; pref. re- re- + stringere to draw, bind, or press together. See Strain, v. t., and cf. Restrict.]

senses.d: The act or process of restraining, or of holding back or hindering from motion or action, in any manner; hindrance of the will, or of any action, physical or mental.
q: No man was altogether above the restrains of law, and no man altogether below its protection.

senses.d: The state of being restrained.
That which restrains, as a law, a prohibition, or the like; limitation; restriction.
q: For one restraint, lords of the world besides.

Restraint.syn: Repression; hindrance; check; stop; curb;�oercion; confinement; limitation; restriction.
Restraint.etym: [OF. restraincte, fr. restrainct, F. restreint, p. p. of restraindre, restrendre. See Restrain.]

senses.d: A rising again; the resumption of vigor.
Especially, the rising again from the dead; the resumption of life by the dead; as, the resurrection of Jesus Christ; the general resurrection of all the dead at the Day of Judgment.
q: Nor after resurrection shall he stay Longer on earth.

senses.d: State of being risen from the dead; future state.
q: In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage.

senses.d: The cause or exemplar of a rising from the dead.
q: I am the resurrection, and the life.

Resurrection.etym: [F. résurrection, L. resurrectio, fr. resurgere, resurrectum, to rise again; pref. re- re- + surgere to rise. See Source.]

senses.d: To continue to hold; to keep in possession; not to lose, part with, or dismiss; to restrain from departure, escape, or the like.
q: Be obedient, and retain Unalterably firm his love entire.
An executor may retain a debt due to him from the testator.

senses.d: To keep in pay; to employ by a preliminary fee paid; to hire; to engage; as, to retain a counselor.
q: A Benedictine convent has now retained the most learned father of their order to write in its defense.

senses.d: To restrain; to prevent.

Retain.syn: To keep; hold; restrain. See Keep.
Retain.etym: [F. retainir, L. retinere; pref. re- re- + tenere to hold, keep. See Tenable, and cf. Rein of a bridle, Retention, Retinue.]

senses.d: To belong; to pertain.
q: A somewhat languid relish, retaining to bitterness.

senses.d: To keep; to continue; to remain.
To withdraw; to take away; — sometimes used reflexively.
q: He . . . retired himself, his wife, and children into a forest.
As when the sun is present all the year, And never doth retire his golden ray.

senses.d: To withdraw from circulation, or from the market; to take up and pay; as, to retire bonds; to retire a note.
To cause to retire; specifically, to designate as no longer qualified for active service; to place on the retired list; as, to retire a military or naval officer.

Retire.etym: [F. retirer; pref. re- re- + tirer to draw. See Tirade.]

senses.d: To go back or return; to draw back or away; to keep aloof; to withdraw or retreat, as from observation; to go into privacy; as, to retire to his home; to retire from the world, or from notice.
q: To Una back he cast him to retire.
The mind contracts herself, and shrinketh in, And to herself she gladly doth retire.

senses.d: To retreat from action or danger; to withdraw for safety or pleasure; as, to retire from battle.
q: Set Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.

senses.d: To withdraw from a public station, or from business; as, having made a large fortune, he retired.
q: And from Britannia's public posts retire.

senses.d: To recede; to fall or bend back; as, the shore of the sea retires in bays and gulfs.
To go to bed; as, he usually retires early.

Retire.syn: To withdraw; leave; depart; secede; recede; retreat; retrocede.

senses.d: The act of retiring, or the state of being retired; also, a place to which one retires.
q: The battle and the retire of the English succors.
discover'd soon the place of her retire.

senses.d: A call sounded on a bugle, announcing to skirmishers that they are to retire, or fall back.
Private; secluded; quiet; as, a retired life; a person of retired habits.
q: A retired part of the peninsula.

senses.d: Withdrawn from active duty or business; as, a retired officer; a retired physician.
To turn back; to go or come again to the same place or condition.
q: On their embattled ranks the waves return.
If they returned out of bondage, it must be into a state of freedom.
Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.

senses.d: To come back, or begin again, after an interval, regular or irregular; to appear again.
q: With the year Seasons return; but not me returns Day or the sweet approach of even or morn.

senses.d: To speak in answer; to reply; to respond.
q: He said, and thus the queen of heaven returned.

senses.d: To revert; to pass back into possession.
q: And Jeroboam said in his heart, Now shall the kingdom return to the house of David.

senses.d: To go back in thought, narration, or argument.

Return.etym: [OE. returnen, retournen, F. retourner; pref. re- re- + tourner to turn. See Turn.]

senses.d: To bring, carry, send, or turn, back; as, to return a borrowed book, or a hired horse.
q: Both fled attonce, ne ever back returned eye.

senses.d: To repay; as, to return borrowed money.
To give in requital or recompense; to requite.
q: The Lord shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head.

senses.d: To give back in reply; as, to return an answer; to return thanks.
To retort; to throw back; as, to return the lie.
q: If you are a malicious reader, you return upon me, that I affect to be thought more impartial than I am.

senses.d: To report, or bring back and make known.
q: And all the people answered together, . . . and Moses returned the words of the people unto the Lord.

senses.d: To render, as an account, usually an official account, to a superior; to report officially by a list or statement; as, to return a list of stores, of killed or wounded; to return the result of an election.
Hence, to elect according to the official report of the election officers.
To bring or send back to a tribunal, or to an office, with a certificate of what has been done; as, to return a writ.
To convey into official custody, or to a general depository.
q: Instead of a ship, he should levy money, and return the same to the treasurer for his majesty's use.

senses.d: To bat (the ball) back over the net.
To lead in response to the lead of one's partner; as, to return a trump; to return a diamond for a club.

Return.syn: To restore; requite; repay; recompense; render; remit; report.

senses.d: The act of returning (intransitive), or coming back to the same place or condition; as, the return of one long absent; the return of health; the return of the seasons, or of an anniversary.
q: At the return of the year the king of Syria will come up against thee.
His personal return was most required and necessary.

senses.d: The act of returning (transitive), or sending back to the same place or condition; restitution; repayment; requital; retribution; as, the return of anything borrowed, as a book or money; a good return in tennis.
q: You made my liberty your late request: Is no return due from a grateful breast?

senses.d: That which is returned.
q: I do expect return Of thrice three times the value of this bond.

senses.d: An answer; as, a return to one's question.

An account, or formal report, of an action performed, of a duty discharged, of facts or statistics, and the like; as, election returns; a return of the amount of goods produced or sold; especially, in the plural, a set of tabulated statistics prepared for general information.
The profit on, or advantage received from, labor, or an investment, undertaking, adventure, etc.
q: The fruit from many days of recreation is very little; but from these few hours we spend in prayer, the return is great.

senses.d: The continuation in a different direction, most often at a right angle, of a building, face of a building, or any member, as a molding or mold; — applied to the shorter in contradistinction to the longer; thus, a facade of sixty feet east and west has a return of twenty feet north and south.
The rendering back or delivery of writ, precept, or execution, to the proper officer or court.

An official account, report, or statement, rendered to the commander or other superior officer; as, the return of men fit for duty; the return of the number of the sick; the return of provisions, etc.
The turnings and windings of a trench or mine.
To make known (that which has been concealed or kept secret); to unveil; to disclose; to show.
q: Light was the wound, the prince's care unknown, She might not, would not, yet reveal her own.

senses.d: Specifically, to communicate (that which could not be known or discovered without divine or supernatural instruction or agency).

Reveal.syn: To communicate; disclose; divulge; unveil; uncover; open; discover; impart; show.
Reveal.etym: [F. révéler, L. revelare, revelatum, to unveil, reveal; pref. re- re- + velare to veil; fr. velum a veil. See Veil.]

senses.d: A revealing; a disclosure.

The side of an opening for a window, doorway, or the like, between the door frame or window frame and the outer surface of the wall; or, where the opening is not filled with a door, etc., the whole thickness of the wall; the jamb.
One who, or that which, reveals.
The act of revealing, disclosing, or discovering to others what was before unknown to them.
That which is revealed.
The act of revealing divine truth.
q: By revelation he made known unto me the mystery, as I wrote afore in few words.

senses.d: Specifically, the last book of the sacred canon, containing the prophecies of St. John; the Apocalypse.

To inflict harm in return for, as an injury, insult, etc.; to exact satisfaction for, under a sense of injury; to avenge; — followed either by the wrong received, or by the person or thing wronged, as the object, or by the reciprocal pronoun as direct object, and a preposition before the wrong done or the wrongdoer.
q: To revenge the death of our fathers.
The gods are just, and will revenge our cause.
Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come, Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius.

senses.d: To inflict injury for, in a spiteful, wrong, or malignant spirit; to wreak vengeance for maliciously.

Revenge.etym: [OF. revengier, F. revancher; pref. re- re- + OF. vengier to avenge, revenge, F. venger, L. vindicare. See Vindicate, Vengerance, and cf. Revindicate.]

senses.d: To take vengeance; — with
The act of revenging; vengeance; retaliation; a returning of evil for evil.
q: Certainly, in taking revenge, a man is even with his enemy; but in passing it over he is superior.

senses.d: The disposition to revenge; a malignant wishing of evil to one who has done us an injury.
q: Revenge now goes To lay a complot to betray thy foes.
The indulgence of revenge tends to make men more savage and cruel.

senses.d: One who revenges.
Executing revenge; revengeful.
That which returns, or comes back, from an investment; the annual rents, profits, interest, or issues of any species of property, real or personal; income.
q: Do not anticipate your revenues and live upon air till you know what you are worth.

senses.d: Hence, return; reward; as, a revenue of praise.
The annual yield of taxes, excise, customs, duties, rents, etc., which a nation, state, or municipality collects and receives into the treasury for public use.

Revenue.etym: [F. revenu, OF. revenue, fr. revenir to return, L. revenire; pref. re- re- + venire to come. See Come.]

senses.d: Profound respect and esteem mingled with fear and affection, as for a holy being or place; the disposition to revere; veneration.
q: If thou be poor, farewell thy reverence.
Reverence, which is the synthesis of love and fear.
When discords, and quarrels, and factions, are carried openly and audaciously, it is a sign the reverence of government islost.

senses.d: The act of revering; a token of respect or veneration; an obeisance.
q: Make twenty reverences upon receiving . . . about twopence.
And each of them doeth all his diligence To do unto the feast reverence.

senses.d: That which deserves or exacts manifestations of reverence; reverend character; dignity; state.
q: I am forced to lay my reverence by.

senses.d: A person entitled to be revered; — a title applied to priests or other ministers with the pronouns his or your; sometimes poetically to a father.
To regard or treat with reverence; to regard with respect and affection mingled with fear; to venerate.
q: Let . . . the wife see that she reverence her husband.
Those that I reverence those I fear, the wise.

senses.d: Worthy of reverence; entitled to respect mingled with fear and affection; venerable.
q: A reverend sire among them came.
They must give good example and reverend deportment in the face of their children.

Reverend.etym: [F. révérend, L. reverendus, fr. revereri. See Revere.]

senses.d: Turned backward; having a contrary or opposite direction; hence; opposite or contrary in kind; as, the reverse order or method.
Turned upside down; greatly disturbed.
q: He found the sea diverse With many a windy storm reverse.

senses.d: Reversed; as, a reverse shell.

Reverse.etym: [OE. revers, OF. revers, L. reversus, p. p. of revertere. See Revert.]

senses.d: That which appears or is presented when anything, as a lance, a line, a course of conduct, etc., is reverted or turned contrary to its natural direction.
q: He did so with the reverse of the lance.

senses.d: That which is directly opposite or contrary to something else; a contrary; an opposite.
q: And then mistook reverse of wrong for right.
To make everything the reverse of what they have seen, is quite as easy as to destroy.

senses.d: The act of reversing; complete change; reversal; hence, total change in circumstances or character; especially, a change from better to worse; misfortune; a check or defeat; as, the enemy met with a reverse.
q: The strange reverse of fate you see; I pitied you, now you may pity me.
By a reverse of fortune, Stephen becomes rich.

senses.d: The back side; as, the reverse of a drum or trench; the reverse of a medal or coin, that is, the side opposite to the obverse. See Obverse.
A thrust in fencing made with a backward turn of the hand; a backhanded stroke.
A turn or fold made in bandaging, by which the direction of the bandage is changed.
To turn back; to cause to face in a contrary direction; to cause to depart.
q: And that old dame said many an idle verse, Out of her daughter's heart fond fancies to reverse.

senses.d: To cause to return; to recall.
q: And to his fresh remembrance did reverse The ugly view of his deformed crimes.

senses.d: To change totally; to alter to the opposite.
q: Reverse the doom of death.
She reversed the conduct of the celebrated vicar of Bray.

senses.d: To turn upside down; to invert.
q: A pyramid reversed may stand upon his point if balanced by admirable skill.

senses.d: Hence, to overthrow; to subvert.
q: These can divide, and these reverse, the state.
Custom . . . reverses even the distinctions of good and evil.

senses.d: To overthrow by a contrary decision; to make void; to under or annual for error; as, to reverse a judgment, sentence, or decree.

Reverse.syn: To overturn; overset; invert; overthrow; subvert; repeal; annul; revoke; undo.

senses.d: To return; to revert.
To become or be reversed.
To address or abuse with opprobrious and contemptuous language; to reproach.
q: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again.

Revile.etym: [Pref. re- + OF. aviler to make vile, depreciate, F. avilir; à (L. ad.) + vil vile. See Vile.]

senses.d: Reproach; reviling.
q: The gracious Judge, without revile, replied.

senses.d: One who reviles.
Reproach; abuse; vilification.
q: Neither be ye afraid of their revilings.

senses.d: Uttering reproaches; containing reproaches.
To return to life; to recover life or strength; to live anew; to become reanimated or reinvigorated.
q: The Lord heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into again, and he revived.

senses.d: Hence, to recover from a state of oblivion, obscurity, neglect, or depression; as, classical learning revived in the fifteenth century.
To recover its natural or metallic state, as a metal.

Revive.etym: [F. revivere, L. revivere; pref. re- re- + vivere to live. See Vivid.]

senses.d: To restore, or bring again to life; to reanimate.
q: Those bodies, by reason of whose mortality we died, shall be revived.

senses.d: To raise from coma, languor, depression, or discouragement; to bring into action after a suspension.
q: Those gracious words revive my drooping thoughts.
Your coming, friends, revives me.

senses.d: Hence, to recover from a state of neglect or disuse; as, to revive letters or learning.
To renew in the mind or memory; to bring to recollection; to recall attention to; to reawaken.
q: The mind has a power in many cases to revive perceptions which it has once had.

senses.d: To restore or reduce to its natural or metallic state; as, to revive a metal after calcination.

Revive.etym: [Cf. F. reviver. See Revive, v. i.]

senses.d: Returning or restoring to life or vigor; reanimating.
To turn away; to abandon or reject something; specifically, to turn away, or shrink, with abhorrence.
q: But this got by casting pearl to hogs, That bawl for freedom in their senseless mood, And still revolt when trith would set them free.
HIs clear intelligence revolted from the dominant sophisms of that time.

senses.d: Hence, to be faithless; to desert one party or leader for another; especially, to renounce allegiance or subjection; to rise against a government; to rebel.
q: Our discontented counties do revolt.
Plant those that have revolted in the van.

senses.d: To be disgusted, shocked, or grossly offended; hence, to feel nausea; — with at; as, the stomach revolts at such food; his nature revolts at cruelty.

Revolt.etym: [Cf. F. révoller, It. rivoltare. See Revolt, n.]

senses.d: To cause to turn back; to roll or drive back; to put to flight.
To do violence to; to cause to turn away or shrink with abhorrence; to shock; as, to revolt the feelings.
q: This abominable medley is made rather to revolt young and ingenuous minds.
To derive delight from what inflicts pain on any sentient creatuure revolted his conscience and offended his reason.

senses.d: The act of revolting; an uprising against legitimate authority; especially, a renunciation of allegiance and subjection to a government; rebellion; as, the revolt of a province of the Roman empire.
q: Who first seduced them to that foul revolt?

senses.d: A revolter.

Revolt.syn: Insurrection; sedition; rebellion; mutiny. See Insurrection.
Revolt.etym: [F. révolte, It. rivolta, fr. rivolto, p. p. fr. L. revolvere, revolutum. See Revolve.]

senses.d: One who revolts.
Causing abhorrence mixed with disgust; exciting extreme repugnance; loathsome; as, revolting cruelty.
To give in return, whether good or evil; — commonly in a good sense; to requite; to recompense; to repay; to compensate.
q: After the deed that is done, one doom shall reward, Mercy or no mercy as truth will accord.
Thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil.
I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me.
God rewards those that have made use of the single talent.

Reward.etym: [OF. rewarder, another form of regarder, of German origin. The original sense is, to look at, regard, hence, to regard as worthy, give a reward to. See Ward, Regard.]

senses.d: Regard; respect; consideration.
q: Take reward of thine own value.

senses.d: That which is given in return for good or evil done or received; esp., that which is offered or given in return for some service or attainment, as for excellence in studies, for the return of something lost, etc.; recompense; requital.
q: Thou returnest From flight, seditious angel, to receive Thy merited reward.
Rewards and punishments do always presuppose something willingly done well or ill.

senses.d: Hence, the fruit of one's labor or works.
q: The dead know not anything, neither have they any more a reward.

senses.d: Compensation or remuneration for services; a sum of money paid or taken for doing, or forbearing to do, some act.

Reward.syn: Recompense; compensation; remuneration; pay; requital; retribution; punishment.
Reward.etym: [See Reward, v., and cf. Regard, n.]

senses.d: One who rewards.
One of the curved bones attached to the vertebral column and supporting the lateral walls of the thorax.
That which resembles a rib in form or use.
The chief nerve, or one of the chief nerves, of a leaf.

In Gothic vaulting, one of the primary members of the vault. These are strong arches, meeting and crossing one another, dividing the whole space into triangles, which are then filled by vaulted construction of lighter material. Hence, an imitation of one of these in wood, plaster, or the like.
Solid coal on the side of a gallery; solid ore in a vein.
A wife; — in allusion to Eve, as made out of Adam's rib.
q: How many have we known whose heads have been broken with their own rib.

Rib.etym: [AS. rib, ribb; akin to D. rib, G. rippe, OHG. rippa, rippi, Dan. ribbe, Icel. rif, Russ. rebro.]

senses.d: To furnish with ribs; to form with rising lines and channels; as, to rib cloth.
To inclose, as with ribs, and protect; to shut in.
q: It were too gross To rib her cerecloth in the obscure grave.

senses.d: A ribbon.
A long, narrow strip of timber bent and bolted longitudinally to the ribs of a vessel, to hold them in position, and give rigidity to the framework.
Having an abundance of material possessions; possessed of a large amount of property; well supplied with land, goods, or money; wealthy; opulent; affluent; — opposed to poor.
q: The rich hath many friends.
As a thief, bent to unhoard the cash Of some rich burgher.

senses.d: Hence, in general, well supplied; abounding; abundant; copious; bountiful; as, a rich treasury; a rich entertainment; a rich crop.
q: If life be short, it shall be glorious; Each minute shall be rich in some great action.
The gorgeous East with richest hand Showers on her kings barbaric pearl and gold.

senses.d: Yielding large returns; productive or fertile; fruitful; as, rich soil or land; a rich mine.
Composed of valuable or costly materials or ingredients; procured at great outlay; highly valued; precious; sumptuous; costly; as, a rich dress; rich silk or fur; rich presents.
q: Like to rich and various gems.

senses.d: Abounding in agreeable or nutritive qualities; — especially applied to articles of food or drink which are high-seasoned or abound in oleaginous ingredients, or are sweet, luscious, and high-flavored; as, a rich dish; rich cream or soup; rich pastry; rich wine or fruit.
q: Sauces and rich spices are fetched from India.

senses.d: Not faint or delicate; vivid; as, a rich color.
Full of sweet and harmonius sounds; as, a rich voice; rich music.
Abounding in beauty; gorgeous; as, a rich landscape; rich scenery.
Abounding in humor; exciting amusement; entertaining; as, the scene was a rich one; a rich incident or character.

Rich.syn: Wealthy; affluent; opulent; ample; copious; abundant; plentiful; fruitful; costly; sumptuous; precious; generous; luscious.
Rich.etym: [OE. riche, AS. rīce rich, powerful; akin to OS. rīki, D. rijk, G. reich, OHG. rīhhi, Icel. rīkr, Sw. rik, Dan. rig, Goth. reiks; from a word meaning, ruler, king, probably borrowed from Celtic, and akin to L. rex, regis, king, regere to guide, rule. √283. See Right, and cf. Derrick, Enrich, Rajah,

senses.d: To enrich.
That which makes one rich; an abundance of land, goods, money, or other property; wealth; opulence; affluence.
q: Riches do not consist in having more gold and silver, but in having more in proportion, than our neighbors.

senses.d: That which appears rich, sumptuous, precious, or the like.
q: The riche of heaven's pavement, trodden gold.
Against the richesses of this world shall they have misease of poverty.
In one hour so great riches is come to nought.
And for that riches where is my deserving?

Riches.syn: Wealth; opulence; affluence; wealthiness; richness; plenty; abundance.
Riches.etym: [OE. richesse, F. richesse, from riche rich, of German origin. See Rich,a.]

senses.d: In a rich manner.
To save; to rescue; to deliver; — with out of.
q: Deliver the poor and needy; rid them out of the hand of the wicked.

senses.d: To free; to clear; to disencumber; — followed by of.
q: In never ridded myself of an overmastering and brooding sense of some great calamity traveling toward me.

senses.d: To drive away; to remove by effort or violence; to make away with; to destroy.
q: I will red evil beasts out of the land.
Death's men, you have rid this sweet young prince!

senses.d: To get over; to dispose of; to dispatch; to finish.
q: Mirth will make us rid ground faster than if thieves were at our tails.

Rid.etym: [OE. ridden, redden, AS. hreddan to deliver, liberate; akin to D. & LG. redden, G. retten, Dan. redde, Sw. rädda, and perhaps to Skr. �rath to loosen.]

senses.d: The act of ridding or freeing; deliverance; a cleaning up or out.
q: Thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field.

senses.d: The state of being rid or free; freedom; escape.
A sieve with coarse meshes, usually of wire, for separating coarser materials from finer, as chaff from grain, cinders from ashes, or gravel from sand.
A board having a row of pins, set zigzag, between which wire is drawn to straighten it.

Riddle.etym: [OE. ridil, AS. hridder; akin to G. reiter, L. cribrum, and to Gr. ��� to distinguish, separate, and G. rein clean. See Crisis, Certain.]

senses.d: To separate, as grain from the chaff, with a riddle; to pass through a riddle; as, riddle wheat; to riddle coal or gravel.
To perforate so as to make like a riddle; to make many holes in; as, a house riddled with shot.
Something proposed to be solved by guessing or conjecture; a puzzling question; an ambiguous proposition; an enigma; hence, anything ambiguous or puzzling.
q: To wring from me, and tell to them, my secret, That solved the riddle which I had proposed.
'T was a strange riddle of a lady.

Riddle.etym: [For riddels, s being misunderstood as the plural ending; OE. ridels, redels. AS. rǣdels; akin to D. raadsel, G. räthsel; fr. AS. rǣdan to counsel or advise, also, to guess. √116. Cf. Read.]

senses.d: To explain; to solve; to unriddle.
q: Riddle me this, and guess him if you can.

senses.d: To speak ambiguously or enigmatically.
To be carried on the back of an animal, as a horse.
q: To-morrow, when ye riden by the way.
Let your master ride on before, and do you gallop after him.

senses.d: To be borne in a carriage; as, to ride in a coach, in a car, and the like. See Synonym, below.
q: The richest inhabitants exhibited their wealth, not by riding in gilden carriages, but by walking the streets with trains of servants.

senses.d: To be borne or in a fluid; to float; to lie.
q: Men once walked where ships at anchor ride.

senses.d: To be supported in motion; to rest.
q: Strong as the exletree On which heaven rides.
On whose foolish honesty My practices ride easy!

senses.d: To manage a horse, as an equestrian.
q: He rode, he fenced, he moved with graceful ease.

senses.d: To support a rider, as a horse; to move under the saddle; as, a horse rides easy or hard, slow or fast.
q: “Will you ride over or drive?” said Lord Willowby to his quest, after breakfast that morning.

Ride.etym: [AS. rīdan; akin to LG. riden, D. rijden, G. reiten, OHG. rītan, Icel. rīða, Sw. rida, Dan. ride; cf. L. raeda a carriage, which is from a Celtic word. Cf. Road.]

senses.d: To sit on, so as to be carried; as, to ride a horse; to ride a bicycle.
q: rend up both rocks and hills, and ride the air In whirlwind.

senses.d: To manage insolently at will; to domineer over.
q: The nobility could no longer endure to be ridden by bakers, cobblers, and brewers.

senses.d: To convey, as by riding; to make or do by riding.
q: Tue only men that safe can ride Mine errands on the Scottish side.

senses.d: To overlap (each other); — said of bones or fractured fragments.
The act of riding; an excursion on horseback or in a vehicle.
A saddle horse.
A road or avenue cut in a wood, or through grounds, to be used as a place for riding; a riding.
One who, or that which, rides.
Formerly, an agent who went out with samples of goods to obtain orders; a commercial traveler.
One who breaks or manages a horse.

An addition or amendment to a manuscript or other document, which is attached on a separate piece of paper; in legislative practice, an additional clause annexed to a bill while in course of passage; something extra or burdensome that is imposed.
q: After the third reading, a foolish man stood up to propose a rider.
This was a rider which Mab found difficult to answer.

senses.d: A problem of more than usual difficulty added to another on an examination paper.
A Dutch gold coin having the figure of a man on horseback stamped upon it.
q: His moldy money ! half a dozen riders.

senses.d: Rock material in a vein of ore, dividing it.
An interior rib occasionally fixed in a ship's hold, reaching from the keelson to the beams of the lower deck, to strengthen her frame.
The second tier of casks in a vessel's hold.
A small forked weight which straddles the beam of a balance, along which it can be moved in the manner of the weight on a steelyard.
A robber.
The back, or top of the back; a crest.
A range of hills or mountains, or the upper part of such a range; any extended elevation between valleys.
q: Part rise crystal wall, or ridge direct.

senses.d: A raised line or strip, as of ground thrown up by a plow or left between furrows or ditches, or as on the surface of metal, cloth, or bone, etc.
The intersection of two surface forming a salient angle, especially the angle at the top between the opposite slopes or sides of a roof or a vault.
The highest portion of the glacis proceeding from the salient angle of the covered way.

Ridge.etym: [OE. rigge the back, AS. hrycg; akin to D. rug, G. rÜcken, OHG. rucki, hrukki, Icel. hryggr, Sw. rugg, Dan. ryg. √16.]

senses.d: To form a ridge of; to furnish with a ridge or ridges; to make into a ridge or ridges.
q: Bristles ranged like those that ridge the back Of chafed wild boars.

senses.d: To form into ridges with the plow, as land.
To wrinkle.
One of the three jurisdictions into which the county of York, in England, is divided; — formerly under the government of a reeve. They are called the North, the East, and the West, Riding.

Riding.etym: [For thriding, Icel. þriðjungr the third part, fr. þriði third, akin to E. third. See Third.]

senses.d: Employed to travel; traveling; as, a riding clerk.
Used for riding on; as, a riding horse.
Used for riding, or when riding; devoted to riding; as, a riding whip; a riding habit; a riding day.
The act or state of one who rides.
A festival procession.
q: When there any riding was in Cheap.

senses.d: Same as Ride, n., 3.
A district in charge of an excise officer.
To seize and bear away by force; to snatch away; to carry off.
q: Till time shall rifle every youthful grace.

senses.d: To strip; to rob; to pillage.
q: Stand, sir, and throw us that you have about ye: If not, we'll make you sit and rifle you.

senses.d: To raffle.

Rifle.etym: [F. rifler to rifle, sweep away; of uncertain origin. CF. Raff.]

senses.d: To raffle.
To commit robbery.
A gun, the inside of whose barrel is grooved with spiral channels, thus giving the ball a rotary motion and insuring greater accuracy of fire. As a military firearm it has superseded the musket.
A body of soldiers armed with rifles.
A strip of wood covered with emery or a similar material, used for sharpening scythes.

Rifle.etym: [Akin to Dan. rifle, or riffel, the rifle of a gun, a chamfer (cf. riffel, riffelbösse, a rifle gun, rifle to rifle a gun, G. riefeln, riefen, to chamfer, groove), and E. rive. See Rive, and cf. Riffle, Rivel.]

senses.d: To grove; to channel; especially, to groove internally with spiral channels; as, to rifle a gun barrel or a cannon.
To whet with a rifle. See Rifle, n., 3.
Straight; direct; not crooked; as, a right line.
Upright; erect from a base; having an upright axis; not oblique; as, right ascension; a right pyramid or cone.
Conformed to the constitution of man and the will of God, or to justice and equity; not deviating from the true and just; according with truth and duty; just; true.
q: That which is conformable to the Supreme Rule is absolutely right, and is called right simply without relation to a special end.

senses.d: Fit; suitable; proper; correct; becoming; as, the right man in the right place; the right way from London to Oxford.
Characterized by reality or genuineness; real; actual; not spurious.
q: In this battle, . . . the Britons never more plainly manifested themselves to be right barbarians.

senses.d: According with truth; passing a true judgment; conforming to fact or intent; not mistaken or wrong; not erroneous; correct; as, this is the right faith.
q: You are right, Justice, and you weigh this well.
If there be no prospect beyond the grave, the inference is . . . right, “Let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we die.”

senses.d: Most favorable or convenient; fortunate.
q: The lady has been disappointed on the right side.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to that side of the body in man on which the muscular action is usually stronger than on the other side; — opposed to left when used in reference to a part of the body; as, the right side, hand, arm. Also applied to the corresponding side of the lower animals.
q: Became the sovereign's favorite, his right hand.

senses.d: Well placed, disposed, or adjusted; orderly; well regulated; correctly done.
Designed to be placed or worn outward; as, the right side of a piece of cloth.
q: “Right,” cries his lordship.

Right.syn: Straight; direct; perpendicular; upright; lawful; rightful; true; correct; just; equitable; proper; suitable; becoming.
Right.etym: [OE. right, riht, AS. riht; akin to D. regt, OS. & OHG. reht, G. recht, Dan. ret, Sw. rätt, Icel. rëttr, Goth. raíhts, L. rectus, p. p. of regere to guide, rule; cf. Skr. ṛju straight, right. √115. Cf. Adroit,Alert, Correct, Dress, Regular, Rector, Recto, Rectum, Regent, Region, Realm, Rich, Royal,

senses.d: In a right manner.
In a right or straight line; directly; hence; straightway; immediately; next; as, he stood right before me; it went right to the mark; he came right out; he followed right after the guide.
q: Unto Dian's temple goeth she right.
Let thine eyes look right on.
Right across its track there lay, Down in the water, a long reef of gold.

senses.d: Exactly; just.
q: Came he right now to sing a raven's note?

senses.d: According to the law or will of God; conforming to the standard of truth and justice; righteously; as, to live right; to judge right.
According to any rule of art; correctly.
q: You with strict discipline instructed right.

senses.d: According to fact or truth; actually; truly; really; correctly; exactly; as, to tell a story right.
q: Right as it were a steed of Lumbardye.
His wounds so smarted that he slept right naught.

senses.d: In a great degree; very; wholly; unqualifiedly; extremely; highly; as, right humble; right noble; right valiant.
q: For which I should be right sorry.
return those duties back as are right fit.

senses.d: That which is right or correct.
q: Seldom your opinions err; Your eyes are always in the right.

senses.d: A just judgment or action; that which is true or proper; justice; uprightness; integrity.
q: Long love to her has borne the faithful knight, And well deserved, had fortune done him right.

senses.d: That to which one has a just claim.
q: There are no rights whatever, without corresponding duties.

senses.d: That which one has a legal or social claim to do or to exact; legal power; authority; as, a sheriff has a right to arrest a criminal.
That which justly belongs to one; that which one has a claim to possess or own; the interest or share which anyone has in a piece of property; title; claim; interest; ownership.
q: Born free, he sought his right.
Hast thou not right to all created things?
Men have no right to what is not reasonable.

senses.d: Privilege or immunity granted by authority.
The right side; the side opposite to the left.
q: Led her to the Souldan's right.

senses.d: In some legislative bodies of Europe (as in France), those members collectively who are conservatives or monarchists. See Center, 5.
The outward or most finished surface, as of a piece of cloth, a carpet, etc.
To bring or restore to the proper or natural position; to set upright; to make right or straight (that which has been wrong or crooked); to correct.
To do justice to; to relieve from wrong; to restore rights to; to assert or regain the rights of; as, to right the oppressed; to right one's self; also, to vindicate.
q: So just is God, to right the innocent.
All experience hath shown that mankind are more disposed to suffer while evils are sufferable, than to right themselves by abolishing the forms to which they are accustomed.

senses.d: To recover the proper or natural condition or position; to become upright.
Hence, to regain an upright position, as a ship or boat, after careening.
Doing, or according with, that which is right; yielding to all their due; just; equitable; especially, free from wrong, guilt, or sin; holy; as, a righteous man or act; a righteous retribution.
q: Fearless in his righteous cause.

Righteous.syn: Upright; just; godly; holy; uncorrupt; virtuous; honest; equitable; rightful.
Righteous.etym: [OE. rightways, rightwise, AS. rightwīs; riht right + wīs wise, having wisdom, prudent. See Right, a., Wise, a.]

senses.d: In a righteous manner; as, to judge righteously.
The quality or state of being righteous; holiness; purity; uprightness; rectitude.
A righteous act, or righteous quality.
q: All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.

senses.d: The act or conduct of one who is righteous.
q: Blessed are they that keep judgment, and he that doeth righteousness at all times.

senses.d: The state of being right with God; justification; the work of Christ, which is the ground of justification.
q: There are two kinds of Christian righteousness: the one without us, which we have by imputation; the other in us, which consisteth of faith, hope, and charity, and other Christian virtues.
Only for the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, and received by faith alone.

Righteousness.syn: Uprightness; holiness; godliness; equity; justice; rightfulness; integrity; honesty; faithfulness.

senses.d: Straightly; directly; in front.
According to justice; according to the divine will or moral rectitude; uprightly; as, duty rightly performed.
Properly; fitly; suitably; appropriately.
q: Eve rightly called, Mother of all mankind.

senses.d: According to truth or fact; correctly; not erroneously; exactly.
q: Thou didst not rightly see.

senses.d: To cause to sound, especially by striking, as a metallic body; as, to ring a bell.
To make (a sound), as by ringing a bell; to sound.
q: The shard-borne beetle, with his drowsy hums, Hath rung night's yawning peal.

senses.d: To repeat often, loudly, or earnestly.

Ring.etym: [AS. hringan; akin to Icel. hringja, Sw. ringa, Dan. ringe, OD. ringhen, ringkelen. √19.]

senses.d: To sound, as a bell or other sonorous body, particularly a metallic one.
q: Now ringen trompes loud and clarion.
Why ring not out the bells?

senses.d: To practice making music with bells.
To sound loud; to resound; to be filled with a ringing or reverberating sound.
q: With sweeter notes each rising temple rung.
The hall with harp and carol rang.
My ears still ring with noise.

senses.d: To continue to sound or vibrate; to resound.
q: The assertion is still ringing in our ears.

senses.d: To be filled with report or talk; as, the whole town rings with his fame.
A sound; especially, the sound of vibrating metals; as, the ring of a bell.
Any loud sound; the sound of numerous voices; a sound continued, repeated, or reverberated.
q: The ring of acclamations fresh in his ears.

senses.d: A chime, or set of bells harmonically tuned.
q: As great and tunable a ring of bells as any in the world.

senses.d: A circle, or a circular line, or anything in the form of a circular line or hoop.
Specifically, a circular ornament of gold or other precious material worn on the finger, or attached to the ear, the nose, or some other part of the person; as, a wedding ring.
q: Upon his thumb he had of gold a ring.
The dearest ring in Venice will I give you.

senses.d: A circular area in which races are or run or other sports are performed; an arena.
q: Place me, O, place me in the dusty ring, Where youthful charioteers contend for glory.

senses.d: An inclosed space in which pugilists fight; hence, figuratively, prize fighting.
A circular group of persons.
q: And hears the Muses in a ring Aye round about Jove's alter sing.

senses.d: The plane figure included between the circumferences of two concentric circles.

An instrument, formerly used for taking the sun's altitude, consisting of a brass ring suspended by a swivel, with a hole at one side through which a solar ray entering indicated the altitude on the graduated inner surface opposite.
An elastic band partly or wholly encircling the spore cases of ferns. See Illust. of Sporangium.
A clique; an exclusive combination of persons for a selfish purpose, as to control the market, distribute offices, obtain contracts, etc.
q: The ruling ring at Constantinople.

Ring.etym: [AS. hring, hrinc; akin to Fries. hring, D. & G. ring, OHG. ring, hring, Icel. hringr, DAn. & SW. ring; cf. Russ. krug'. Cf. Harangue, Rank a row,Rink.]

senses.d: To surround with a ring, or as with a ring; to encircle.
To make a ring around by cutting away the bark; to girdle; as, to ring branches or roots.
To fit with a ring or with rings, as the fingers, or a swine's snout.
To rise in the air spirally.
The leader of a circle of dancers; hence, the leader of a number of persons acting together; the leader of a herd of animals.
q: A primacy of order, such an one as the ringleader hath in a dance.

senses.d: Opprobriously, a leader of a body of men engaged in the violation of law or in an illegal enterprise, as rioters, mutineers, or the like.
q: The ringleaders were apprehended, tried, fined, and imprisoned.

senses.d: Ring-streaked.
q: Cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.

senses.d: To wash lightly; to cleanse with a second or repeated application of water after washing.
To cleancse by the introduction of water; — applied especially to hollow vessels; as, to rinse a bottle.

Rinse.etym: [OE., fr. OF. rincer, rimser, reinser, raïncier, F. rincer; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: The act of rinsing.
Wanton or unrestrained behavior; uproar; tumult.
q: His headstrong riot hath no curb.

senses.d: Excessive and exxpensive feasting; wild and loose festivity; revelry.
q: Venus loveth riot and dispense.
The lamb thy riot dooms to bleed to-day.

senses.d: The tumultuous disturbance of the public peace by an unlawful assembly of three or more persons in the execution of some private object.

Riot.etym: [OF. riote, of uncertain origin; cf. OD. revot, ravot.]

senses.d: To engage in riot; to act in an unrestrained or wanton manner; to indulge in excess of luxury, feasting, or the like; to revel; to run riot; to go to excess.
q: Now he exact of all, wastes in delight, Riots in pleasure, and neglects the law.
No pulse that riots, and no blood that glows.

senses.d: To disturb the peace; to raise an uproar or sedition. See Riot, n., 3.
To spend or pass in riot.
q: had rioted his life out.

senses.d: Involving, or engaging in, riot; wanton; unrestrained; luxurious.
q: The younger son . . . took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.

senses.d: Partaking of the nature of an unlawful assembly or its acts; seditious.
A wicker fish basket.

Rip.etym: [Cf. Icel. hrip a box or basket; perhaps akin to E. corb. Cf. Ripier.]

senses.d: To divide or separate the parts of, by cutting or tearing; to tear or cut open or off; to tear off or out by violence; as, to rip a garment by cutting the stitches; to rip off the skin of a beast; to rip up a floor; — commonly used with up, open, off.
To get by, or as by, cutting or tearing.
q: He 'll rip the fatal secret from her heart.

senses.d: To tear up for search or disclosure, or for alteration; to search to the bottom; to discover; to disclose; — usually with up.
q: They ripped up all that had been done from the beginning of the rebellion.
For brethern to debate and rip up their falling out in the ear of a common enemy . . . is neither wise nor comely.

senses.d: To saw (wood) lengthwise of the grain or fiber.

Rip.etym: [Cf. AS. rȳpan, also Sw. repa to ripple flax, D. repelen, G. reffen, riffeln, and E. raff, raffle. Cf. Raff, Ripple of flax.]

senses.d: A rent made by ripping, esp. by a seam giving way; a tear; a place torn; laceration.
A term applied to a mean, worthless thing or person, as to a scamp, a debauchee, or a prostitute, or a worn-out horse.
A body of water made rough by the meeting of opposing tides or currents.
The bank of a river.
Ready for reaping or gathering; having attained perfection; mature; — said of fruits, seeds, etc.; as, ripe grain.
q: So mayst thou live, till, like ripe fruit, thou drop Into thy mother's lap.

senses.d: Advanced to the state of fitness for use; mellow; as, ripe cheese; ripe wine.
Having attained its full development; mature; perfected; consummate.
q: He was a scholar, and a ripe and good one.

senses.d: Maturated or suppurated; ready to discharge; — said of sores, tumors, etc.
Ready for action or effect; prepared.
q: While things were just ripe for a war.
I am not ripe to pass sentence on the gravest public bodies.

senses.d: Like ripened fruit in ruddiness and plumpness.
q: Those happy smilets, That played on her ripe lip.

senses.d: Intoxicated.

Ripe.etym: [AS. rīpe; akin to OS. rīpi, D. rijp, G. rief, OHG. rīft; cf. AS. rīp harvest, rīpan to reap. Cf. Reap.]

senses.d: To ripen; to grow ripe.
To mature; to ripen.
To grow ripe; to become mature, as grain, fruit, flowers, and the like; as, grapes ripen in the sun.
To approach or come to perfection.
To cause to mature; to make ripe; as, the warm days ripened the corn.
To mature; to fit or prepare; to bring to perfection; as, to ripen the judgment.
q: When faith and love, which parted from thee never, Had ripined thy iust soul to dwell with God.

senses.d: A bough or branch; a twig.
q: As white as is the blossom upon the ris.

Ris.etym: [AS. hrīs; akin to D. rils, G. reis, OHG. hrīs.]

senses.d: To move from a lower position to a higher; to ascend; to mount up. Specifically: — (a) To go upward by walking, climbing, flying, or any other voluntary motion; as, a bird rises in the air; a fish rises to the bait.
To ascend or float in a fluid, as gases or vapors in air, cork in water, and the like.
To move upward under the influence of a projecting force; as, a bullet rises in the air.
To grow upward; to attain a certain height; as, this elm rises to the height of seventy feet.
To reach a higher level by increase of quantity or bulk; to swell; as, a river rises in its bed; the mercury rises in the thermometer.
To become erect; to assume an upright position; as, to rise from a chair or from a fall.
To leave one's bed; to arise; as, to rise early.
q: He that would thrive, must rise by five.

senses.d: To tower up; to be heaved up; as, the Alps rise far above the sea.
To slope upward; as, a path, a line, or surface rises in this direction.
To retire; to give up a siege.
q: He, rising with small honor from Gunza, . . . was gone.

senses.d: To swell or puff up in the process of fermentation; to become light, as dough, and the like.
To have the aspect or the effect of rising.

Rise.syn: To arise; mount; ascend; climb; scale.
Rise.etym: [AS. rīsan; akin to OS. rīsan, D. rijzen, OHG. rīsan to rise, fall, Icel. rīsa, Goth. urreisan, G. reise journey. CF. Arise, Raise, Rear, v.]

senses.d: The act of rising, or the state of being risen.
The distance through which anything rises; as, the rise of the thermometer was ten degrees; the rise of the river was six feet; the rise of an arch or of a step.
Land which is somewhat higher than the rest; as, the house stood on a rise of land.
Spring; source; origin; as, the rise of a stream.
q: All wickednes taketh its rise from the heart.

senses.d: Appearance above the horizon; as, the rise of the sun or of a planet.
Increase; advance; augmentation, as of price, value, rank, property, fame, and the like.
q: The rise or fall that may happen in his constant revenue by a Spanish war.

senses.d: Increase of sound; a swelling of the voice.
q: The ordinary rises and falls of the voice.

senses.d: Elevation or ascent of the voice; upward change of key; as, a rise of a tone or semitone.
The spring of a fish to seize food (as a fly) near the surface of the water.
To go up; to ascend; to climb; as, to rise a hill.
To cause to rise; as, to rise a fish, or cause it to come to the surface of the water; to rise a ship, or bring it above the horizon by approaching it; to raise.
q: Until we rose the bark we could not pretend to call it a chase.

senses.d: Attaining a higher place; taking, or moving in, an upward direction; appearing above the horizon; ascending; as, the rising moon.
Increasing in wealth, power, or distinction; as, a rising state; a rising character.
q: Among the rising theologians of Germany.

senses.d: Growing; advancing to adult years and to the state of active life; as, the rising generation.
More than; exceeding; upwards of; as, a horse rising six years of age.
The act of one who, or that which, rises (in any sense).
That which rises; a tumor; a boil.

The act of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept, or custom; a formal act of religion or other solemn duty; a solemn observance; a ceremony; as, the rites of freemasonry.
q: He looked with indifference on rites, names, and forms of ecclesiastical polity.

Rite.etym: [L. ritus; cf. Skr. rīti a stream, a running, way, manner, ri to flow: cf. F. rit, rite. CF. Rivulet.]

senses.d: To rend asunder by force; to split; to cleave; as, to rive timber for rails or shingles.
q: I shall ryve him through the sides twain.
The scolding winds have rived the knotty oaks.
Brutus hath rived my heart.

Rive.etym: [Icel. rīfa, akin to Sw. rifva to pull asunder, burst, tear, Dan. rive to rake, pluck, tear. Cf. Reef of land, Rifle a gun, Rift, Rivel.]

senses.d: To be split or rent asunder.
q: Freestone rives, splits, and breaks in any direction.

senses.d: A place torn; a rent; a rift.
One who rives or splits.
A large stream of water flowing in a bed or channel and emptying into the ocean, a sea, a lake, or another stream; a stream larger than a rivulet or brook.
q: Transparent and sparkling rivers, from which it is delightful to drink as they flow.

senses.d: Fig.: A large stream; copious flow; abundance; as, rivers of blood; rivers of oil.

River.etym: [F. rivère a river, LL. riparia river, bank of a river, fr. L. riparius belonging to a bank or shore, fr. ripa a bank or shore; of uncertain origin. Cf. Arrive, Riparian.]

senses.d: To hawk by the side of a river; to fly hawks at river fowl.
A journey, or stage of a journey.
q: With easy roads he came to Leicester.

senses.d: An inroad; an invasion; a raid.
A place where one may ride; an open way or public passage for vehicles, persons, and animals; a track for travel, forming a means of communication between one city, town, or place, and another.
q: The most villainous house in all the London road.

senses.d: A place where ships may ride at anchor at some distance from the shore; a roadstead; — often in the plural; as, Hampton Roads.
q: Now strike your saile, ye jolly mariners, For we be come unto a quiet rode .

Road.syn: Way; highway; street; lane; pathway; route; passage; course. See Way.
Road.etym: [AS. rād a riding, that on which one rides or travels, a road, fr. rīdan to ride. See Ride, and cf. Raid.]

senses.d: To cry with a full, loud, continued sound.
q: Roaring bulls he would him make to tame.

senses.d: To cry loudly, as in pain, distress, or anger.
q: Sole on the barren sands, the suffering chief Roared out for anguish, and indulged his grief.
He scorned to roar under the impressions of a finite anger.

senses.d: To make a loud, confused sound, as winds, waves, passing vehicles, a crowd of persons when shouting together, or the like.
q: The brazen throat of war had ceased to roar.
How oft I crossed where carts and coaches roar.

senses.d: To be boisterous; to be disorderly.
q: It was a mad, roaring time, full of extravagance.

senses.d: To laugh out loudly and continuously; as, the hearers roared at his jokes.
To make a loud noise in breathing, as horses having a certain disease. See Roaring, 2.

Roar.etym: [OE. roren, raren, AS. rārian; akin to G. röhten, OHG. r�r�n. √112.]

senses.d: To cry aloud; to proclaim loudly.
q: This last action will roar thy infamy.

senses.d: The sound of roaring.
The deep, loud cry of a wild beast; as, the roar of a lion.
The cry of one in pain, distress, anger, or the like.
A loud, continuous, and confused sound; as, the roar of a cannon, of the wind, or the waves; the roar of ocean.
q: Arm! arm! it is, it is the cannon's opening roar!

senses.d: A boisterous outcry or shouting, as in mirth.
q: Pit, boxes, and galleries were in a constant roar of laughter.

senses.d: A loud, deep, prolonged sound, as of a large beast, or of a person in distress, anger, mirth, etc., or of a noisy congregation.
An affection of the windpipe of a horse, causing a loud, peculiar noise in breathing under exertion; the making of the noise so caused. See Roar, v. i., 5.
To cook by exposure to radiant heat before a fire; as, to roast meat on a spit, or in an oven open toward the fire and having reflecting surfaces within; also, to cook in a close oven.
To cook by surrounding with hot embers, ashes, sand, etc.; as, to roast a potato in ashes.
q: In eggs boiled and roasted there is scarce difference to be discerned.

senses.d: To dry and parch by exposure to heat; as, to roast coffee; to roast chestnuts, or peanuts.
Hence, to heat to excess; to heat violently; to burn.
To dissipate by heat the volatile parts of, as ores.
To banter severely.

Roast.etym: [OE. rosten, OF. rostir, F. rôtir; of German origin; cf. OHG. rōsten, G. rösten, fr. OHG. rōst, rōsta, gridiron, G. rost; cf. AS. hyrstan to roast.]

senses.d: To cook meat, fish, etc., by heat, as before the fire or in an oven.
q: He could roast, and seethe, and broil, and fry.

senses.d: To undergo the process of being roasted.
That which is roasted; a piece of meat which has been roasted, or is suitable for being roasted.
q: A fat swan loved he best of any roost .

senses.d: Roasted; as, roast beef.
The inspissated juice of ripe fruit, obtained by evaporation of the juice over a fire till it acquires the consistence of a sirup. It is sometimes mixed with honey or sugar.

Rob.etym: [F.; cf. Sp. rob, It. rob, robbo, Pg. robe, arrobe, Ar. rubb, robb, Per. rub.]

senses.d: To take (something) away from by force; to strip by stealing; to plunder; to pillage; to steal from.
q: Who would rob a hermit of his weeds, His few books, or his beads, or maple dish?
He that is robbed, not wanting what is stolen, Let him not know it, and he's not robbed at all.
To be executed for robbing a church.

senses.d: To take the property of (any one) from his person, or in his presence, feloniously, and against his will, by violence or by putting him in fear.
To deprive of, or withhold from, unjustly or injuriously; to defraud; as, to rob one of his rest, or of his good name; a tree robs the plants near it of sunlight.
q: I never robbed the soldiers of their pay.

Rob.etym: [OF. rober, of German origin; cf. OHG. roub�n, G. rauben, and OHG. roub robbing, booty, G. raub. √114. See Reave,and cf. Robe.]

senses.d: To take that which belongs to another, without right or permission, esp. by violence.
q: I am accursed to rob in that thief's company.

senses.d: One who robs; in law, one who feloniously takes goods or money from the person of another by violence or by putting him in fear.
q: Some roving robber calling to his fellows.

Robber.syn: Thief; depredator; despoiler; plunderer; pillager; rifler; brigang; freebooter; pirate. See Thief.

senses.d: The act or practice of robbing; theft.
q: Thieves for their robbery have authority When judges steal themselves.

senses.d: The crime of robbing. See Rob, v. t., 2.

Robbery.syn: Theft; depredation; spoliation; despoliation; despoilment; plunder; pillage; rapine; larceny; freebooting; piracy.

senses.d: An outer garment; a dress of a rich, flowing, and elegant style or make; hence, a dress of state, rank, office, or the like.
q: Through tattered clothes small vices do appear; Robes and furred gowns hide all.

senses.d: A skin of an animal, especially, a skin of the bison, dressed with the fur on, and used as a wrap.

Robe.etym: [F., fr. LL. rauba a gown, dress, garment; originally, booty, plunder. See Rob, v. t., and cf. Rubbish.]

senses.d: To invest with a robe or robes; to dress; to array; as, fields robed with green.
q: The sage Chaldeans robed in white appeared.
Such was his power over the expression of his countenance, that he could in an instant shake off the sternness of winter, and robe it in the brightest smiles of spring.

senses.d: A distaff used in spinning; the staff or frame about which flax is arranged, and from which the thread is drawn in spinning.
q: Sad Clotho held the rocke, the whiles the thread By grisly Lachesis was spun with pain, That cruel Atropos eftsoon undid.

Rock.etym: [OE. rocke; akin to D. rok, rokken, G. rocken, OHG. roccho, Dan. rok, Icel. rokkr. Cf. Rocket a firework.]

senses.d: A large concreted mass of stony material; a large fixed stone or crag. See Stone.
q: Come one, come all! this rock shall fly From its firm base as soon as I.

senses.d: Any natural deposit forming a part of the earth's crust, whether consolidated or not, including sand, earth, clay, etc., when in natural beds.
That which resembles a rock in firmness; a defense; a support; a refuge.
q: The Lord is my rock, and my fortress.

senses.d: Fig.: Anything which causes a disaster or wreck resembling the wreck of a vessel upon a rock.
The striped bass. See under Bass.

Rock.etym: [OF. roke, F. roche; cf. Armor. roc'h, and AS. rocc.]

senses.d: To cause to sway backward and forward, as a body resting on a support beneath; as, to rock a cradle or chair; to cause to vibrate; to cause to reel or totter.
q: A rising earthquake rocked the ground.

senses.d: To move as in a cradle; hence, to put to sleep by rocking; to still; to quiet.

Rock.etym: [AS. roccian; akin to Dan. rokke to move, to snake; cf. Icel. rukkja to pull, move, G. rücken to move, push, pull.]

senses.d: To move or be moved backward and forward; to be violently agitated; to reel; to totter.
q: The rocking town Supplants their footsteps.

senses.d: To roll or saway backward and forward upon a support; as, to rock in a rocking-chair.
A straight and slender stick; a wand; hence, any slender bar, as of wood or metal (applied to various purposes).
q: He that spareth his rod hateth his son.

senses.d: A kind of sceptor, or badge of office; hence, figuratively, power; authority; tyranny; oppression.
A support for a fishing line; a fish pole.
A member used in tension, as for sustaining a suspended weight, or in tension and compression, as for transmitting reciprocating motion, etc.; a connecting bar.
An instrument for measuring.
A measure of length containing sixteen and a half feet; — called also perch, and pole.

Rod.etym: [The same word as rood. See Rood.]

senses.d: Redness; complexion.
A roebuck. See Roebuck.
The female of any species of deer.

Roe.etym: [OE. ro, AS. rāh; akin to D. ree, G. reh, Icel. rā, SW. rå.]

senses.d: The ova or spawn of fishes and amphibians, especially when still inclosed in the ovarian membranes. Sometimes applied, loosely, to the sperm and the testes of the male.
A mottled appearance of light and shade in wood, especially in mahogany.

Roe.etym: [For roan, OE. rowne, akin to G. rogen, OHG. rogan, Icel. hrogn, Dan. rogn, ravn, Sw. rom; of uncertain origin; cf. Gr. ��� pebble, Skr. �arkarā gravel.]

senses.d: A small European and Asiatic deer (Capreolus capræa) having erect, cylindrical, branched antlers, forked at the summit. This, the smallest European deer, is very nimble and graceful. It always prefers a mountainous country, or high grounds.
To cause to revolve by turning over and over; to move by turning on an axis; to impel forward by causing to turn over and over on a supporting surface; as, to roll a wheel, a ball, or a barrel.
To wrap round on itself; to form into a spherical or cylindrical body by causing to turn over and over; as, to roll a sheet of paper; to roll parchment; to roll clay or putty into a ball.
To bind or involve by winding, as in a bandage; to inwrap; — often with up; as, to roll up a parcel.
To drive or impel forward with an easy motion, as of rolling; as, a river rolls its waters to the ocean.
q: The flood of Catholic reaction was rolled over Europe.

senses.d: To utter copiously, esp. with sounding words; to utter with a deep sound; — often with forth, or out; as, to roll forth some one's praises; to roll out sentences.
q: Who roll'd the psalm to wintry skies.

senses.d: To press or level with a roller; to spread or form with a roll, roller, or rollers; as, to roll a field; to roll paste; to roll steel rails, etc.
To move, or cause to be moved, upon, or by means of, rollers or small wheels.
To beat with rapid, continuous strokes, as a drum; to sound a roll upon.

To apply (one line or surface) to another without slipping; to bring all the parts of (one line or surface) into successive contact with another, in suck manner that at every instant the parts that have been in contact are equal.
To turn over in one's mind; to revolve.
q: Full oft in heart he rolleth up and down The beauty of these florins new and bright.

Roll.etym: [OF. roeler, roler, F. rouler, LL. rotulare, fr. L. royulus, rotula, a little wheel, dim. of rota wheel; akin to G. rad, and to Skr. ratha car, chariot. Cf. Control, Roll, n., Rotary.]

senses.d: To move, as a curved object may, along a surface by rotation without sliding; to revolve upon an axis; to turn over and over; as, a ball or wheel rolls on the earth; a body rolls on an inclined plane.
q: And her foot, look you, is fixed upon a spherical stone, which rolls, and rolls, and rolls.

senses.d: To move on wheels; as, the carriage rolls along the street.
To be wound or formed into a cylinder or ball; as, the cloth rolls unevenly; the snow rolls well.
To fall or tumble; — with over; as, a stream rolls over a precipice.
To perform a periodical revolution; to move onward as with a revolution; as, the rolling year; ages roll away.
To turn; to move circularly.
q: And his red eyeballs roll with living fire.

senses.d: To move, as waves or billows, with alternate swell and depression.
q: What different sorrows did within thee roll.

senses.d: To incline first to one side, then to the other; to rock; as, there is a great difference in ships about rolling; in a general semse, to be tossed about.
q: Twice ten tempestuous nights I rolled.

senses.d: To turn over, or from side to side, while lying down; to wallow; as, a horse rolls.
To spread under a roller or rolling-pin; as, the paste rolls well.
To beat a drum with strokes so rapid that they can scarcely be distinguished by the ear.
To make a loud or heavy rumbling noise; as, the thunder rolls.
q: Man shall not suffer his wife go roll about.

senses.d: The act of rolling, or state of being rolled; as, the roll of a ball; the roll of waves.
That which rolls; a roller.
That which is rolled up; as, a roll of fat, of wool, paper, cloth, etc.
q: Busy angels spread The lasting roll, recording what we say.

senses.d: Hence, an official or public document; a register; a record; also, a catalogue; a list.
q: The rolls of Parliament, the entry of the petitions, answers, and transactions in Parliament, are extant.
The roll and list of that army doth remain.

senses.d: A quantity of cloth wound into a cylindrical form; as, a roll of carpeting; a roll of ribbon.
A cylindrical twist of tobacco.
A kind of shortened raised biscuit or bread, often rolled or doubled upon itself.
The oscillating movement of a vessel from side to side, in sea way, as distinguished from the alternate rise and fall of bow and stern called pitching.
A heavy, reverberatory sound; as, the roll of cannon, or of thunder.
The uniform beating of a drum with strokes so rapid as scarcely to be distinguished by the ear.
Part; office; duty; rôle.

Roll.syn: List; schedule; catalogue; register; inventory. See List.
Roll.etym: [F. rôle a roll (in sense 3), fr. L. rotulus � little wheel, LL., a roll, dim. of L. rota a wheel. See Roll, v., and cf. Rôle, Rouleau, Roulette.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, rolls; especially, a cylinder, sometimes grooved, of wood, stone, metal, etc., used in husbandry and the arts.
A bandage; a fillet; properly, a long and broad bandage used in surgery.
One of series of long, heavy waves which roll in upon a coast, sometimes in calm weather.
A long, belt-formed towel, to be suspended on a rolling cylinder; — called also roller towel.
A cylinder coated with a composition made principally of glue and molassess, with which forms of type are inked previously to taking an impression from them.
A long cylinder on which something is rolled up; as, the roller of a map.
A small wheel, as of a caster, a roller skate, etc.
ANy insect whose larva rolls up leaves; a leaf roller. see Tortrix.
Any one of numerous species of Old World picarian birds of the family Coraciadæ. The name alludes to their habit of suddenly turning over or “tumbling” in flight.
Any species of small ground snakes of the family Tortricidæ.
Rotating on an axis, or moving along a surface by rotation; turning over and over as if on an axis or a pivot; as, a rolling wheel or ball.
Moving on wheels or rollers, or as if on wheels or rollers; as, a rolling chair.
Having gradual, rounded undulations of surface; as, a rolling country; rolling land.
Of or pertaining to Rome, or the Roman people; like or characteristic of Rome, the Roman people, or things done by Romans; as, Roman fortitude; a Roman aqueduct; Roman art.
Of or pertaining to the Roman Catholic religion; professing that religion.
Upright; erect; — said of the letters or kind of type ordinarily used, as distinguished from Italic characters.

Roman.etym: [L. Romanus, fr. Roma Rome: cf. F. romain. Cf. Romaic, Romance, Romantic.]

senses.d: A native, or permanent resident, of Rome; a citizen of Rome, or one upon whom certain rights and privileges of a Roman citizen were conferred.
Roman type, letters, or print, collectively; — in distinction from Italics.

The cover of any building, including the roofing (see Roofing) and all the materials and construction necessary to carry and maintain the same upon the walls or other uprights. In the case of a building with vaulted ceilings protected by an outer roof, some writers call the vault the roof, and the outer protection the roof mask. It is better, however, to consider the vault as the ceiling only, in cases where it has farther covering.
That which resembles, or corresponds to, the covering or the ceiling of a house; as, the roof of a cavern; the roof of the mouth.
q: The flowery roof Showered roses, which the morn repaired.

senses.d: The surface or bed of rock immediately overlying a bed of coal or a flat vein.

Roof.etym: [OE. rof, AS. hr�f top, roof; akin to D. roef cabin, Icel. hr�f a shed under which ships are built or kept; cf. OS. hr�st roof, Goth. hr�t. Cf. Roost.]

senses.d: To cover with a roof.
q: I have not seen the remains of any Roman buildings that have not been roofed with vaults or arches.

senses.d: To inclose in a house; figuratively, to shelter.
q: Here had we now our country's honor roofed.

senses.d: Unobstructed spase; space which may be occupied by or devoted to any object; compass; extent of place, great or small; as, there is not room for a house; the table takes up too much room.
q: Lord, it is done as thou hast commanded, and yet there is room.
There was no room for them in the inn.

senses.d: A particular portion of space appropriated for occupancy; a place to sit, stand, or lie; a seat.
q: If he have but twelve pence in his purse, he will give it for the best room in a playhouse.
When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room.

senses.d: Especially, space in a building or ship inclosed or set apart by a partition; an apartment or chamber.
q: I found the prince in the next room.

senses.d: Place or position in society; office; rank; post; station; also, a place or station once belonging to, or occupied by, another, and vacated.
q: When he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judea in the room of his father Herod.
Neither that I look for a higher room in heaven.
Let Bianca take her sister's room.

senses.d: Possibility of admission; ability to admit; opportunity to act; fit occasion; as, to leave room for hope.
q: There was no prince in the empire who had room for such an alliance.

Room.etym: [OE. roum, rum, space, AS. rūm; akin to OS., OFries. & Icel. rūm, D. ruim, G. raum, OHG. rūm, Sw. & Dan. rum, Goth. rūms, and to AS. rūm, adj., spacious, D. ruim, Icel. rūmr, Goth. rūms; and prob. to L. rus country (cf. Rural), Zend ravaṅh wide, free, open, ravan a plain.]

senses.d: To occupy a room or rooms; to lodge; as, they arranged to room together.
Spacious; roomy.
q: No roomer harbour in the place.

senses.d: To turn up the earth with the snout, as swine.
Hence, to seek for favor or advancement by low arts or groveling servility; to fawn servilely.

Root.etym: [AS. wrōtan; akin to wrōt a snout, trunk, D. wroeten to root, G. rüssel snout, trunk, proboscis, Icel. rōta to root, and perhaps to L. rodere to gnaw (E. rodent) or to E. root, n.]

senses.d: To turn up or to dig out with the snout; as, the swine roots the earth.
The underground portion of a plant, whether a true root or a tuber, a bulb or rootstock, as in the potato, the onion, or the sweet flag.
An edible or esculent root, especially of such plants as produce a single root, as the beet, carrot, etc.; as, the root crop.

That which resembles a root in position or function, esp. as a source of nourishment or support; that from which anything proceeds as if by growth or development; as, the root of a tooth, a nail, a cancer, and the like.
q: They were the roots out of which sprang two distinct people.

senses.d: A primitive form of speech; one of the earliest terms employed in language; a word from which other words are formed; a radix, or radical.
The cause or occasion by which anything is brought about; the source.
q: The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

senses.d: That factor of a quantity which when multiplied into itself will produce that quantity; thus, 3 is a root of 9, because 3 multiplied into itself produces 9; 3 is the cube root of 27.
The fundamental tone of any chord; the tone from whose harmonics, or overtones, a chord is composed.
The lowest place, position, or part.
The time which to reckon in making calculations.
q: When a root is of a birth yknowe .

Root.etym: [Icel. rōt (for vrōt); akin to E. wort, and perhaps to root to turn up the earth. See Wort.]

senses.d: To fix the root; to enter the earth, as roots; to take root and begin to grow.
q: In deep grounds the weeds root deeper.

senses.d: To be firmly fixed; to be established.
q: If any irregularity chanced to intervene and to cause misappehensions, he gave them not leave to root and fasten by concealment.

senses.d: To plant and fix deeply in the earth, or as in the earth; to implant firmly; hence, to make deep or radical; to establish; — used chiefly in the participle; as, rooted trees or forests; rooted dislike.
To tear up by the root; to eradicate; to extirpate; — with up, out, or away.
q: The Lord rooted them out of their land . . . and cast them into another land.

senses.d: To shout for, or otherwise noisly applaud or encourage, a contestant, as in sports; hence, to wish earnestly for the success of some one or the happening of some event, with the superstitious notion that this action may have efficacy; — usually with for; as, the crowd rooted for the home team.
Having taken root; firmly implanted; fixed in the heart.
A large, stout cord, usually one not less than an inch in circumference, made of strands twisted or braided together. It differs from cord, line, and string, only in its size. See Cordage.
A row or string consisting of a number of things united, as by braiding, twining, etc.; as, a rope of onions.
The small intestines; as, the ropes of birds.

Rope.etym: [AS. rāp; akin to D. reep, G. reif ring hoop, Icel. reip rope, Sw. rep, Dan. reb, reeb Goth. skaudaraip latchet.]

senses.d: To be formed into rope; to draw out or extend into a filament or thread, as by means of any glutinous or adhesive quality.
q: Let us not hang like ropingicicles Upon our houses' thatch.

senses.d: To bind, fasten, or tie with a rope or cord; as, to rope a bale of goods.
To connect or fasten together, as a party of mountain climbers, with a rope.
To partition, separate, or divide off, by means of a rope, so as to include or exclude something; as, to rope in, or rope off, a plot of ground; to rope out a crowd.
To lasso (a steer, horse).
To draw, as with a rope; to entice; to inveigle; to decoy; as, to rope in customers or voters.
To prevent from winning (as a horse), by pulling or curbing.
A flower and shrub of any species of the genus Rosa, of which there are many species, mostly found in the morthern hemispere
A knot of ribbon formed like a rose; a rose knot; a rosette, esp. one worn on a shoe.
A rose window. See Rose window, below.
A perforated nozzle, as of a pipe, spout, etc., for delivering water in fine jets; a rosehead; also, a strainer at the foot of a pump.
The erysipelas.
The card of the mariner's compass; also, a circular card with radiating lines, used in other instruments.
The color of a rose; rose-red; pink.
A diamond. See Rose diamond, below.

Rose.etym: [AS. rose, L. rosa, probably akin to Gr. �, Armor. vard, OPer. vareda; and perhaps to E. wort: cf. F. rose, from the Latin. Cf. Copperas, Rhododendron.]

senses.d: To render rose-colored; to redden; to flush.
To perfume, as with roses.

To undergo a process common to organic substances by which they lose the cohesion of their parts and pass through certain chemical changes, giving off usually in some stages of the process more or less offensive odors; to become decomposed by a natural process; to putrefy; to decay.
q: Fixed like a plant on his peculiar spot, To draw nutrition, propagate, and rot.

senses.d: Figuratively: To perish slowly; to decay; to die; to become corrupt.
q: Four of the sufferers were left to rot in irons.
Rot, poor bachelor, in your club.

Rot.etym: [OE. rotien, AS. rotian; akin to D. rotten, Prov. G. rotten, OHG. rozz�n, G. rösten to steep flax, Icel. rotna to rot, Sw. ruttna, Dan. raadne, Icel. rottin rotten. √117. Cf. Ret, Rotten.]

senses.d: To make putrid; to cause to be wholly or partially decomposed by natural processes; as, to rot vegetable fiber.
To expose, as flax, to a process of maceration, etc., for the purpose of separating the fiber; to ret.
Process of rotting; decay; putrefaction.
A disease or decay in fruits, leaves, or wood, supposed to be caused by minute fungi. See Bitter rot, Black rot, etc., below.
A fatal distemper which attacks sheep and sometimes other animals. It is due to the presence of a parasitic worm in the liver or gall bladder. See 1st Fluke, 2.
q: His cattle must of rot and murrain die.

senses.d: Having rotted; putrid; decayed; as, a rotten apple; rotten meat.
Offensive to the smell; fetid; disgusting.
q: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate As reek of the rotten fens.

senses.d: Not firm or trusty; unsound; defective; treacherous; unsafe; as, a rotten plank, bone, stone.

Rotten.syn: Putrefied; decayed; carious; defective; unsound; corrupt; deceitful; treacherous.
