Rotten.etym: [Icel. rotinn; akin to Sw. rutten, Dan. radden. See Rot.]

senses.d: Having inequalities, small ridges, or points, on the surface; not smooth or plain; as, a rough board; a rough stone; rough cloth.
Not polished; uncut; — said of a gem; as, a rough diamond.
Tossed in waves; boisterous; high; — said of a sea or other piece of water.
q: More unequal than the roughest sea.

senses.d: Marked by coarseness; shaggy; ragged; disordered; — said of dress, appearance, or the like; as, a rough coat.
Hence, figuratively, lacking refinement, gentleness, or polish.
q: A fiend, a fury, pitiless and rough.
A surly boatman, rough as wayes or winds.

senses.d: Marked by severity or violence; harsh; hard; as, rough measures or actions.
q: On the rough edge of battle.
A quicker and rougher remedy.
Kind words prevent a good deal of that perverseness which rough and imperious usage often produces.

senses.d: Loud and hoarse; offensive to the ear; harsh; grating; — said of sound, voice, and the like; as, a rough tone; rough numbers.
Austere; harsh to the taste; as, rough wine.
Tempestuous; boisterous; stormy; as, rough weather; a rough day.
q: He stayeth his rough wind.
Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.

senses.d: Hastily or carelessly done; wanting finish; incomplete; as, a rough estimate; a rough draught.

Rough.etym: [OE. rou�, rou, row, rugh, ruh, AS. r�h; akin to LG. rug, D. rug, D. ruig, ruw, OHG. r�h, G. rauh, rauch; cf. Lith. raukas wrinkle, rukti to wrinkle. √ 18. Cf. Rug, n.]

senses.d: Boisterous weather.
A rude fellow; a coarse bully; a rowdy.
q: Contemplating the people in the rough.

senses.d: In a rough manner; rudely; roughly.
q: Sleeping rough on the trenches, and dying stubbornly in their boats.

senses.d: To render rough; to roughen.
To break in, as a horse, especially for military purposes.
To cut or make in a hasty, rough manner; — with out; as, to rough out a carving, a sketch.
In a rough manner; unevenly; harshly; rudely; severely; austerely.
To whisper.
q: The Bishop of Glasgow rounding in his ear, “Ye are not a wise man,” . . . he rounded likewise to the bishop, and said, “Wherefore brought ye me here?”

senses.d: Having every portion of the surface or of the circumference equally distant from the center; spherical; circular; having a form approaching a spherical or a circular shape; orbicular; globular; as, a round ball.
q: Upon the firm opacous globe Of this round world.

senses.d: Having the form of a cylinder; cylindrical; as, the barrel of a musket is round.

Having a curved outline or form; especially, one like the arc of a circle or an ellipse, or a portion of the surface of a sphere; rotund; bulging; protuberant; not angular or pointed; as, a round arch; round hills.
Full; complete; not broken; not fractional; approximately in even units, tens, hundreds, thousands, etc.; — said of numbers.
q: Pliny put a round number near the truth, rather than the fraction.

senses.d: Not inconsiderable; large; hence, generous; free; as, a round price.
q: Three thousand ducats; 'tis a good round sum.
Round was their pace at first, but slackened soon.

senses.d: Uttered or emitted with a full tone; as, a round voice; a round note.
Modified, as a vowel, by contraction of the lip opening, making the opening more or less round in shape; rounded; labialized; labial. See Guide to Pronunciation, § 11.
Outspoken; plain and direct; unreserved; unqualified; not mincing; as, a round answer; a round oath.
q: Sir Toby, I must be round with you.

senses.d: Full and smoothly expanded; not defective or abrupt; finished; polished; — said of style, or of authors with reference to their style.
q: In his satires Horace is quick, round, and pleasant.

senses.d: Complete and consistent; fair; just; — applied to conduct.
q: Round dealing is the honor of man's nature.

Round.syn: Circular; spherical; globular; globase; orbicular; orbed; cylindrical; full; plump; rotund.
Round.etym: [OF. roond, roont, reond, F. rond, fr. L. rotundus, fr. rota wheel. See Rotary, and cf. Rotund, roundel, Rundlet.]

senses.d: Anything round, as a circle, a globe, a ring. “The golden round” .
q: In labyrinth of many a round self-rolled.

senses.d: A series of changes or events ending where it began; a series of like events recurring in continuance; a cycle; a periodical revolution; as, the round of the seasons; a round of pleasures.
A course of action or conduct performed by a number of persons in turn, or one after another, as if seated in a circle.
q: Women to cards may be compared: we play A round or two; which used, we throw away.
The feast was served; the bowl was crowned; To the king's pleasure went the mirthful round.

senses.d: A series of duties or tasks which must be performed in turn, and then repeated.
q: the trivial round, the common task.

senses.d: A circular dance.
q: Come, knit hands, and beat the ground, In a light fantastic round.

senses.d: That which goes round a whole circle or company; as, a round of applause.
Rotation, as in office; succession.
The step of a ladder; a rundle or rung; also, a crosspiece which joins and braces the legs of a chair.
q: All the rounds like Jacob's ladder rise.

senses.d: A course ending where it began; a circuit; a beat; especially, one freguently or regulary traversed; also, the act of traversing a circuit; as, a watchman's round; the rounds of the postman.

A walk performed by a guard or an officer round the rampart of a garrison, or among sentinels, to see that the sentinels are faithful and all things safe; also, the guard or officer, with his attendants, who performs this duty; — usually in the plural.
A short vocal piece, resembling a catch in which three or four voices follow each other round in a species of canon in the unison.
The time during which prize fighters or boxers are in actual contest without an intermission, as prescribed by their rules; a bout.
On all sides; around.
q: Round he throws his baleful eyes.

senses.d: Circularly; in a circular form or manner; by revolving or reversing one's position; as, to turn one's head round; a wheel turns round.
In circumference; as, a ball is ten inches round.
From one side or party to another; as to come or turn round, — that is, to change sides or opinions.
By or in a circuit; by a course longer than the direct course; back to the starting point.
Through a circle, as of friends or houses.
q: The invitations were sent round accordingly.

senses.d: Roundly; fully; vigorously.
On every side of, so as to encompass or encircle; around; about; as, the people atood round him; to go round the city; to wind a cable round a windlass.
q: The serpent Error twines round human hearts.

senses.d: To make circular, spherical, or cylindrical; to give a round or convex figure to; as, to round a silver coin; to round the edges of anything.
q: Worms with many feet, which round themselves into balls, are bred chiefly under logs of timber.
The figures on our modern medals are raised and rounded to a very great perfection.

senses.d: To surround; to encircle; to encompass.
q: The inclusive verge Of golden metal that must round my brow.

senses.d: To bring to fullness or completeness; to complete; hence, to bring to a fit conclusion.
q: We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.

senses.d: To go round wholly or in part; to go about (a corner or point); as, to round a corner; to round Cape Horn.
To make full, smooth, and flowing; as, to round periods in writing.
To grow round or full; hence, to attain to fullness, completeness, or perfection.
q: The queen your mother rounds apace.
So rounds he to a separate mind, From whence clear memory may begin.

senses.d: To go round, as a guard.
q: They . . . nightly rounding walk.

senses.d: To go or turn round; to wheel about.
To pull or haul strongly and all together, as upon a rope, without the assistance of mechanical appliances.

Rouse.etym: [Perhaps the same word as rouse to start up, “buckle to.”]

senses.d: A bumper in honor of a toast or health.
A carousal; a festival; a drinking frolic.
q: Fill the cup, and fill the can, Have a rouse before the morn.

Rouse.etym: [Cf. D. roes drunkeness, icel. r�ss, Sw. rus, G. rauchen, and also E. rouse, v.t., rush, v.i. Cf. Row a disturbance.]

senses.d: To cause to start from a covert or lurking place; as, to rouse a deer or other animal of the chase.
q: Like wild boars late roused out of the brakes.
Rouse the fleet hart, and cheer the opening hound.

senses.d: To wake from sleep or repose; as, to rouse one early or suddenly.
To excite to lively thought or action from a state of idleness, languor, stupidity, or indifference; as, to rouse the faculties, passions, or emotions.
q: To rouse up a people, the most phlegmatic of any in Christendom.

senses.d: To put in motion; to stir up; to agitate.
q: Blustering winds, which all night long Had roused the sea.

senses.d: To raise; to make erect.

Rouse.etym: [Probably of Scan. origin; cf. Sw. rusa to rush, Dan. ruse, AS. hreósan to fall, rush. Cf. Rush, v.]

senses.d: To get or start up; to rise.
q: Night's black agents to their preys do rouse.

senses.d: To awake from sleep or repose.
q: Morpheus rouses from his bed.

senses.d: To be exited to thought or action from a state of indolence or inattention.
One who practices robbery on the seas; a pirate.
q: Yet Pompey the Great deserveth honor more justly for scouring the seas, and taking from the rovers 846 sail of ships.

senses.d: One who wanders about by sea or land; a wanderer; a rambler.
Hence, a fickle, inconstant person.
A ball which has passed through all the hoops and would go out if it hit the stake but is continued in play; also, the player of such a ball.
Casual marks at uncertain distances.
A sort of arrow.
q: All sorts, flights, rovers, and butt shafts.

Rover.etym: [D. roover a robber. See Rove, v. i.]

senses.d: Rough; stern; angry.
A noisy, turbulent quarrel or disturbance; a brawl.
A series of persons or things arranged in a continued line; a line; a rank; a file; as, a row of trees; a row of houses or columns.
q: And there were windows in three rows.
The bright seraphim in burning row.

Row.etym: [OE. rowe, rawe, rewe, AS. rāw, r�w; probably akin to D. rij, G. reihe; cf. Skr. r�khā a line, stroke.]

senses.d: To propel with oars, as a boat or vessel, along the surface of water; as, to row a boat.
To transport in a boat propelled with oars; as, to row the captain ashore in his barge.

Row.etym: [AS. r�wan; akin to D. roeijen, MHG. rüejen, Dan. roe, Sw. ro, Icel. r�a, L. remus oar, Gr. �, Skr. aritra. √8. Cf. Rudder.]

senses.d: To use the oar; as, to row well.
To be moved by oars; as, the boat rows easily.
The act of rowing; excursion in a rowboat.
Formed into a row, or rows; having a row, or rows; as, a twelve-rowed ear of corn.
One who rows with an oar.
Kingly; pertaining to the crown or the sovereign; suitable for a king or queen; regal; as, royal power or prerogative; royal domains; the royal family; royal state.
Noble; generous; magnificent; princely.
q: How doth that royal merchant, good Antonio?

senses.d: Under the patronage of royality; holding a charter granted by the sovereign; as, the Royal Academy of Arts; the Royal Society.

Royal.syn: Kingly; regal; monarchical; imperial; kinglike; princely; august; majestic; superb; splendid; illustrious; noble; magnanimous.
Royal.etym: [OE. roial, riall, real, OF. roial. reial, F. royal, fr. L. regalis, fr. rex, regis, king. See Rich, and cf. regal, real a coin, Rial.]

senses.d: Printing and writing papers of particular sizes. See under paper, n.
A small sail immediately above the topgallant sail.
One of the upper or distal branches of an antler, as the third and fourth tynes of the antlers of a stag.
A small mortar.
One of the soldiers of the first regiment of foot of the British army, formerly called the Royals, and supposed to be the oldest regular corps in Europe; — now called the Royal Scots.
An old English coin. See Rial.
A royal spade.

To subject (a body) to the action of something moving over its surface with pressure and friction, especially to the action of something moving back and forth; as, to rub the flesh with the hand; to rub wood with sandpaper.
q: It shall be expedient, after that body is cleaned, to rub the body with a coarse linen cloth.

senses.d: To move over the surface of (a body) with pressure and friction; to graze; to chafe; as, the boat rubs the ground.
To cause (a body) to move with pressure and friction along a surface; as, to rub the hand over the body.
q: Two bones rubbed hard against one another.

senses.d: To spread a substance thinly over; to smear.
q: The smoothed plank, . . . New rubbed with balm.

senses.d: To scour; to burnish; to polish; to brighten; to cleanse; — often with up or over; as, to rub up silver.
q: The whole business of our redemption is to rub over the defaced copy of the creation.

senses.d: To hinder; to cross; to thwart.
q: 'T is the duke's pleasure, Whose disposition, all the world well knows, Will not be rubbed nor stopped.

Rub.etym: [Probably of Celtic origin; cf. W. rhwbiaw, gael. rub.]

senses.d: To move along the surface of a body with pressure; to grate; as, a wheel rubs against the gatepost.
To fret; to chafe; as, to rub upon a sore.
To move or pass with difficulty; as, to rub through woods, as huntsmen; to rub through the world.
The act of rubbing; friction.
That which rubs; that which tends to hinder or obstruct motion or progress; hindrance; obstruction, an impediment; especially, a difficulty or obstruction hard to overcome; a pinch.
q: Every rub is smoothed on our way.
To sleep, perchance to dream; ay, there's the rub.
Upon this rub, the English ambassadors thought fit to demur.
One knows not, certainly, what other rubs might have been ordained for us by a wise Providence.

senses.d: Inequality of surface, as of the ground in the game of bowls; unevenness.
Something grating to the feelings; sarcasm; joke; as, a hard rub.
Imperfection; failing; fault.
A chance.
q: Flight shall leave no Greek a rub.

senses.d: A stone, commonly flat, used to sharpen cutting tools; a whetstone; — called also rubstone.
Waste or rejected matter; anything worthless; valueless stuff; trash; especially, fragments of building materials or fallen buildings; ruins; débris.
q: What rubbish and what offal!
he saw the town's one half in rubbish lie.

Rubbish.etym: [OE. robows, robeux, rubble, originally an Old French plural from an assumed dim. of robe, probably in the sense of trash; cf. It. robaccia trash, roba stuff, goods, wares, robe. Thus, etymologically rubbish is the pl. of rubble. See Robe, and cf. Rubble.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to rubbish; of the quality of rubbish; trashy.
A precious stone of a carmine red color, sometimes verging to violet, or intermediate between carmine and hyacinth red. It is a red crystallized variety of corundum.
q: Of rubies, sapphires, and pearles white.

senses.d: The color of a ruby; carmine red; a red tint.
q: The natural ruby of your cheeks.

senses.d: That which has the color of the ruby, as red wine. Hence, a red blain or carbuncle.
Any species of South American humming birds of the genus Clytolæma. The males have a ruby-colored throat or breast.

Ruby.etym: [F. rubis (cf. Pr. robi), LL. rubinus, robinus, fr. L. rubeus red, reddish, akin to ruber. See Rouge, red.]

senses.d: Ruby-colored; red; as, ruby lips.
To make red; to redden.
Redness; blush.
Ruddle; red ocher.
The rudd.

Rud.etym: [AS. rudu, akin to reád red. √113. See Red, and cf. Ruddy.]

senses.d: To make red.

A fresh-water European fish of the Carp family (Leuciscus erythrophthalmus). It is about the size and shape of the roach, but it has the dorsal fin farther back, a stouter body, and red irises. Called also redeye, roud, finscale, and shallow. A blue variety is called azurine, or blue roach.
A riddle or sieve.

The mechanical appliance by means of which a vessel is guided or steered when in motion. It is a broad and flat blade made of wood or iron, with a long shank, and is fastened in an upright position, usually by one edge, to the sternpost of the vessel in such a way that it can be turned from side to side in the water by means of a tiller, wheel, or other attachment.
Fig.: That which resembles a rudder as a guide or governor; that which guides or governs the course.
q: For rhyme the rudder is of verses.

Rudder.etym: [OE. rother, AS. rōðer a paddle; akin to D. roer rudder, oar, G. ruder, OHG. roadar, Sw. roder, ror, Dan. roer, ror. √ 8. See Row to propel with an oar, and cf. Rother. ]

senses.d: In an aircraft, a surface the function of which is to exert a turning moment about an axis of the craft.
Of a red color; red, or reddish; as, a ruddy sky; a ruddy flame.
q: They were more ruddy in body than rubies.

senses.d: Of a lively flesh color, or the color of the human skin in high health; as, ruddy cheeks or lips.
To make ruddy.
Characterized by roughness; umpolished; raw; lacking delicacy or refinement; coarse.
q: Such gardening tools as art, yet rude, . . . had formed.

senses.d: Unformed by taste or skill; not nicely finished; not smoothed or polished; — said especially of material things; as, rude workmanship.
q: Rude and unpolished stones.
The heaven-born child All meanly wrapt in the rude manger lies.

senses.d: Of untaught manners; unpolished; of low rank; uncivil; clownish; ignorant; raw; unskillful; — said of persons, or of conduct, skill, and the like.
q: He was but rude in the profession of arms.
the rude forefathers of the hamlet sleep.

senses.d: Violent; tumultuous; boisterous; inclement; harsh; severe; — said of the weather, of storms, and the like; as, the rude winter.
q: pushed with winds, rude in their shock.
The rude agitation breaks it into foam.

senses.d: Barbarous; fierce; bloody; impetuous; — said of war, conflict, and the like; as, the rude shock of armies.
Not finished or complete; inelegant; lacking chasteness or elegance; not in good taste; unsatisfactory in mode of treatment; — said of literature, language, style, and the like.
q: Rude am I in my speech.
Unblemished by my rude translation.

Rude.syn: Impertinent; rough; uneven; shapeless; unfashioned; rugged; artless; unpolished; uncouth; inelegant; rustic; coarse; vulgar; clownish; raw; unskillful; untaught; illiterate; ignorant; uncivil; impolite; saucy; impudent; insolent; surly; currish; churlish; brutal; uncivilized; barbarous; savage; violent; fierce; tumultuous; turbulent; impetuous; boisterous; harsh; inclement; severe. See Impertiment.

senses.d: That which is unformed or undeveloped; the principle which lies at the bottom of any development; an unfinished beginning.
q: but I will bring thee where thou soon shalt quit Those rudiments, and see before thine eyes The monarchies of the earth.
the single leaf is the rudiment of beauty in landscape.

senses.d: Hence, an element or first principle of any art or science; a beginning of any knowledge; a first step.
q: This boy is forest-born, And hath been tutored in the rudiments of many desperate studies.
There he shall first lay down the rudiments Of his great warfare.

senses.d: An imperfect organ or part, or one which is never developed.

Rudiment.etym: [L. rudimentum, fr. rudis unwrought, ignorant, rude: cf. F. rudiment. See Rude.]

senses.d: To furnish with first principles or rules; to insrtuct in the rudiments.
A perennial suffrutescent plant (Ruta graveolens), having a strong, heavy odor and a bitter taste; herb of grace. It is used in medicine.
q: Then purged with euphrasy and rue The visual nerve, for he had much to see.
They are to try the devil by holy water, incense, sulphur, rue, which from thence, as we suppose, came to be called herb of grace.

senses.d: Fig.: Bitterness; disappointment; grief; regret.

Rue.etym: [F. rue, L. ruta, akin to Gr. ρυτἥ; cf. AS. rūde.]

senses.d: To lament; to regret extremely; to grieve for or over.
q: I wept to see, and rued it from my heart.
Thy will Chose freely what it now so justly rues.

senses.d: To cause to grieve; to afflict.
To repent of, and withdraw from, as a bargain; to get released from.

Rue.etym: [OE. rewen, reouwen, to grive, make sorry, AS. hreówan; akin to OS. hrewan, D. rouwen, OHG. hriuwan, G. reuen, Icel. hryggr grieved, hrygð sorrow. √ 18. Cf. Ruth.]

senses.d: To have compassion.
q: God so wisly [i.e., truly] on my soul rue.
Which stirred men's hearts to rue upon them.

senses.d: To feel sorrow and regret; to repent.
q: Work by counsel and thou shalt not rue.
Old year, we'll dearly rue for you.

senses.d: Sorrow; repetance.
The act of falling or tumbling down; fall.

Such a change of anything as destroys it, or entirely defeats its object, or unfits it for use; destruction; overthrow; as, the ruin of a ship or an army; the ruin of a constitution or a government; the ruin of health or hopes.

That which is fallen down and become worthless from injury or decay; as, his mind is a ruin; especially, in the plural, the remains of a destroyed, dilapidated, or desolate house, fortress, city, or the like.
q: The Veian and the Gabian towers shall fall, And one promiscuous ruin cover all; Nor, after length of years, a stone betray The place where once the very ruins lay.
The labor of a day will not build up a virtuous habit on the ruins of an old and vicious character.

senses.d: The state of being dcayed, or of having become ruined or worthless; as, to be in ruins; to go to ruin.
That which promotes injury, decay, or destruction.
q: The errors of young men are the ruin of business.

Ruin.syn: Destruction; downfall; perdition; fall; overthrow; subversion; defeat; bane; pest; mischief.
Ruin.etym: [OE. ruine, F. ruine, fr. L. ruina, fr. ruere, rutum, to fall with violence, to rush or tumble down.]

senses.d: To bring to ruin; to cause to fall to pieces and decay; to make to perish; to bring to destruction; to bring to poverty or bankruptcy; to impair seriously; to damage essentially; to overthrow.
q: this mortal house I'll ruin.
By thee raised, I ruin all my foes.
The eyes of other people are the eyes that ruin us.
By the fireside there are old men seated, Seeling ruined cities in the ashes.

Ruin.etym: [Cf. F. ruiner, LL. ruinare. See Ruin, n.]

senses.d: To fall to ruins; to go to ruin; to become decayed or dilapidated; to perish.
q: Though he his house of polished marble build, Yet shall it ruin like the moth's frail cell.
If we are idle, and disturb the industrious in their business, we shall ruin the faster.

senses.d: Causing, or tending to cause, ruin; destructive; baneful; pernicious; as, a ruinous project.
q: After a night of storm so ruinous.

senses.d: Characterized by ruin; ruined; dilapidated; as, an edifice, bridge, or wall in a ruinous state.
Composed of, or consisting in, ruins.
q: Behold, Damascus . . . shall be a ruinous heap.

Ruinous.syn: Dilapidated; decayed; demolished; pernicious; destructive; baneful; wasteful; mischievous.
Ruinous.etym: [L. ruinosus: cf. F. ruineux. See Ruin.]

senses.d: That which is prescribed or laid down as a guide for conduct or action; a governing direction for a specific purpose; an authoritative enactment; a regulation; a prescription; a precept; as, the rules of various societies; the rules governing a school; a rule of etiquette or propriety; the rules of cricket.
q: We profess to have embraced a religion which contains the most exact rules for the government of our lives.

senses.d: Uniform or established course of things.
q: 'T is against the rule of nature.

senses.d: Systematic method or practice; as, my ule is to rise at six o'clock.
Ordibary course of procedure; usual way; comon state or condition of things; as, it is a rule to which there are many exeptions.
Conduct in general; behavior.
q: This uncivil rule; she shall know of it.

senses.d: The act of ruling; administration of law; government; empire; authority; control.
q: Obey them that have the rule over you.
His stern rule the groaning land obeyed.

senses.d: An order regulating the practice of the courts, or an order made between parties to an action or a suit.
A determinate method prescribed for performing any operation and producing a certain result; as, a rule for extracting the cube root.

A general principle concerning the formation or use of words, or a concise statement thereof; thus, it is a rule in England, that s or es , added to a noun in the singular number, forms the plural of that noun; but “man” forms its plural “men”, and is an exception to the rule.
A straight strip of wood, metal, or the like, which serves as a guide in drawing a straight line; a ruler.
q: A judicious artist will use his eye, but he will trust only to his rule.

senses.d: A thin plate of metal (usually brass) of the same height as the type, and used for printing lines, as between columns on the same page, or in tabular work.

Rule.syn: regulation; law; precept; maxim; guide; canon; order; method; direction; control; government; sway; empire.
Rule.etym: [OE. reule, riule, OF. riule, reule, F. régle, fr. L. regula a ruler, rule, model, fr. regere, rectum, to lead straight, to direct. See Right, a., and cf. Regular.]

senses.d: To control the will and actions of; to exercise authority or dominion over; to govern; to manage.
q: A bishop then must be blameless; . . . one that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection.

senses.d: To control or direct by influence, counsel, or persuasion; to guide; — used chiefly in the passive.
q: I think she will be ruled In all respects by me.

senses.d: To establish or settle by, or as by, a rule; to fix by universal or general consent, or by common practice.
q: That's are ruled case with the schoolmen.

senses.d: To require or command by rule; to give as a direction or order of court.

To mark with lines made with a pen, pencil, etc., guided by a rule or ruler; to print or mark with lines by means of a rule or other contrivance effecting a similar result; as, to rule a sheet of paper of a blank book.

Rule.etym: [Cf. OF. riuler, ruiler, L. regulare. See Rule, n., and cf. Regulate.]

senses.d: To have power or command; to exercise supreme authority; — often followed by over.
q: By me princes rule, and nobles.
We subdue and rule over all other creatures.

senses.d: To lay down and settle a rule or order of court; to decide an incidental point; to enter a rule.
To keep within a (certain) range for a time; to be in general, or as a rule; as, prices ruled lower yesterday than the day before.
One who rules; one who exercises sway or authority; a governor.
q: And he made him ruler over all the land.
A prince and ruler of the land.

senses.d: A straight or curved strip of wood, metal, etc., with a smooth edge, used for guiding a pen or pencil in drawing lines. Cf. Rule, n., 7 (a).
Predominant; chief; reigning; controlling; as, a ruling passion; a ruling sovereign.
Used in marking or engraving lines; as, a ruling machine or pen.

Ruling.syn: Predominant; chief; controlling; directing; guiding; governing; prevailing; prevalent.

senses.d: The act of one who rules; ruled lines.
A decision or rule of a judge or a court, especially an oral decision, as in excluding evidence.
To make a low, heavy, continued sound; as, the thunder rumbles at a distance.
q: In the mean while the skies 'gan rumble sore.
The people cried and rombled up and down.

senses.d: To murmur; to ripple.
q: To rumble gently down with murmur soft.

Rumble.etym: [OE. romblen, akin to D. rommelen, G. rumpeln, Dan. rumle; cf. Icel. rymja to roar.]

senses.d: A noisy report; rumor.
q: Delighting ever in rumble that is new.

senses.d: A low, heavy, continuous sound like that made by heavy wagons or the reverberation of thunder; a confused noise; as, the rumble of a railroad train.
q: Clamor and rumble, and ringing and clatter.
Merged in the rumble of awakening day.

senses.d: A seat for servants, behind the body of a carriage.
q: Kit, well wrapped, . . . was in the rumble behind.

senses.d: A rotating cask or box in which small articles are smoothed or polished by friction against each other.
To cause to pass through a rumble, or shaking machine. See Rumble, n., 4.
The end of the backbone of an animal, with the parts adjacent; the buttock or buttocks.
Among butchers, the piece of beef between the sirloin and the aitchbone piece. See Illust. of Beef.
The hind or tail end; a fag-end; a remnant.

Rump.etym: [OE. rumpe; akin to D. romp trunk, body, LG. rump, G. rumpf, Dan. rumpe rump, Icel. rumpr, Sw. rumpa rump, tail.]

senses.d: To move, proceed, advance, pass, go, come, etc., swiftly, smoothly, or with quick action; — said of things animate or inanimate. Hence, to flow, glide, or roll onward, as a stream, a snake, a wagon, etc.; to move by quicker action than in walking, as a person, a horse, a dog.
To go swiftly; to pass at a swift pace; to hasten.
q: “Ha, ha, the fox!” and after him they ran.

senses.d: To flee, as from fear or danger.
q: As from a bear a man would run for life.

senses.d: To steal off; to depart secretly.
q: My conscience will serve me to run from this jew.

senses.d: To contend in a race; hence, to enter into a contest; to become a candidate; as, to run for Congress.
q: Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.

senses.d: To pass from one state or condition to another; to come into a certain condition; — often with in or into; as, to run into evil practices; to run in debt.
q: Have I not cause to rave and beat my breast, to rend my heart with grief and run distracted?

senses.d: To exert continuous activity; to proceed; as, to run through life; to run in a circle.
To pass or go quickly in thought or conversation; as, to run from one subject to another.
q: Virgil, in his first Georgic, has run into a set of precepts foreign to his subject.

senses.d: To discuss; to continue to think or speak about something; — with on.
To make numerous drafts or demands for payment, as upon a bank; — with on.
To creep, as serpents.
To flow, as a liquid; to ascend or descend; to course; as, rivers run to the sea; sap runs up in the spring; her blood ran cold.
q: The fire ran along upon the ground.

Run.etym: [OE. rinnen, rennen (imp. ran, p. p. runnen, ronnen). AS. rinnan to flow (imp. ran, p. p. gerunnen), and iernan, irnan, to run (imp. orn, arn, earn, p. p. urnen); akin to D. runnen, rennen, OS. & OHG. rinnan, G. rinnen, rennen, Icel. renna, rinna, Sw. rinna, ränna, Dan. rinde, rende, Goth. rinnan, a

senses.d: To cause to run (in the various senses of Run, v. i.); as, to run a horse; to run a stage; to run a machine; to run a rope through a block.
To pursue in thought; to carry in contemplation.
q: To run the world back to its first original.
I would gladly understand the formation of a soul, and run it up to its “punctum saliens.”

senses.d: To cause to enter; to thrust; as, to run a sword into or through the body; to run a nail into the foot.
q: You run your head into the lion's mouth.
Having run his fingers through his hair.

senses.d: To drive or force; to cause, or permit, to be driven.
q: They ran the ship aground.
A talkative person runs himself upon great inconveniences by blabbing out his own or other's secrets.
Others, accustomed to retired speculations, run natural philosophy into metaphysical notions.

senses.d: To fuse; to shape; to mold; to cast; as, to run bullets, and the like.
q: The purest gold must be run and washed.

senses.d: To cause to be drawn; to mark out; to indicate; to determine; as, to run a line.
To cause to pass, or evade, offical restrictions; to smuggle; — said of contraband or dutiable goods.
q: Heavy impositions . . . are a strong temptation of running goods.

senses.d: To go through or accomplish by running; as, to run a race; to run a certain career.
To cause to stand as a candidate for office; to support for office; as, to run some one for Congress.
To encounter or incur, as a danger or risk; as, to run the risk of losing one's life. See To run the chances, below.
To put at hazard; to venture; to risk.
q: He would himself be in the Highlands to receive them, and run his fortune with them.

senses.d: To discharge; to emit; to give forth copiously; to be bathed with; as, the pipe or faucet runs hot water.
q: At the base of Pompey's statua, Which all the while ran blood, great Cæsar fell.

senses.d: The act of running; as, a long run; a good run; a quick run; to go on the run.
A small stream; a brook; a creek.
That which runs or flows in the course of a certain operation, or during a certain time; as, a run of must in wine making; the first run of sap in a maple orchard.
A course; a series; that which continues in a certain course or series; as, a run of good or bad luck.
q: They who made their arrangements in the first run of misadventure . . . put a seal on their calamities.

senses.d: State of being current; currency; popularity.
q: It is impossible for detached papers to have a general run, or long continuance, if not diversified with humor.

senses.d: Continued repetition on the stage; — said of a play; as, to have a run of a hundred successive nights.
q: A canting, mawkish play . . . had an immense run.

senses.d: A continuing urgent demand; especially, a pressure on a bank or treasury for payment of its notes.
A range or extent of ground for feeding stock; as, a sheep run.
The aftermost part of a vessel's hull where it narrows toward the stern, under the quarter.
A pleasure excursion; a trip.
q: I think of giving her a run in London.

senses.d: The horizontal distance to which a drift may be carried, either by license of the proprietor of a mine or by the nature of the formation; also, the direction which a vein of ore or other substance takes.
A roulade, or series of running tones.
Melted, or made from molten material; cast in a mold; as, run butter; run iron or lead.
Smuggled; as, run goods.
A number of cards of the same suit in sequence; as, a run of four in hearts.
The movement communicated to a golf ball by running.
To strike (the ball) in such a way as to cause it to run along the ground, as when approaching a hole.
Moving or advancing by running.
Successive; one following the other without break or intervention; — said of periods of time; as, to be away two days running; to sow land two years running.
Flowing; easy; cursive; as, a running hand.
Continuous; keeping along step by step; as, he stated the facts with a running explanation.
q: What are art and science if not a running commentary on Nature?

senses.d: Extending by a slender climbing or trailing stem; as, a running vine.
Discharging pus; as, a running sore.
The act of one who, or of that which runs; as, the running was slow.
That which runs or flows; the quantity of a liquid which flows in a certain time or during a certain operation; as, the first running of a still.
The discharge from an ulcer or other sore.
A name given to many aquatic or marsh-growing endogenous plants with soft, slender stems, as the species of Juncus and Scirpus.
The merest trifle; a straw.
q: John Bull's friendship is not worth a rush.

Rush.etym: [OE. rusche, rische, resche, AS. risce, akin to LG. rusk, risch, D. & G. rusch; all probably fr. L. ruscum butcher's broom; akin to Goth. raus reed, G. rohr.]

senses.d: To move forward with impetuosity, violence, and tumultuous rapidity or haste; as, armies rush to battle; waters rush down a precipice.
q: Like to an entered tide, they all rush by.

senses.d: To enter into something with undue haste and eagerness, or without due deliberation and preparation; as, to rush business or speculation.
q: They . . . never think it to be a part of religion to rush into the office of princes and ministers.

Rush.etym: [OE. ruschen; cf. AS. hryscan to make a noise, D. ruischen to rustle, G. rauschen, MHG. rūschen to rush, to rustle, LG. rusken, OSw. ruska, Icel. & Sw. ruska to shake, Dan. ruske to shake, and E. rouse.]

senses.d: To push or urge forward with impetuosity or violence; to hurry forward.
To recite (a lesson) or pass (an examination) without an error.
A moving forward with rapidity and force or eagerness; a violent motion or course; as, a rush of troops; a rush of winds; a rush of water.
q: A gentleman of his train spurred up his horse, and, with a violent rush, severed him from the duke.

senses.d: Great activity with pressure; as, a rush of business.
A perfect recitation.
A rusher; as, the center rush, whose place is in the center of the rush line; the end rush.
Abounding or covered with rushes.
The reddish yellow coating formed on iron when exposed to moist air, consisting of ferric oxide or hydroxide; hence, by extension, any metallic film of corrosion.

A minute mold or fungus forming reddish or rusty spots on the leaves and stems of cereal and other grasses (Trichobasis Rubigo-vera), now usually believed to be a form or condition of the corn mildew (Puccinia graminis). As rust, it has solitary reddish spores; as corn mildew, the spores are double and blackish.
That which resembles rust in appearance or effects.
q: Sacred truths cleared from all rust and dross of human mixtures.

Rust.etym: [AS. rust; akin to D. roest, G. & Sw. rost, Icel. ryð; — named from its color, and akin to E. red. √113. See Red.]

senses.d: To contract rust; to be or become oxidized.
q: If gold ruste, what shall iron do?
Our armors now may rust.

senses.d: To be affected with the parasitic fungus called rust; also, to acquire a rusty appearance, as plants.
To degenerate in idleness; to become dull or impaired by inaction.
q: Must I rust in Egypt? never more Appear in arms, and be the chief of Greece?

senses.d: To cause to contract rust; to corrode with rust; to affect with rust of any kind.
q: Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them.

senses.d: To impair by time and inactivity.
Sorrow for the misery of another; pity; tenderness.
q: To stir up gentle ruth, Both for her noble blood, and for her tender youth.

senses.d: That which causes pity or compassion; misery; distress; a pitiful sight.
q: It had been hard this ruth for to see.
With wretched miseries and woeful ruth.

Ruth.etym: [From Rue, v.: cf. Icel. hryggð, hrygð.]
